{"artifact_digest":"sha256:eff8a3c12bf8b61692949a4612a1c89f574447289a791fad4e379b81394ac8d6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ef/eff8a3c12bf8b61692949a4612a1c89f574447289a791fad4e379b81394ac8d6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:db4315b575d251e8436b83b02ffb4957ac7546b6d5a9b968b916c9f8a8fc957c","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c09","bundle_id":"population.t309-ordinary-empirical-centered-equilateral-random-init-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-centered-equilateral-empirical-random-initialization","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Own work draft; proof (unaudited), T309-w721-C09 v2, Target 2.

# Ordinary empirical DDPM GD: the centered equilateral random-initialization case

This builds on unaudited C07 v2 and C08 v2. It replaces the population gradient by the ordinary empirical gradient, without orbit augmentation. It does not solve the unrestricted K=3 target. The centroid is constrained to zero, weights and covariance are known, radius is known, and the true triangle is equilateral. No novelty or bit-complexity claim is made.

## 1. Statement and objective

Let the original teacher be (1/3)sum_j N(R E u_j,I_d), d>=2, R>=1 known, E^T E=I_2 and u_j the unit equilateral vertices. Choose a at the inverse-polynomial-in-d scale of C08, with its absolute constant reduced as needed below. Set tau=a/R and sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2. Draw n iid pairs (X_i,Y_i), where X_i is an original teacher sample and Y_i~N(0,I_d) independently. Put W_i=tau X_i+sigma Y_i. The loss is the usual single-time empirical DDPM objective

    Lhat(Z)=(1/n)sum_i ||s_{M(Z)}(W_i)+Y_i/sigma||^2,
    M(Z)=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T,

where V=sqrt(2/3)U^T, as in C07. This is Eq. (5) with the Eq. (9) mixture-score student. Initialization has iid N(0,1/d) entries in Z_0 and is independent of these pairs.

For each 0<epsilon<1 and 0<eta<=1/100, there is an n polynomial in d,1/a,1/epsilon,1/eta such that physical unit-step GD on the centered parameters satisfies

    min_pi ||M_T-M_teacher,pi||_F<=a epsilon          (1)

with probability at least 7/20-eta, after

    T=O(a^(-2)log d+a^(-4)log(C/epsilon)).             (2)

In particular the success probability exceeds 1/3. Both sample count and real-arithmetic work are polynomial in d,1/epsilon,1/eta because a is inverse polynomial in d. Arithmetic evaluations of the score and its gradient, including exponentials, are counted here; no finite-precision runtime theorem is asserted. Rescaling the means by R/a gives original mean error R epsilon and hence TV at most R epsilon/2 after matching, by Gaussian KL and Pinsker. For a prescribed original-law error, choose epsilon accordingly. There is no claim of exact convergence for a fixed finite sample.

## 2. Polynomial uniform gradient approximation

Write F_a(Z) for the population excess score risk in C07. The conditional-expectation identity for DDPM gives E grad Lhat=grad F_a; the difference between their population losses is constant in Z. Define the rescaled fields

    f_a(Z)=-a^(-4)grad_Z F_a(Z),
    fhat(Z)=-a^(-4)grad_Z Lhat(Z).

For each 0<zeta<1, a polynomial n suffices for

    sup_{||Z||_F<=5} ||fhat(Z)-f_a(Z)||_F<=zeta       (3)

with probability at least 1-eta. Here are explicit deliberately loose polynomial choices and a proof.

Take B=C_0(d+a^(-1)+zeta^(-1)+eta^(-1)+1)^2 and n=ceil(B^80), with C_0 an absolute sufficiently large constant. A pair is safe when ||W||,||Y||<=B. Marginally W is a three-component unit-covariance Gaussian mixture with means of norm a; Y is standard Gaussian. Their correlation is irrelevant to the union bound. For a standard d-Gaussian G, direct Gaussian integration gives E exp(||G||^2/4)=2^(d/2). Markov, B>=2a, and a union bound yield unsafe probability at most C exp(-c B^2), provided B^2 exceeds a sufficiently large constant times d.

Uniformly on the model ball and safe pairs, the rescaled per-pair gradient and its Z Lipschitz constant are bounded by C B^12. To verify a polynomial envelope, let b_M(w)=sum_j p_j(w)m_j be the posterior mean correction in s_M=-w+b_M. Since ||m_j||<=C a, the residual norm is at most C B. The first Z derivative of b has operator norm at most C a(1+aB+a^2); differentiating the logits once introduces a(w-m_j). A second derivative has a bound C a^2(1+B)^3. These follow by differentiating the three softmax weights, whose values lie in [0,1]. The gradient of a squared residual is twice the score Jacobian adjoint applied to the residual; its Hessian is twice the Jacobian square plus twice the residual paired with the score Hessian. Multiplying their bounds by a^(-4), and using B>=1/a, gives the stated looser B^12 bound in Frobenius/operator norm. These bounds do not introduce an exponential of a logit or an unbounded number of components.

Multiply the per-pair field by the safe-pair indicator for the purpose of the proof only. The truncated expectation differs from f_a by at most zeta/10 uniformly on the ball. Indeed the same derivative formulas give a fixed polynomial envelope in ||W||+||Y||, multiplied by a^(-4). Its second moment is bounded by a fixed polynomial in d and 1/a. Cauchy--Schwarz and the unsafe probability bound give polynomial(d,1/a)*exp(-cB^2), which is below zeta/10 for the stated B and large C_0. The algorithm itself does not truncate: with probability at least 1-eta/4 all n pairs are safe, since n exp(-cB^2)<=eta/4.

Choose a model net of mesh zeta/(100 C B^12) in the radius-5 ball of R^(2d), and a 1/2-net of the unit sphere in the same space. The elementary disjoint-ball packing argument bounds the two cardinalities by (1+C B^12/zeta)^(2d) and 5^(2d). Their combined logarithm is at most C d log B<=C B^2. At each model and direction net point the truncated scalar field is bounded by C B^12. For independent bounded scalars in [-G,G],

    P(|sample mean-expectation|>u)<=2exp(-n u^2/(2G^2)).

For clarity, this bound can be proved directly: the second derivative of the log moment-generating function is a tilted variance, bounded by G^2 for a variable in [-G,G]. Integrating twice from zero bounds the centered log MGF by t^2 G^2/2. Chernoff optimization for the independent sum and the two signs gives the displayed inequality. No Gaussianity of the gradient is assumed.

Apply this at tolerance a small constant times zeta and union bound over both nets. Since zeta>=1/B and n>=B^80, the tail exponent is at least cB^54, dominating the net logarithm and log(1/eta). The direction net converts scalar to vector bounds with factor at most two. The model Lipschitz bound extends to the whole ball, with error at most zeta/10. Adding the truncated-expectation bias and the all-samples-safe event proves (3), after allocating the failure probabilities below eta. All estimates hold at once over parameters, so no independence between later GD iterates and the samples is needed.

## 3. Entry still has polynomial cost

On (3), the empirical unit-step update is

    Z_{k+1}=Z_k+gamma[f(Z_k)+R_a(Z_k)+e(Z_k)],
    gamma=2a^2/3, ||R_a||<=C a^2, ||e||<=zeta,

where f=(P-ZZ^T)Z. C07's stopped flow comparison on its logarithmic rescaled entry interval now gives error at most

    C(a^2+zeta)exp(76(S+1)).

Set zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon, with c_* small, and reduce the absolute constant in C07's choice of a. This comparison is then still at most rho/4. The same norm-4 initialization event, tube entry and angular error transfer apply to the empirical trajectory. In particular the good surrogate-flow angle event in C08 has probability at least 7/20. It is not claimed that the empirical objective is rotation invariant.

## 4. Stable recurrences with persistent error

Use C08's branch, subspace L, normalized radius r, normal error w, and nearest-sector-minimum angle alpha. As long as the trajectory is in the tube, (3) and the normal contraction imply

    ||w_{k+1}||<=(1-c gamma)||w_k||+gamma zeta,
    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c gamma k)+C zeta.             (4)

The exact population tangent correction remains quadratic in w, by C08's self-adjoint Hessian and invariant-subspace argument. The empirical field adds at most zeta directly. Thus the angular error from the restricted map is bounded by the sum of a transient term Cgamma rho^2 exp(-c gamma k) and a persistent term Cgamma zeta, since zeta^2<=zeta. The transient has total sum at most C rho^2; choose the fixed rho to make this at most delta/8, where delta=pi/24.

The persistent term cannot simply be summed over all time. Instead, near a sector boundary at angular margin in [delta/2,3delta/4], the restricted map moves inward by at least c gamma a^2 delta. Choosing zeta<=c' a^2 makes that inward drift dominate its persistent perturbation. A precise moving barrier is b_k=3delta/4 minus the partial sum of the transient error bounds; it stays above 5delta/8. The restricted boundary-distance map is increasing and moves b_k inward by the stated amount. Subtracting the persistent perturbation still leaves at least b_k, and subtracting the current transient leaves at least b_{k+1}. Induction therefore keeps the margin at least delta/2. This closes the angular barrier without incorrectly claiming a summable persistent error.

The radial annulus also remains invariant: its leading field (1-r^2)r has fixed inward margins at 0.9 and 1.1, and its perturbations are bounded by C(a^2+||w||^2+zeta). Choose the constants small, exactly as in C08. This and (4) close the tube induction simultaneously.

Within the sector, the angle recurrence is

    alpha_{k+1}<=(1-c gamma a^2)alpha_k
                      +Cgamma rho^2 exp(-c' gamma k)
                      +Cgamma zeta.

Its geometric-series solution is

    alpha_k<=C exp(-c'' gamma a^2 k)+C zeta/a^2.       (5)

The first convolution is bounded uniformly because its forcing decays on the faster normal scale. The constant forcing has exactly the slow-rate denominator a^2; it is not being discarded.

Writing b=r-1, C08's radial estimate now reads

    |b_{k+1}|<=(1-c gamma)|b_k|
                      +Cgamma a^2 alpha_k^2
                      +Cgamma ||w_k||^2+Cgamma zeta.

Using (4),(5) and zeta<=a^2 gives

    |b_k|+alpha_k+||w_k||
       <=C exp(-c_1 gamma a^2 k)+C_1 zeta/a^2.        (6)

For example the persistent radial contribution is bounded by C(zeta+zeta^2/a^2), at most C'zeta; angular error is the larger floor. Choose c_* in zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon to make the last term of (6) a small enough multiple of epsilon. The factor-to-means isometry then proves (1) after the time in (2).

## 5. Probability, scope, and review

The surrogate initialization-and-angle event has probability at least 7/20 and uniform empirical control fails with probability at most eta. A union bound gives success at least 7/20-eta. No conditional independence or product of success probabilities is required. With eta<=1/100 this is at least 17/50>1/3.

This supplies a candidate polynomial empirical result for the centered equilateral case, with enormous polynomial exponents. It removes orbit augmentation and a known teacher plane from C04. It does not release the centroid constraint, identify an unknown radius, allow unequal weights, or resolve general well-separated K=3 mixtures. In particular C06's anisotropic high-noise local minimum remains an obstruction to a naive generalization.

The least trusted steps for review are the global polynomial gradient envelope and net extension in Section 2, the moving angular barrier with persistent error, and closure of the radial/normal tube. There is no computer-assisted bound here: this is an analytic argument using explicit polynomial domination. No training run, numerical concentration estimate, Lean certificate, or reviewer PASS is offered. Work as d->infinity with integers N=N(d)->infinity and M=M(d)>=1. Let (X_d,nu_d) and (Omega_d,tau_d) be probability spaces and sigma_d in L2(nu_d times tau_d). Use its singular expansion sigma_d(x,theta)=sum_j sqrt(mu_j) psi_j(x) phi_j(theta), with ordered nonnegative mu_j, sum_j mu_j<infinity, positive mu_(M+1) and positive denominators in the displayed tail conditions, and orthonormal families psi_j in L2(nu_d), phi_j in L2(tau_d). Let D_d be the closed span of the psi_j and P_<=M its orthogonal projection onto the first M modes. Define the feature kernel U_d(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu_d sigma_d(x,theta)sigma_d(x,thetaprime), its spectral tail U_>r=sum_(j>r) mu_j phi_j phi_j^T, and kappa_r=sum_(j>r)mu_j>0 for each cutoff used. Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau_d and let K_ij=U_d(theta_i,theta_j). All stochastic rates below are as d->infinity. (H) There is one sequence u(d)>=M(d) such that, for every fixed real q>=1, all g in span{phi_1,...,phi_u} satisfy ||g||_(L2q(tau_d))<=C_q||g||_(L2(tau_d)), with C_q independent of d and g. (E) For the same u there is a fixed delta_E>0 such that N^(2+delta_E)<=kappa_u^2/sum_(j>u)mu_j^2 eventually. (Dupper) For every epsilon>0, max_i U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M=O_P(N^epsilon). (Dlower) For every epsilon>0, min_i U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M=Omega_P(N^(-epsilon)), where Omega_P means that the reciprocal divided by N^epsilon is stochastically bounded. (Sa) There is a fixed delta_a>0 with N^(1+delta_a)<=kappa_M/mu_(M+1) eventually. (Sb) There is a fixed delta_b>0 with M<=N^(1-delta_b) and kappa_M/mu_M<=N^(1-delta_b) eventually. Assumption6 consists of H,E,Dupper,Dlower; Assumption7 consists of Sa,Sb. Results using only some clauses retain exactly their listed subsets. The divergence N(d)->infinity is explicit here as the asymptotic feature-count regime. No coordinate independence of the vector (phi_j(theta)) is imposed.

DRAFT; independent mathematical review pending. For iid finite nonnegative nondegenerate weights on nearest-neighbor Z^2, choose finite 0<=a<b with q=P(t<=a)>0 and p=P(t>=b)>0, integer L>=2 with L(b-a)>2a, R=2(L+1), D=1+2R(R+1), and eta=p^L q^(L+2). For any deterministic finite dictionary P_N of simple N-edge paths, P(some member is a geodesic) <= |P_N|(1-eta)^ceil(floor(N/L)/D). Thus if these products tend to zero, almost surely there is no geodesic ray starting at a specified vertex whose N-edge prefix belongs to P_N for every N. In particular subexponential dictionary cardinality suffices. The result excludes bigeodesics only when one of their tails is covered by such dictionaries.
Not a proof of the unrestricted no-bigeodesics conjecture; see the exact hypotheses in the statement.

[Corollary 46 of arXiv:2609.02819, 'Adelic Points and Unramified Brauer Approximation for Classifying Stacks'] The following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $S$ contains a finite place, then
\[
 B\PGL_n(k)\longrightarrow B\PGL_n(\bA_k^S)
\]
is surjective.
\item Suppose that $S$ contains no finite place.  Then the localization map is
surjective if and only if $n=2$ and $S$ contains a real place.
\item In particular, if $S=\Omega_k^\infty$, then plain strong approximation
holds for $B\PGL_n$ exactly when $n=2$ and $k$ has a real place.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2607.17030, 'Stationary measures for log-gamma polymer on a strip and in half-space'] Assume  
$\alpha,u,v\in\RR$ are such that $\alpha>0$, $\alpha+u>0$
  and  $\alpha+v>0$.
 Furthermore, we assume that
 $u,v\not\in \ZZ_{\leq 0}$ 
  and if $u<0$ and $v<0$, we assume that  $v-u\not\in\ZZ$.
Then 
  \begin{multline}
     \GG_N(\alpha ,u ,v )
     =\tfrac{1}{2\pi \Gamma(u+v)}\int_{0}^\infty \left|\Gamma(\alpha +\i x)\right|^{2N}\,\tfrac{|\Gamma(v+\i x)|^2|\Gamma(u +\i x )|^2}{|\Gamma(2\i x)|^2}\d x \\ +\mathbb{D}_N(\alpha,u,v)+ \mathbb{D}_N(\alpha,v,u),
  \end{multline}
where
\begin{equation}
   \mathbb{D}_N(\alpha,u,v)=\sum_{j\in \ZZ\cap[0,-v )} m_j(u,v) \Gamma(\alpha+v+j)^{N}\Gamma(\alpha-v-j)^{N}\nonumber
\end{equation}
   with
    \begin{equation}
    
    m_j(u,v)
    =\tfrac{-2(v+j )}{j!}\cdot \tfrac{ \Gamma(u-v)}{\Gamma (1-2 v ) }\cdot\tfrac{ (v+u)_j(2 v )_j }{ (v-u+1)_j},\; j\in \ZZ\cap[0,-v ).
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 7 (Peskun--Tierney optimality of the multi-judge $N$-vote rule) of arXiv:2609.00905, 'When Metropolis and Hastings Meet Bradley and Terry: Exact MCMC From Preference Voting'] Fix a proposal kernel $q$ and a comparison budget $N\geq 1$ per judge. Among all
exact acceptance rules satisfying detailed balance with respect to $\pi_m$, that
use the same proposal kernel and only the outcomes of exactly $N$ judge queries
per judge per proposal, the multi-judge $N$-vote rule Peskun--Tierney dominates
every competitor. Equivalently, for every proposed move $x\to x'$, we have
\[
\mathbb P_{\text{multi-judge $N$-vote}}
(\textup{accept }x'\mid x,x'\textup{ proposed})
\geq
\mathbb P_{\text{competitor}}
(\textup{accept }x'\mid x,x'\textup{ proposed}).
\]

[Mainthm thm:smallmu of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $d\ge2$ and $\eta,r,\lambda>0$ with $\lambda<\infty$. There is
$\mu_*(\lambda)=\mu_*(\lambda;\eta,r,d)>0$ such that for every $\mu\le\mu_*(\lambda)$ the
finite-rate infection started from a single particle at the origin survives with positive
probability, and moreover
\[
  \mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\mu}_\eta\Big(\liminf_{t\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{rad}(I_t)}{t}>0\Big)\ >\ 0 .
\]
In particular $\mu_c(\lambda,\eta)\ge\mu_*(\lambda)>0$ for every $\eta>0$ and every
$\lambda\in(0,\infty)$. Consequently
\[
  \lim_{\mu\downarrow0}\eta_c(\lambda,\mu)\ =\ 0\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in(0,\infty] .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition notation:binom of arXiv:2511.15893, 'On a Class of Dynamical Poisson-Voronoi Tessellations'] For $l,r,k\in \{1,2\}$ with $l\neq r$, we say that an intersection is of type $\binom{k}{l,r}$, if it is the $k$-th intersection between the radial birds of type $l$ and $r$. \!\!\! In the combinatorial like notation $\binom{k}{l,r}$, the fact that the position of $l$ is on the \textbf{left} means that the head of the bird of type $l$ is on the left of the head of the bird of type $r$, which is on the \textbf{right}. The two values of $k$ refer to the two intersections, as in ((eq:HOs of the paper)), of radial birds of two different types, where $k=1$ means the left intersection and $k=2$ means the right intersection. We call intersections of these type \textbf{mixed intersections} and the handovers given by these intersections as \textbf{mixed handovers}.

body: [Lemma lem:gamma(s)nonnul of arXiv:2411.02156, 'Martin boundary of a degenerate Reflected Brownian Motion in a wedge'] For all $n \geq 1$ and $s \in (\max(s_{min}, s^{**}), \min(s_{max}, s^*))$, we have $\gamma_1(s - 2n) \neq 0$ and $\gamma_2(\zeta(s - 2n)) \neq 0$. Furthermore, $\gamma_2(s), \gamma_2(\zeta s), \gamma_1(s), \gamma_1(\eta s)$ are also non-zero.

body:
[Lemma halfspace of arXiv:2608.12056, 'Deviation inequalities for U-processes of growing order, with applications to half-space d'] Assume that $\frac{\max(t,d)m^2}{N}\leq c$ for sufficiently small $c>0$ and that $\mathbb E\left|\dotp{X}{u}\right|^p<\infty$ for some $p>4$. Then for any $\varepsilon>0$, 
\begin{multline*}  
R_{N,m}\leq \frac{ 1 + \alpha_m}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{\frac{dm}{N}} +
\sqrt{\frac{2tm}{N}} \right]
\\
+C\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}+\sqrt{\frac{dm^2\log(m)}{N}}\right)\frac{tm}{N}
    +\frac{Cd}{N}\log^{3/2}(m).
\end{multline*}
with probability at least $1-2e^{-t}$.
Here, 
\[
\alpha_m = \left| \phi_m(0) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right| + C(p)\max\left(\frac{1}{m^{1/4}},\frac{\sqrt{d}}{N^{1/4}}\right)\log^{1/2}(dm)
\]
where $C(p)$ also depends on the distribution $F_1$ of the random variable $\dotp{X}{u}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem Lemma: Measurability over homogeneous factor of arXiv:2605.16921, '${\ASL_n}(\mathbb Z)$ invariant random subsets of $\mathbb Z^n$'] Let $(X, \nu)$ be an $\SL_d(\mathbb{Z})$-ergodic system, $N$ a connected simply connected nilpotent Lie group, $\Gamma \subset N$ a lattice, and $\alpha: \SL_d(\mathbb{Z}) \times X \to \Aut(N, \Gamma)$ a cocycle valued in the stabiliser of $\Gamma$ in $\Aut(N)$. Up to a compact extension of $X$, there exist a homomorphism $\pi: \SL_d(\mathbb{Z}) \to \Aut(N)$ with image contained in a closed subgroup $H \subseteq \Aut(N)$, and an $\SL_d(\mathbb{Z})$-equivariant measurable map
    $$ \Phi: X \longrightarrow H/\Gamma_H, \qquad \Gamma_H := H \cap \Aut(N, \Gamma),$$
    such that $\alpha$ factors through $\Phi$ and is given by the constant cocycle $\alpha(\gamma, x) = \pi(\gamma)$.

[Lemma Ap1 of arXiv:2411.05369, 'Stochastic games of parental vaccination decision making and bounded rationality'] Consider a function $f\in C([0,\infty)\times \Omega,(0,\infty))$. Let $a(t)$ be a sequence such that $\lim_{t \to \infty} \dfrac{a(t)}{t}=a$ a.s. and let $a$ and $b$ be two positive constants such that
$$\log(f(t))\geq (\leq) \, a(t)-b\int_0^t f(s)ds $$
for all $t\geq 0$ a.s. Then
$$\liminf_{t\to \infty} (\limsup_{t\to \infty})\, \frac{1}{t} \int_0^t f(s)ds\geq (\leq) \, \dfrac{a}{b} \quad a.s.$$

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2603.26303, 'Spectral Gap of Biased Adjacent-Transposition Chains'] Let $n\ge 3$.
    Suppose that the smallest positive eigenvalue of $K$ is $(1-2m_{\mathbf p}\cos(\tfrac{{\pi}}{n}))/(n-1)$ with corresponding eigenvector $f$.
    Then $S_f$ is non-empty and
    \[
    \sqrt{p_{i,j}p_{j,k}p_{k,i} + p_{k,j}p_{j,i}p_{i,k}} = m_{\mathbf p}
    \]
    for all $i<j<k$ such that $\{(i,j),(i,k),(j,k)\} \cap S_f \ne \emptyset$.
    Furthermore, if $\mathbf p$ is regular and $m_{\mathbf p}=1/2$, then 
    
    
    the lexicographically minimal element of $S_f$ has the form $(1,b)$ and, if $b = n$ then $[2,n-1] \subseteq H_{\mathbf p}$, otherwise $b \in H_{\mathbf p}$.
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2603.26303

body:
[Proposition prop:lipptx3 of arXiv:2411.10235, '\textbf{Smooth transport map via diffusion process}'] Let $l,h\in L^2_p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with
$h \in \mathcal{H}_{1}^{1}(B^d(0,1))$.
Then, for $t\in [0,1),z\in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\theta_1,\theta_2\in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying (equation eq:onremetlacontrainte of the paper), in the case $\beta\geq 1$ we have 
    \begin{align*}
        &\|\int (l(y)-l(z))h(y)(p^{t,\theta_1}(y)-p^{t,\theta_2}(y))d\lambda^d(y)\|\\
         \leq &C_\epsilon \left(\int\|l(y)-l(y+t(\theta_2-\theta_1))\|^2dp^{t,\theta_1}(y)\right)^{1/2}\sum_{i=1}^2\left(\int\|h(y)\|^2p^{t,\theta_i}(y) \right)^{1/2}\\
        & +C_\epsilon\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|\left(\left(\int\|l(y)-l(z)\|^2dp^{t,\theta_2}(y) \right)^{1/2}+\exp(-\frac{(1-t^2)^{-1/4}}{8})\right)
    \end{align*}
    and in the case $\beta\in (0,1)$, $l(y)-l(z)=y-t\theta_1$, $h(y)=H(y,\theta_2)$ we have
    \begin{align*}
        &\|\int (y-t\theta_1)\left(H(y,\theta_2)\right)(p^{t,\theta_1}(y)-p^{t,\theta_2}(y))d\lambda^d(y)\|\\
         \leq &C\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|\left(\|\int H(y,\theta_2)dp^{t,\theta_2}(y) \|+\|\int \left(y-t\theta_1 \right)dp^{t,\theta_2}(y)\|\right)\\
        & +C_\epsilon\frac{\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|^{\beta}}{\log(\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|^{-1})^{\theta}}\left(\left(\int\|y-t\theta_2\|^2dp^{t,\theta_2}(y) \right)^{1/2}+\exp(-\frac{(1-t^2)^{-1/4}}{8})\right)\left(\int\|H(y,\theta_2)\|^2p^{t,\theta_1}(y) \right)^{1/2}.
    \end{align*}
title: Proposition prop:lipptx3 of arXiv:2411.10235

[Prop 7 of arXiv:2608.25829, 'Topology of low-dimensional generalized Ricci solitons and string backgrounds'] Let $(M^n, g, H, f)$ be a compact GRS.  Then $Y_{[g]} \geq 0$, with equality if and only if the soliton is trivial.
\begin{proof} Choose a Yamabe minimizer $u$.  Then we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \brs{\brs{u}}_{L^{2n/n-2}}^2 Y_{[g]} =&\ \int_M \left( R_g u^2 + 4 \frac{n-1}{n-2} \brs{\N u}^2 \right)\\
    \geq&\ \int_M \left( R_g u^2 + 4 \brs{\N u}^2 \right)\\
    =&\ \mathcal F(g, H, -2 \ln u)\\
    \geq&\ \gl(g, H) \brs{\brs{u}}_{L^2}^2.
\end{align*}
Both claims now follow immediately from Lemma \ref{l:lambdasign}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 7 of arXiv:2608.25829

body: [Lemma lemma_backward_tree of arXiv:2604.04672, 'Connected components and topological ends of stationary planar forests'] Almost surely, $\mathrm{Pend}(v)$ is finite for each $v\in V$. In particular, for every compact set $K\subset \mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathrm{Pend}(K)$ is a.s.\ finite. Furthermore, for any compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ and vertex $v\in V_1\setminus\mathrm{Pend}(K)$, $\pi_v$ avoids $K$.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2609.01473, 'Keller sequences of exact $\infty$-categories'] Suppose that the localisation $p^l\colon \cal{C} \to \cal{B}^l$ sends cocartesian squares in $\cal{C}$ with parallel maps inclusions to cocartesian squares in $\cal{B}^l$.
If $f\colon x \to y$ in $\cal{B}^l$ is the image of some inclusion in $\cal{C}$ then for every $\tilde x\in \cal{C}$ lifting $x$ we can lift $f$ to an inclusion $\tilde f\colon \tilde x \mono \tilde y$ with domain $\tilde x$. 

Dually, if $p^r\colon \cal{C} \to \cal{B}^r$ sends cartesian squares in $\cal{C}$ with parallel maps projections to cartesian squares in $\cal{B}^r$ then any map in $\cal{B}^{r}$ which is the image of some projection in $\cal{C}$ can be lifted to a projection in $\cal{C}$ with any prescribed lift of its codomain.

body:
[Lemma lem:dense-rare of arXiv:2605.21744, 'Return Probability for the Switch--Walk--Switch Lamplighter Walk on a Regular Tree'] For every $a\in(0,1)$, there are constants $r_0=r_0(d,a)$ and $c=c(d,a)>0$ such that, for every $r\ge r_0$,
\[
        \mathbb P\left(|C_\omega(o)\cap B(o,r)|\ge a b^r\right)
        \le
        \exp(-c b^r ),
\]
where $C_\omega(o)$ is the open cluster of $o$, interpreted as empty when $o$ is closed.

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.03902, 'Bundles of Probability Schemes'] For any bundle $\pi \colon \gv{\Omega,\pr} \to \gv{\Omega',\pr'}$,
  \begin{enumerate}[i.]
    \item $\pi_{\flat}\pi^{\sharp}$ is the identity map on $\Rr^{\Omega'}$.
      
    \item Both $\pi^{\sharp}$ and $\pi_{\flat}$ preserve expectation.
      
    \item $\pi_{\flat}$ is an $\Rr^{\Omega'}$-module map. 
    \item The operators $\pi^{\sharp}$ and $\pi_{\flat}$ form an adjoint pair.
      
    \item $\E_{\pi}:=\pi^{\sharp}\pi_{\flat}$ is the orthogonal projection of
      $\Rr^{\Omega}$ to $\cA_{\pi}$. 
    \item $\pi^{\sharp}$ is an isometry. 
  \end{enumerate}

body: [Proposition prop:normalized of arXiv:2606.28869, '\bfseries A General Theory of Paths:\\ \large Signatures, Jump Lifts, and Expected Signatu'] Under the characteristic-kernel hypotheses of [chevyrev2022], there is a tensor normalization $\Lambda$ for which $\Lambda(\mathrm{Sig}(X))$ is uniformly bounded on the relevant path space, so $\mathbb{E}[\Lambda(\mathrm{Sig}(X))]$ exists for every probability law. The induced maximum mean discrepancy is a metric on laws. In particular, for heavy-tailed drivers excluded by the stable threshold in (thm:stable-threshold of the paper), where raw coordinates $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Sig}^k]$ may diverge, the law can still be characterized by the normalized expected signature.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.01594, '2609.01594'] For integers $A_1,\ldots,A_k,S,T$ with $S\neq0$, we have
\[
 A_1,\ldots,A_k\in\Sq(\Z) \ \land\  S\mid T
 \iff
 \exists m\ [H_k(A_1,\ldots,A_k,S,T,m)=0].
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 H_k(A_1,\ldots,A_k,0,T,m)=T^{2^k}.
\end{equation}

[Definition 16 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] We use $B$ to denote a standard Brownian motion on $\mbb R^2$. For any $x,y\in\mbb R^2$ and $t>0$,
we let $B^x=(B|B(0)=x)$ denote the Brownian motion started at $x$, and let $B^{x,y}_t=(B|B(0)=x,~B(t)=y)$
denote the Brownian bridge from $x$ to $y$ on the time interval $[0,t]$. Finally, when we require multiple
independent copies of Brownian motion, we use the notation ${_1}B,{_2}B,{_3}B,\ldots$
(in particular, we use ${_i}B^{x_i}$ and ${_i}B^{x_i,y_i}_t$, $i\geq1$, to denote independent Brownian motions
started at $x_i$ and independent Brownian bridges from $x_i$ to $y_i$ on the time interval $[0,t]$).

[Theo thm:regularforitselfregularlyvarying of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $\Psi=\Sigma-\Phi$ and $\hat{\Psi}=\hat\Sigma-\hat\Phi$ be mechanisms such that 
\[\Phi(y)=y^{\alpha}\ell(y), \ y\in [0,\infty) \text{ and } \hat\Sigma(x)=x^{2-\alpha}\hat{L}(x), \ x\in [0,\infty) \text{ with } \alpha\in (0,1)\]
where $\ell$ and $\hat{L}$ are slowly varying respectively at $0$ and $\infty$.
Assume 

\[1/\Gamma(\alpha)<\underline{\xi}=\underset{z\rightarrow 0}{\liminf} \frac{\ell(z)}{\hat{L}(1/z)}\leq \overline{\xi}=\underset{z\rightarrow 0}{\limsup} \frac{\ell(z)}{\hat{L}(1/z)}<\Gamma(2-\alpha),\] then :
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\Sigma\equiv 0$, $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$  has $\infty$ regular-for-itself and  $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$  non-sticky.
    \item If $\hat\Phi\equiv 0$, $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$ regular-for-itself and $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$  has $\infty$ non-sticky. 
\end{enumerate}
When
\begin{center}
$\Psi=-\Phi$ and $\hat{\Psi}=\hat{\Sigma}$, \end{center} the boundaries $\infty$ of $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ and $0$ of $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ are both regular-for-itself and non-sticky.

body: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space on a set X is a Hilbert space H of functions f : X -> R (or C) in which every evaluation functional f -> f(x) is bounded. By Riesz representation there is then a unique kernel k(x, .) in H with the reproducing property f(x) = <f, k(x, .)> for all f in H; the function k(x, y) = <k(y, .), k(x, .)> is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
title: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space

Let (T, d) be a pseudo-metric space and epsilon > 0. The covering number N(T, d, epsilon) is the minimal number of open balls of radius epsilon whose union covers T. The packing number P(T, d, epsilon) is the maximal number of points in T whose pairwise distances are all strictly greater than epsilon. The quantity H(T, d, epsilon) = log N(T, d, epsilon) is the metric entropy of T.

body:
Let (a_n)_{n >= 1} be a sequence of reals with a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1. Then lim_{n -> infinity} a_n / n exists in [-infinity, +infinity) and equals inf_{n >= 1} a_n / n. In particular the limit is finite if and only if a_n / n is bounded below. The SUPERadditive version, a_{m+n} >= a_m + a_n, gives lim a_n/n = sup_n a_n/n in (-infinity, +infinity]. The lemma requires nothing beyond subadditivity - no monotonicity, no positivity, no continuity - and the limit can be minus infinity, as with a_n = -n^2. Fekete's lemma is the deterministic skeleton of Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem: applying it to a_n = E[X_{0,n}] gives the existence of the constant that the ergodic theorem then identifies as the almost sure limit. [Fekete (1923); standard, e.g. Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, Chapter 1]
a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1
nothing else; the limit may be -infinity

body: [Lemma 8 of arXiv:2609.02283, 'The game chromatic number of generalized Mycielski graphs of paths and cycles'] Consider a coloring game on $M_k(C_6)$ with three colors, where $k\geq2$. Suppose that $v_i^0$ and $v_{i+2}^0$ have distinct colors $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and denote the third color by $\gamma$. Suppose that $v_{i+1}^0$ and $v_{i+1}^1$ are uncolored and that, for some $p,q\in\{i,i+2\}$, the vertices $v_p^1$ and $v_q^2$ are uncolored and $\gamma$ is legal at both of them. Then Bob has a winning strategy.

[Definition def:continuous_continuous_coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let
  $(x_0, (\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0)), (\tilde x_0,(\tilde \sigma^1_0,
  \tilde \sigma^2_0)) \in [0, \ell] \times \Sigma$ be given. Let
  $s^1, s^2, \tilde s^1, \tilde s^2$ be four independent Markov jump
  processes with the transition rates of figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper) (resp. figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)) and respective
  initial states
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0, \tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde \sigma^2_0$. Set
  $\tau_i = \inf \{t \ge 0: s_i(t) = \tilde s_i(t)\}$ and define
\begin{align*}
  \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for } t \ge 0, \quad \quad \tilde \sigma^i(t) = \tilde s^i(t) \text{ for } t \le \tau_i \text{ and } \tilde \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for } t\ge \tau_i.
\end{align*}

Finally set $X = \mathcal X(\sigma^1, \sigma^2, x_0, \ell)$ and
$\tilde X = \mathcal X (\tilde \sigma^1, \tilde \sigma^2, \tilde x_0,
\ell)$.

Assume $u, v = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. Let $P^{(u)}$ and $Q$ be the mode-$1$ matricization of ${\cal P}^{(u)}$ and the transition matrix of the reduced first order chain $Y$, respectively. Then, 
\be

P^{(u+v)}=P^{(u)}Q^v.
\ee
In particular, we have 
\be

P^{(v)}=P^{(0)}Q^v
\ee
for any $v=0, 1, 2, \ldots$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2607.25986, 'Asymptotics of a two-species particle system associated to the doubly parabolic Keller-Seg'] Consider the process $(U^{1,N,M,\e}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ defined by
\begin{align*}
U^{1,N,M,\e}_t=&(\nu^{1,N,M,\e}_t\ast \nabla \phi_{\e})(X^{1,N,M,\e}_t)-(\nabla \phi_{\e}\ast b^{c_0,\theta,\lambda}_t)(X^{1,N,M,\e}_t)\\
&-\frac1{N-1} \sum_{j \in I_N,j\neq 1}\int_0^t (\nabla \phi_\e\ast K^{\theta,\lambda}_{t-s})(X^{1,N,M,\e}_t-X^{j,N,M,\e}_s)\dd s.
\end{align*}
For any $\sigma\in (0,\frac12]$, any $T>0$, there exists a constant
$A_{\sigma,T}$ (also depending on $\lambda,\theta,c_0$) such that for all $N\geq 2$, all $M>0$, all $\e\in (0,1]$,
$$
\sup_{t\in [0,T]}\E[|U^{1,N,M,\e}_t|^2] \leq \frac{A_{\sigma,T}}{(NM \e^{\frac12})^{2}}
+\frac{A_{\sigma,T}}{NM \e^{3+\sigma}}+\frac{A_{\sigma,T}}{NM^{1+\sigma}\e^{2+\sigma}}.

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Let $f:\Pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cone-additive function such that $|f(\pi)|$ grows at most polynomially in the length of $\pi\in \Pi$. Furthermore, assume that the power series $G(o,o|z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\P[X_n=o]\cdot z^n$ has radius of convergence strictly bigger than $1$.
Then there exists some constant $\mathfrak{c}\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr) = 
\mathfrak{c}\quad \textrm{almost surely}.
$$    
Moreover, if $f$ is strictly positive  then $\mathfrak{c}>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 1 of arXiv:2605.31300

[Theorem t:tara of arXiv:2505.11389, '\bf The Poisson Multiplication Formula'] Let $\gamma$ be a Poisson measure on a measurable space $(\mathcal{A} , \mathscr{A})$, with $\sigma$-finite intensity $\nu$. Assume that $G = G(\gamma)$ is such that $\mathbb{E}|G| < \infty$. Then, for all all $p\in [1,2]$ one has that
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\left| G \right|^p  \leq \left| 
\mathbb{E}[G] \right| ^p +  2^{2-p} \int_\mathcal{A} \mathbb{E}[ |D_a^+ G|^p]\, \nu(da).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.03243, 'Weighted Ces\`aro type operators on the weighted Bergman spaces in the unit ball'] Let $\alpha>-1$, $\beta>0$ and   $0<q<p\leq\infty$. Suppose $\mu$ is a positive Borel measure on $[0,1)$.
Then $\mathcal{C}_{\mu,\beta}^{\xi}: A_{\alpha}^p(\mathbb{B}_n)\to A_{\alpha}^q(\mathbb{B}_n)$ is bounded if and only if $\mu$ is finite and 
\begin{equation}
    \int_{0}^1\left(\frac{\hat{\mu}(r)}{(1-r)^{\lambda}}\right)^{\theta}\frac{{\rm d}r}{1-r}<\infty.
\end{equation}
Here
  \[
    \frac{1}{\theta}=\frac{1}q-\frac{1}p
    \quad \text{and}\quad
    \lambda=\beta+(n+1+\alpha)\Big(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\Big)
    =\beta-\frac{n+1+\alpha}{\theta}.
\]
For finite $\mu$, condition~\eqref{equa1.1} is equivalent to
\[
    \left\{\frac{\hat\mu(r_k)}{\delta_k^\lambda}\right\}_{k\geq1}
    \in\ell^\theta.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem bbmHydroAppendix of arXiv:2605.04860, 'Branching Brownian motion with rank-based selection and reaction-diffusion equations'] Let $\rho^N$ be a sequence of probability measures such that $\rho^N$ is the sum of $N$ atoms of weight $1/N$, and such that $\rho^N\Rightarrow \rho\ll\lambda$ as $N\to\infty$. Consider a branching Brownian motion $\{B^N_i(t):i\in \mathcal{U}^N(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ which initially has $N$ particles and empricial distribution $\rho^N$, and in which each particle branches at time-dependent rate $r(t)$. Define
    $$\eta_t^N:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in \mathcal{U}^N(t)}\delta_{B^N_i(t)},$$
    so that $\eta_0^N=\rho^N$, and $(\eta_t^N)_{t\geq 0}$ is the empirical measure-valued process describing the system. Let $\mathcal{L}^N_T$ be the law of $(\eta_t^N)_{t\in [0,T]}$. Then $\mathcal{L}^N_T$ converges weakly to $\mathcal{L}^\infty_T$ in the Skorokhod topology, and if $(\eta_t)_{t\in [0,T]}\sim \mathcal{L}^\infty_T$, then $\eta_t(dx)=u(x,t)dx$ where $u$ is the unique classical solution to the PDE $u_t = \frac12 u_{xx}+ r(t)u$ for $(x,t)\in \mathbb{R}\times (0,T)$ and $u(x,0)=\rho(x)$.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Let $(b_n)_{n\in \N}\subset \R$ be a sequence  satisfying $b_n >0$ and $\sum_{n\in\N} b_n <\infty$. Consider a sequence of nonnegative random variables $U_n$ satisfying, for some $c,C>0$ and for all $u\geq 0$,
\[
  \P(U_n>u) \leq C b_n^{-2} e^{-cu^2/b_n^2}\,.
\]
Then $U\coloneqq \sup_{n\in\N} U_n$ satisfies $\E e^{\lambda U}<\infty$ for all $\lambda>0$.
\begin{proof}
We compute the tail of $U$ via union bound:
\[
  \P(U > u) \leq C \sum_{n\in\N} b_n^{-2} e^{-c u^2/b_n^2}\,.
\]
Observe that  $v^{3} e^{-cv^2/2} \leq C'$ for some constant $C'>0$ and all $v \geq 0$, and thus for all $u, n\geq 1$,
\[
  b_n^{-2} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2b_n^2}}\leq C' u^{-3} b_n\,.
\]
Since $b_n \to 0$, we have $\eta \coloneqq \sup_{n\in\N} b_n <\infty$. It follows that, for $u\geq 1$,
\[
    \P(U>u) \ll u^{-3} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2\eta^2}} \sum_{n\in \N} b_n \ll u^{-3} e^{-\frac{cu^2}{2\eta^2}} \,.
\]
This implies the exponential moment bound for any $\lambda >0$ via the layer-cake formula.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[\tanh(\rl)^2(Y(t)-\tanh(\rl)^{-2})^2=\frac{1-\tanh^2(\rl)}{\tanh(\rl)^2}+(X(t)-1)^2,~~~\forall t\in[0,1].\]
The map  $Y$ can be expressed in terms of $X$. We have $X(t)=x\in[0,2]$ iff
\[  t=\frac {\rl-{\rm arcsinh} \left(\sinh \left( \rl \right) x- \sinh \left( \rl \right) \right)}{2\rl},  \]
and then
 \beq Y(x)=x-2\,{\frac {  \dis\sinh \left( \frac \rl2+\frac12\,{\rm arcsinh} \left(\sinh
 \left( \rl \right)  \left( x-1 \right) \right) \right)  ^{2}}{
\sinh \left( \rl \right)   ^{2}}},~~~ 0\leq x \leq 2.\eq
The area   and affine length of ${\cal H}_{\lambda}$ are given by
   \beq
   {\A}({\cal H}_\lambda)=  \rl {\frac {\cosh \left(\rl \right)  }{ 
\sinh \left( \rl \right)  ^{3}} \left( {\frac{\sinh \left( 2\,\rl \right)}{2\rl}}-1\right) }  =\rl \la  \frac {\cosh \left( \rl \right)  }{ 
\sinh \left( \rl \right)  ^{3}}
=\frac{\lambda}{(\lambda+1)^3}\frac{\cosh(\rl)^4}{\rl^2}    \eq
and

\beq 
\L_\lambda:= \L({\cal H}_\lambda)
=  2\prod_{k\geq 0} 2 \l(  \frac{\cosh(\rl/2^k)}{2(\cosh(\rl/2^k)+1)^2}\r)^{1/3} =\frac{2\rl\cosh(\rl)^{1/3}}{\sinh(\rl)} =  
\frac{2 \cosh(\rl)^{4/3}}{\lambda+1}.
\eq
For all $t\in[0,1]$,
\beq {Y''(t)X'(t)-X''(t)Y'(t)}  = \L_\lambda^3.
\eq (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theo 5 of arXiv:2510.26330

body: The Paris-Harrington theorem strengthens the finite Ramsey theorem. Call a finite set Y of positive integers relatively large if its size is at least as large as its minimum element. The strengthened statement asserts: for all positive integers n, k, m there is an N such that for every coloring of the k-element subsets of {1,...,N} with m colors, some relatively large subset Y of {1,...,N} with at least n elements is homogeneous, meaning every k-element subset of Y receives the same color. This statement is true, provable in second-order arithmetic, but Paris and Harrington proved in 1977 it is not provable in first-order Peano arithmetic, a natural combinatorial example of incompleteness.
title: Paris-Harrington theorem
Corollary 7 of arXiv:2608.06038

body: [Definition def:regular-loop-family of arXiv:2608.15923, 'Universality of two-dimensional Markovian holonomy fields'] A finite family of based rectifiable loops $L=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r)$ is called \emph{regular} if its image is contained in $\operatorname{int}(\Sigma)$ and the union of the images of its loops is a finite embedded ribbon graph $\Gamma(L)\subset\operatorname{int}(\Sigma).$ The vertices are the base point, the self-intersection points and the mutual intersection points. The edges are embedded piecewise-smooth arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors. We always take $\Gamma(L)$ to be minimal: all unmarked vertices of degree two are suppressed.
title: Definition def:regular-loop-family of arXiv:2608.15923

body:
[Theorem thm:intrinsicfreeness of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] Let $X$ be a $d\times d$ random matrix with jointly gaussian entries (not necessarily centered or self-adjoint), we have
\begin{equation}
    \Big| \mathbb{E}\|X\| - \|X_{\mathrm{free}}\|\Big| \leq C\tilde{v}(X)(\log d)^{\frac34},
\end{equation}
and, for all $t\geq 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{P}\left[ \Big| \mathbb{E}\|X\| - \|X_{\mathrm{free}}\|\Big| > C\tilde{v}(X)(\log d)^{\frac34} + 
    C\sigma_\ast(X)t
   \right] \leq \exp(-t^2),
\end{equation}
where $C$ is a universal constant, $\tilde{v}(X) = \sqrt{v(X)\sigma(X)}$ and $\sigma(X),v(X),\sigma_{\ast}(X)$ are as in Definition~(def:sigmaandv(X) of the paper). Recall that $\sigma(X)\leq\|X_{\mathrm{free}}\|\leq2\sigma(X)$.

If $X$ is self-adjoint the same inequalities hold replacing $\|X\|$, $\|X_{\mathrm{free}}\|$ by $\lambda_{\max}(X)$, $\lambda_{\max}(X_{\mathrm{free}})$ or by $\lambda_{\min}(X)$, $\lambda_{\min}(X_{\mathrm{free}})$.

For self-adjoint $X$ we also have:
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}\left[ d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathrm{sp}(X),\mathrm{sp}(X_{\mathrm{free}}) \right) > C\tilde{v}(X)(\log d)^{\frac34} + 
    C\sigma_\ast(X)t \right]\leq \exp(-t^2),
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{sp}(M)$ denotes the spectrum of $M$ and
\[
d_{\mathrm{H}}(A,B) \coloneqq \inf\left\{ \varepsilon>0:\, A\subseteq B + [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] \text{ and } B\subseteq A + [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] \right\} ,
\]
denotes the Hausdorff distance between two subsets of the real line. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Intrinsic Freeness~\cite{bandeira2023free,bandeira2024free2}

[Thm 23 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $A, B$ be  standard graded $\KK$-algebras, with $B$ a graded subalgebra of $A$. Suppose we can find homogeneous elements $a_1, \dots, a_m \in A$ with 
        $a_i B = B a_i$ for each $i$ which induce a direct sum decomposition 
        $A = \bigoplus_i a_i B$.
        If $B$ is Koszul, then $A$ is Koszul if and only if the quotient 
        $C = A/(B_+)$ is Koszul.
        Here $(B_+) = AB_+ = B_+A = AB_+A$.

[Definition 20 of arXiv:2609.02755, 'The Sharp Rate of Probabilistically Strong Convergence to the KPZ Equation'] We define $\tcT_1$ to be the set of trees $\tau = \mcI_{(\mfl, \partial)}^k \sigma \cdot \eta$ where $\eta \in \mcT_+$ conforms to $R$ and $\mcI_{(\mfl, \partial)}^k \sigma$ conforms to $R^\partial$ and satisfies $o(\mcI_\mfl^k \sigma) := \max\{\gamma_{\mcI_\mfl^k \sigma}, |\mcI_\mfl^k \sigma|_\mfs\} > 0$.  We define $\mcT_1$ similarly.
	
	Furthermore, for a tree $\tau$ conforming to $R$ and an edge $e$ of $\tau$ that is adjacent to the root, we write $\partial_e \tau$ for the tree obtained by replacing the type $\mfl$ of $e$ with $(\mfl, \partial)$. When the edge $e$ is clear from context (for example when $\tau$ is planted), we will sometimes simply write $\partial$ to avoid unnecessarily introducing variable names for edges.

body: [Proposition 13 of arXiv:2608.13358, 'Extreme points of sets of probability measures and $\phi$-divergences'] The extreme points of $\cP_q$ are precisely the measures $q_A$, where $A$ ranges over all $q$-atoms.\ In particular, $\cP_q$ has no extreme points if $q$ is atomless.

body:
[Definition 41 of arXiv:2608.29086, '2608.29086'] [$FLOW(M)$]
Given $M \subset M_0$ and $\Psi \subset TRAJ(M)$ (Definition \ref{def_traj}). $\Psi$ is called a \textit{flow} on $M$ if the trajectories of $\Psi$ do not intersect and $\Psi$ covers the entire $M$. i.e.,
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $\forall \psi_1,\psi_2 \in \Psi$, $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ share no triangles if  $\psi_1 \neq \psi_2$,
\item For $\forall abc \in Tri(M),\ \exists \psi \in \Psi$ uniquely such that $abc \in \psi$.
\end{enumerate}
A flow may have isolated triangles, terminal triangles, regular triangles, and branch triangles. $FLOW(M)$ denotes the collection of all flows on $M$.
title: Definition 41 of arXiv:2608.29086

body:
[Lemma 7 (Multinomial as conditional Poisson) of arXiv:2606.20816, 'Spectral Properties of Dense Barab\'asi--Albert Graphs'] Let $X_1, \dots, X_k$ be independent random variables with $X_j \sim \mathrm{Poisson} \left(\lambda_j\right)$ for $j = 1, \dots, k$, and set $\Lambda := \sum_{j = 1}^k \lambda_j$. Then, for any $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and any $\left(x_1, \dots, x_k\right) \in \mathbb{N}^k$ satisfying $\sum_{j = 1}^k x_j = m$,
\[
\P \left[
X_1
\ = \
x_1, \dots, X_k
\ = \
x_k \,\middle|\, \sum_{j = 1}^k X_j
\ = \
m
\right]
\ = \
\frac{m!}{x_1! \cdots x_k!}
\prod_{j = 1}^k \left(\frac{\lambda_j}{\Lambda}\right)^{x_j}.
\]
More concisely, conditional on $\sum_{j = 1}^k X_j = m$, the random vector $\left(X_1, \dots, X_k\right)$ has the probability distribution described by $\mathrm{Multinomial} \left(m; \frac{\lambda_1}{\Lambda}, \dots, \frac{\lambda_k}{\Lambda}\right)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Multinomial as conditional Poisson

[Defi app_def_indivGraph of arXiv:2411.16464, 'Generating social networks with static and dynamic utility-maximization approaches'] For a given individuals space $\mathcal{I}$ and a given individuals set $\mathscr{I} \in \mathcal{I}^I$, an \textbf{individual graph} is a 3-tuple $\mathcal{G}(\mathscr{I} , \alpha, C)$ with $\alpha, C$ two vectors of $(\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+})^{n_I}$ and $(\mathbb{R}_{+})^{n_I}$) with $n_I=\binom{I}{2} = \frac{I^2-I}{2}$ :
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\alpha$ is a \textbf{weight list}. $$\alpha = (\alpha_{1,2}, \hdots, \alpha_{1,I},  \alpha_{2,3}, \hdots, \alpha_{2,I}, \hdots,\alpha_{I-1,I} )^T$$
    with $\alpha_{i,j}$ the edge weight between agent i and j
    \item $\chi(i,j) = \innerproduct{P_i}{P_j}\mathbbm{1}(i\neq j)$ is the \textbf{compatibility function}, with $(i,j)\in \mathscr{I}^2$ and $P_i$ the first component of i (in $\mathcal{E}$).
    \item $C$ is a \textbf{compatibility list} $$C = (c_{1,2}, \hdots, c_{1,I},  c_{2,3}, \hdots, c_{2,I}, \hdots,c_{I-1,I} )^T$$ with $c_{i,j} = \chi(i,j) = \innerproduct{P_i}{P_j}$.
    
\end{itemize}

On each graph is defined $d : \mathcal{I}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ a distance between agents $i$ and $j$: the smallest number of intermediary non-null edges it takes to reach a vertex from another.
title: Individuals graph

[Theorem 14 (Secant-Gram metric domination for nonlinear RG) of arXiv:2606.07931, 'Pointwise Complexity for Gaussian Fields:\\Upper Envelopes, Algorithmic Lower Bounds, and '] Fix \(g\) and a finite neighborhood \(\mathcal N(g,\varepsilon)\).  Assume that for each \(j\): 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the later RG flow is locally stable: for every \(g'\in\mathcal N(g,\varepsilon)\) and all states \(U,V\) arising along the corresponding hybrid trajectories,
\[
\rho\bigl(\mathcal R_{J-1:j+1}^{g'}(U),\mathcal R_{J-1:j+1}^{g'}(V)\bigr)
\le M_{j\to J}(g,\varepsilon)\|U-V\|_{j+1};
\]
\item the scale-\(j\) finite replacement is dominated by a positive semidefinite secant Gram \(\Gamma_j(g,\varepsilon)\):
\[
\bigl\|\mathcal R_j^{g'_j}(S_j^{(j)})-
\mathcal R_j^{g_j}(S_j^{(j)})\bigr\|_{j+1}^2
\le
(g'_j-g_j)^\top\Gamma_j(g,\varepsilon)(g'_j-g_j).
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then all \(g'\in\mathcal N(g,\varepsilon)\) satisfy
\begin{equation}
\rho(S_J(g'),S_J(g))^2
\le
\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}
(g'_j-g_j)^\top G_j(g,\varepsilon)(g'_j-g_j),
\qquad
G_j:=J\,M_{j\to J}(g,\varepsilon)^2\Gamma_j(g,\varepsilon).
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:full-linear-reference of arXiv:2606.29557, 'Propagation of chaos for Belavkin equations beyond pure states'] For every $t\in[0,T]$,  define the random map
\[
  \Psi_t^{N,\eta}:\vartheta
  \longmapsto
  \widehat R_t^{N,\vartheta}.
\]
Then the map is linear and positive (almost surely).  Moreover, for every
$\vartheta\in\mathcal L^+(\mathcal H_N)$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[
    \mathrm{Tr}(\widehat R_t^{N,\vartheta})
  \right]
  =
  \mathrm{Tr}(\vartheta).
  
\end{equation}
title: Lemma lem:full-linear-reference of arXiv:2606.29557

[Definition 2 (Finite-stride convolution) of arXiv:2609.03361, 'Grassmann--Pl\"ucker Parametrization of Convolutional Filter Subspaces:\ Regularity and Cl'] For a filter
\[
  w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{k-1})\in\cK
\]
and an input
\[
  x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{d-1})\in E,
\]
define $C_wx\in F$ by
\begin{equation}
  (C_wx)_i=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w_jx_{si+j},
  \qquad 0\leq i\leq d'-1.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:length-relation}, if $0\leq i\leq d'-1$ and
$0\leq j\leq k-1$, then
\[
  0\leq si+j\leq s(d'-1)+k-1=d-1,
\]
so every input coordinate in \eqref{eq:convolution} is defined.
title: Finite-stride convolution

[Definition deftt of arXiv:2606.15203, 'The existence of invariant sublinear expectations for $G\text{-}$SDEs'] The operator $T_t$ is called a sublinear Markovian semigroup if for any $\varphi \in B_b(\mathbb{R}^d)$, it satisfies\\
\rm{(1)}. For each fixed $(t,x)\in \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^d$, $(T_t\varphi)(x)$ is an SE defined on $B_b(\mathbb{R}^d)$;\\
\rm{(2)}. $T_0\varphi=\varphi$;\\
\rm{(3)}. $t \to T_t\varphi$ satisfies the following Chapman semigroup formula,
\begin{equation*}
    (T_t \circ T_s)(\varphi)=T_{t+s}\varphi,\ t,s\geq 0. 
\end{equation*}
title: Sublinear Markovian semigroup \cite{Peng2005}

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] Let $S_{\nu} \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{<I}$ be fixed but arbitrary. 
	Let $\nu = \Ncal(m_{\nu}, C_{\nu}) \in \Gauss(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$, where $m_{\nu} \in \Hcal$, $C_{\nu} = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\nu})C_{*}^{1/2}$.
	Let $S, S_1,S_2 \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{< I}$. Let
	$\mu = \Ncal(m,C)$, $\mu_i = \Ncal(m_i, C_i) \in \Gauss(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$, $C= C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S)C_{*}^{1/2}$, $C_i = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_i)C_{*}^{1/2}$, $i=1,2$.
	Then, with $u_{\nu} = C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\nu} - m_{*})$, $u_i = C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_i - m_{*})$, $i=1,2$,
	\begin{align}
		&\left\la \log\left\{{\frac{d\mu_1}{d\mu_{*}}(x)}\right\}, \log\left\{{\frac{d\mu_2}{d\mu_{*}}(x)}\right\}\right\ra_{\Lcal^2(\Hcal,\nu)} 
		\\
		&
		= \frac{1}{2}\trace[(I-S_{\nu})S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}(I-S_{\nu})S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}]
		\nonumber
		
		
		
		\\
		& \quad +\left\la (I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}(I-S_1)^{-1}u_1 - (I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}u_{\nu}, \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad \quad \left.(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}(I-S_2)^{-1}u_2 - (I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}u_{\nu}\right\ra
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad + \frac{1}{4}\left[\la u_{\nu}, S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}u_{\nu}\ra-2\la (I-S_1)^{-1}u_1, u_{\nu}\ra \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad \quad \left. -  \trace(S_{\nu}S_1(I-S_1)^{-1})-	\log\dettwo[(I-S_1)^{-1} \right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \quad \times \left[\la u_{\nu}, S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}u_{\nu}\ra-2\la (I-S_2)^{-1}u_2, u_{\nu}\ra \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad \quad \left. - \trace(S_{\nu}S_2(I-S_2)^{-1})-	\log\dettwo[(I-S_2)^{-1}\right].
		\nonumber
	\end{align} 
	In particular, for $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu = \Ncal(m,C)$, $m_1 = m_2 = m$, $u_1 = u_2 = u = C_{*}^{-1/2}(m-m_{*})$, $S_1 = S_2 = S$,
	\begin{align}
		&\left\|\log\left\{\frac{d\mu}{d\mu_{*}}(x)\right\}\right\|^2_{\Lcal^2(\Hcal,\nu)} 
		\\
			&
		= \frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}S(I-S)^{-1}(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}||^2_{\HS}
		\nonumber
		
		
		
		\\
		& \quad +||(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}(I-S)^{-1}u - (I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}S(I-S)^{-1}u_{\nu}||^2
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad + \frac{1}{4}\left[\la u_{\nu}, S(I-S)^{-1}u_{\nu}\ra-2\la (I-S)^{-1}u, u_{\nu}\ra \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad \quad \left. -  \trace(S_{\nu}S(I-S)^{-1})-	\log\dettwo[(I-S)^{-1} \right]^2.
		\nonumber
	\end{align}
	Consequently,
	\begin{align}
		&\left\| \log\left\{{\frac{d\mu_1}{d\mu_{*}}(x)}\right\}- \log\left\{{\frac{d\mu_2}{d\mu_{*}}(x)}\right\}\right\|^2_{\Lcal^2(\Hcal,\nu)}
		\\
		&= \frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}[S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}-S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}](I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}||^2_{\HS}
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad + ||(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}[(I-S_1)^{-1}u_1 - (I-S_2)^{-1}u_2] 
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad -(I-S_{\nu})^{1/2}[S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}-S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}]u_{\nu}||^2
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad + \frac{1}{4}\left(\log\dettwo(I-S_1)^{-1}- \log\dettwo(I-S_2)^{-1} \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad+ \trace[S_{\nu}[S_1(I-S_1)^{-1}-S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}]]
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\quad \quad - \la u_{\nu}, [S_1(I-S_1)-S_2(I-S_2)^{-1}]u_{\nu}\ra 
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \quad \left.+ 2 \la (I-S_1)^{-1}u_1 - (I-S_2)^{-1}u_2, u_{\nu}\ra\right)^2.
		\nonumber
	\end{align}
	Furthermore,

		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad +[4||I-S_{\nu}||+8||u_{\nu}||^2] ||(I-S_2)^{-1}||^2||u_1 - u_2||^2. 
		\nonumber
	\end{align}

[Corollary 34 of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] Fix \(1\le m\le n\) and \(k\ge0\). If \((Q^{(m)})^{*k}=U\), then
\[
\|(Q^{(m)})^{*k}-U\|_{\TV}=0.
\]
Assume \((Q^{(m)})^{*k}\neq U\), and define
\[
w_{n,k}^{(m)}
:=
\min\left\{\ell\in\{0,\dots,n\}:\ \sum_{u=0}^{\ell}P_k^{(m)}(u)\,u!\,p^u>1\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\|(Q^{(m)})^{*k}-U\|_{\TV}
=
1-\sum_{u=0}^{w_{n,k}^{(m)}-1}P_k^{(m)}(u)
+\frac{1}{w_{n,k}^{(m)}!\,p^{w_{n,k}^{(m)}}}
\left(\sum_{u=0}^{w_{n,k}^{(m)}-1}P_k^{(m)}(u)\,u!\,p^u-1\right).
\]

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and in its classical strong form also gives a tail comparison, typically under an additional nonnegative-correlation condition. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances or a correlation-sign condition; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.

[Definition d:p-independent of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] A map $\bphi=(\phi_1,\dots, \phi_n):X\to \mathbb{R}$ with $ \phi_i\in \mathcal{F}_p$ for all $i=1,\dots,n$ is called $p$-independent in a measurable set $A\subset X$, if 
		\[
		\bigwedge^{\Lambda_{\bphi}}_{\blambda \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \frac{d\Gamma_p\langle \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \phi_i\rangle}{d\Lambda_{\bphi}}>0  \ \ \ \ \ \Lambda_{\bphi}\text{-a.e. in } A
		\]
		where $\blambda = (\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\in  \mathbb{S}^{n-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and
		$\Lambda_{\bphi} =\sum_{i=1}^n \Gamma_p\langle\phi_i\rangle$.
title: Definition d:p-independent of arXiv:2510.13659

[Cor gausssubexp of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Let $\boldsymbol{G}^N$ and $\boldsymbol{s}$ be defined as in Theorem 
(thm:maingauss of the paper). For any sequence of noncommutative polynomials 
$P_N\in\mathrm{M}_{D_N}(\mathbb{C})\otimes 
\mathbb{C}\langle\boldsymbol{s}\rangle$ of degree $O(1)$ and matrix 
coefficients of dimension $D_N=e^{o(N)}$, we have
$$
	\|P_N(\boldsymbol{G}^N)\|=(1+o(1))\|P_N(\boldsymbol{s})\|
	\quad\text{a.s.} \quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.
$$
Consequently, for any noncommutative polynomial 
$Q\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\boldsymbol{s}\rangle$ with
coefficients in a subexponential operator space $\mathbf{W}$, we have
$$
	\frac{1}{C(\mathbf{W})}
	\|Q(\boldsymbol{s})\|_{\rm min} \le
	\liminf_{N\to\infty}\|Q(\boldsymbol{G}^N)\|
	\le
	\limsup_{N\to\infty}\|Q(\boldsymbol{G}^N)\|
	\le C(\mathbf{W}) \|Q(\boldsymbol{s})\|_{\rm min}
	\text{ a.s.},
$$
where $C(\mathbf{W})$ denotes the subexponential constant of

body:
[Dfn 113 (temporal smoothing) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the spatially smoothed quantities specified by Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}. Recall the function $\sphicirc$ from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}, and let
	\[\tphi(t)
	\equiv
	\frac{2}{\tep}
	\sphicirc\lt(\frac{2
		t}{\tep}-1\rt)\,,\] so that $\tphi$ integrates to one and has support $[0,\tep]$. We define temporally smoothed coefficients by simply convolving with $\tphi$ in the time coordinate:
	\[\tB^N(t,y)
	\equiv\int_{\R} 
        \tphi(s) 
        \sB^N(t-s,y)\,ds
	= \tE\Big[ \sB^N(t-\sss,y)\Big]	\,,\]
where $\tE$ refers to expectation over the law of the random variable $\sss$ sampled from density $\tphi$. We define analogously $\tV^N$, $\tU^N$, $\trrr^N$,and $\twww^N$.  Recalling \eqref{e:qbar.and.qstar}, we will view all these quantities as being defined only for $t\in [q_*,1]$, so its definition only involves the values $\sbbb^N(t-s)$ for $t-s\in [\bar q,1]$, thus avoiding any temporal boundary issues. We then define 
	\begin{align*}
	\tbbb^N(t,y)
	&\equiv\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2} }\,,\\
	\tvvv^N(t,y)
	&\equiv \frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t) } 
	\,,\\
	\tuuu^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}} \,.
	\end{align*}
We abbreviate $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$. Recalling \eqref{e:sp.smoothed.F.N} we let
	\beq
	\tF^N(t,y)
\equiv\Big\{ \tV^N+2\tU^N+\trrr^N
\Big\}(t,y)+2\eta^{1/2}\,,
	\eeq
and we note that $\tF^N$ can be obtained by convolving $\sF^N$ with $\tphi$ in the time coordinate. In particular, since $\sF^N\ge0$, it follows that $\tF^N\ge0$ also.
title: temporal smoothing

body: A finite normal-form (strategic-form) game is a tuple (N, (S_i)_{i in N}, (u_i)_{i in N}) where N = {1,...,n} is a finite, nonempty set of players; for each player i, S_i is a finite, nonempty set of pure strategies; and for each player i, u_i: S_1 x S_2 x ... x S_n -> R is a payoff function assigning a real number to every strategy profile s = (s_1,...,s_n), one strategy per player. A mixed strategy for player i is a probability distribution sigma_i over S_i, and the expected payoff to player i under a profile of mixed strategies sigma = (sigma_1,...,sigma_n), with players randomizing independently, is the expectation of u_i(s_1,...,s_n) over s_i drawn from sigma_i for each i.
title: Finite Normal-Form Game

    There exist $K,C,c > 0$ such that, for any $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$, $s \geq K$ and $t \geq s + Ks^\kappa$, we have

	\varphi_0 \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( \frac{\vartheta_2 y}{t^{\kappa/2}} \aftergroup\egroup\originalright)}
    \nonumber \\

[Theorem thm:global-convergence of arXiv:2411.01364, 'Global Dynamics of Granular Media Equations via Stochastic Order'] Under Assumption (asp:potential of the paper), the following statements hold for the equation (equation eq:mvsystem of the paper).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item \textnormal{(Total Orderedness and Finiteness)} The set of invariant measures $\mathcal M$ is a finite set, totally ordered with respect to the stochastic order, and $\mathcal M\subset\mathcal P_{\8}(\mathbb R)$;
\item \textnormal{(Global Convergence to Order Interval)} $\inf_{\leq_{\mathrm{st}}}\mathcal M$ and $\sup_{\leq_{\mathrm{st}}}\mathcal M$ exist.
We denote them by $\underline{\nu}$ and $\overline{\nu}$ respectively.
Then for all bounded sets $B\subset\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)$,
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*B,[\underline{\nu},\overline{\nu}])\to0\ \text{ as $t\to\8$};
\]
\item \textnormal{(Globally Attracting from Below/Above)} For all $\mu\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\underline{\nu}$,
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\underline{\nu})\to0\text{ as }t\to\8,
\]
and for all $\mu\geq_{\mathrm{st}}\overline{\nu}$,
\[
\mathcal W_2(P_t^*\mu,\overline{\nu})\to0\text{ as }t\to\8.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:global-convergence of arXiv:2411.01364

[Definition 97 (Bottleneck profile) of arXiv:2507.07702, 'Observables of random spanning trees in random environment'] \sloppy 
Let $(G, \weight)$ be an electric network with weights $\weight = (\weight(e))_{e \in E}$ and consider the corresponding lazy random walk with stationary measure $\pi$. For $\pi_{\mathrm{min}} \leq r \leq 1/2$ define the quantity
\begin{equation*}
    \Phi_{(G, \weight)}(r) := \min\limits_{0 < \pi(S) \leq r} \Phi_{(G, \weight)}(S),
\end{equation*}
and for $r \geq 1/2$, let $\Phi_{(G, \weight)}(r) := \Phi_{(G, \weight)}(1/2) = \Phi_{(G, \weight)}$.

$x_{1,n},\ldots,x_{n,n}$. They are positive and simple.

body:
[Exlem 8 of arXiv:2506.13661, 'Box-Covariances of Hyperuniform Point Processes'] Let $\eta=\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$ be a stationary point process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $k$-th factorial cumulant measure $\gamma^{(k)}$. For any distribution $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ define the perturbation $\tilde \eta=\sum_i\delta_{X_i+Y_i}$ for i.i.d.~$Y_i\sim\mu$. Then,
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item The process $\tilde \eta$ has factorial cumulant measure $\tilde\gamma^{(k)}=\gamma^{(k)}\ast\mu^{\otimes k}$, where $\ast$ is the convolution on $(\mathbb{R}^d)^k$.
    \item The process $\tilde \eta$ has 
$\tilde\gamma^{(k)}_!=\gamma^{(k)}_!\ast\mu^{\Delta}$, where $\mu^\Delta$ is the distribution of $(Y_1-Y_k,\dots,Y_{k-1}-Y_k)$.
    \item If $\eta$  is Brillinger-mixing, then also $\tilde\eta$ is Brillinger-mixing. If for all $k\ge 2$, the measure $\gamma_!^{(k)}$ has a uniform sign, then the converse is also true.
    \item Let $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ have regularly varying density $f$ of order ${a-2}$ for $a\in (0,1)$ and $\eta$ on $\mathbb{R}$ be hyperuniform and Brillinger-mixing with $0\le -\frac{\mathrm d \beta }{\mathrm d x}(x)=o(f(x))$, such as the $\mathsf{sine}_2$ process. Then, $\tilde \eta$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm:CLT}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Exlem 8 of arXiv:2506.13661

[Corollary cor:Borel-faces of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Let $X$ be a topological space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The sets $R$ and $P\!_\tau$ are faces of the simplex $P$ of Borel probability measures.
They are linearly compact, $k$-neighborly simplices for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$. 
\item 
The extreme points are $\ext R=\ext P\!_\tau=P_1$ (Tops{\o}e).
\end{enumerate}
Consider moment constraints on the ambient space $Q=R$ or $Q=P\!_\tau$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(3)]
We have $\ext G(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$.
\item[(4)] 
We have $\ext G(C)=G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$ if $C$ is a singleton.
\item[(5)]
The constrained set $G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures is a face of $G(C)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Thm Weak Convergence of Approximate Tridiagonal Entries of arXiv:2411.01633, 'On the Limit of the Tridiagonal Model \\for $\beta$-Dyson Brownian Motion'] Fix a $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $T>0$ and define a vector of approximated tridiagonal entry processes,
\begin{equation*}
    \Tilde{E}_n(t):=\left(\Tilde{a}_1(t),\dots ,\Tilde{a}_k(t), \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(\Tilde{b}_1(t)^2-n),\dots ,\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(\Tilde{b}_k(t)^2-n)\right).
\end{equation*} Then, $\Tilde{E}_n(t)$ converges weakly in $C[0,T]$ to a vector process $E(t)=(A_1(t),\dots ,A_k(t),B_1(t),\dots,B_k(t))$, distributed as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}E(t) \sim \mathbf{OU}_{2k}(1,3,\dots ,2k-1,2,4,\dots ,2k)$. More explicitly, the components $A_j(t) \in C[0,T]$ and $B_j(t) \in C[0,T]$ are jointly-independent centered Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes with covariances $\mathrm{Cov}(A_j(t),A_j(s))=2e^{-(2j-1)|t-s|}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(B_j(t),B_j(s))=2e^{-2j|t-s|}$, for $j=1,\dots ,k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Weak Convergence of Approximate Tridiagonal Entries

Let $A \! \subseteq \! T$ be a non-empty subset. 

\smallskip

\begin{compactenum} 

\item[$(a)$] The \emph{total height} of $A$ is  $\mathtt{Ht}_{d,\rho} (A) \! = \!  \sup_{\sigma \in A} d(\rho, \sigma) \in [0, \infty]$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(b)$] The \emph{subtree spanned by $A$} is the smallest connected subset containing $A$ and $\rho$. Namely, $\mathtt{Span} (A) \! = \!  \bigcup_{\sigma \in A} [\![ \rho , \sigma ]\!]  $. We also denote by $\mathtt{S}\, \overline{\! \mathtt{pan}\!  }\,  (A)$ the closure of $\mathtt{Span} (A)$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(c)$] We say that a subtree $\mathtt{t}\! \subseteq \! T$ (i.e.~a connected subset containing $\rho$) is \emph{of finite type} if there is a finite subset $A\! \subseteq \! T$ such that $\mathtt{t} \! = \!  \mathtt{Span} (A)$. $\hfill \square$ 

\end{compactenum}

[Proposition 40 (Lipschitz dependence) of arXiv:2609.01826, 'An extension theory for fully fractional Schr\"odinger equations with memory'] Let $0<s\le\frac12$, equivalently $0\le a<1$, and let $p$, $q$, $r$ be
as in part (i) of Theorem~\ref{T:memory-wp}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{(1) The subcritical case $1<p<p_c$.} For every $M>0$ there exist
$T=T(d,a,p,\mu,M)>0$ and $C=C(d,a,p,\mu,M)>0$, both independent of the
individual data within the ball of radius $M$, such that the following holds
with $I=[0,T]$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] \emph{(half-space problem)} if $U,\widetilde U$ are the mild
solutions of \eqref{cp02} on $I$ with initial data
$U_0,\widetilde U_0\in L^2_a(\RN)$ of norm at most $M$, then
\[
\|U-\widetilde U\|_{\mathcal X_T}
\leq C\|U_0-\widetilde U_0\|_{L^2_a(\RN)};
\]
\item[(ii)] \emph{(memory problem)} consequently, if $u,\widetilde u$ are the
mild solutions of \eqref{E:nonlinear-memory} corresponding to histories
$u_0,\widetilde u_0\in\mathcal H^s$ of norm at most $M$, then
\[
\|u-\widetilde u\|_{L^q_t(I;L^r_x(\Rd))}
\leq C\|u_0-\widetilde u_0\|_{\mathcal H^s}.
\]
\end{itemize}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{(2) The critical case $p=p_c$.} The same two estimates hold for
every $M\le\varepsilon_0$, with $\varepsilon_0$ as in
Theorem~\ref{T:memory-wp}(i)(a), on $I=[0,T]$ for every $T<\infty$, with a
constant $C=C(d,a,p,\mu)$ independent of $T$.

\smallskip
\noindent
The restriction on $M$ in (2) is not technical: for $p=p_c$ and $M>\varepsilon_0$
Theorem~\ref{T:memory-wp} produces no solutions to be compared, and at the
scaling-critical exponent the existence time is in any case not a function of
the size of the datum alone. No separate Lipschitz estimate for the
$-1<a<0$ regime is asserted here; the two-exponent contraction used in
\cite[Theorem~2.9]{GS2} is not rewritten as a separate continuous-dependence
statement.

[Lemma L:jensen of arXiv:2609.03939, 'Arithmetic probability measures'] Let $K \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a compact set with $c(K)>0$, and let $Q \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ be a nonzero polynomial. 
Then
\[
\int \log |Q(z)| \, d {\nu_K}(z)= \log |\ell_Q| + \deg Q \log c(K) + \sum_{Q(r)=0} g_K(r, \infty).
\]
where $\ell_Q$ is the leading coefficient of $Q$, and the sum is taken over the zeros of $Q$, 
counted with multiplicity.

body: Let F, G: C -> D be functors between the same two categories. A natural transformation eta: F => G assigns to every object c of C a morphism eta_c: F(c) -> G(c) in D, called the component of eta at c, such that for every morphism f: c -> c' in C, the naturality square commutes: G(f) o eta_c = eta_{c'} o F(f), both sides being morphisms F(c) -> G(c') in D. If every component eta_c is an isomorphism in D, eta is called a natural isomorphism, and F, G are said to be naturally isomorphic.
title: Natural Transformation

body:
[Proposition p:difference of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] In the setting of Definition (def:vary of the paper), let $\overline{\delta_0}, \overline{\delta_1}$, $\overline{\delta_2}$ be deterministic drift functions such that $\overline{\delta_0}(x)>0$ on ${\mathbb R}$.  Let $r_0\in {\mathbb R}$ be a constant and $r_1\ge r_0$ be an $\mathcal F$-stopping time. We write $Y=(Y_x,\, x\ge r_0)$ for the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})$ flow line  starting at $(0,r_0)$ and we let $\mathcal S$ be the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_2})$ flow, both driven by $\mathcal W$. Let $\mathcal W^-_Y$ and $\mathcal W^+_Y$ defined as in (equation eq:W- of the paper) and (equation eq:W+ of the paper) from $(\mathcal W,Y)$ in place of $(\mathcal W,S)$. We extend $Y$ to ${\mathbb R}$ by setting $Y_x=0$ when $x<r_0$.  Consider the collection of processes 
 \begin{align*}
\mathcal S^+_{r,x}(a) &:=\mathcal S_{r,x}(a+ Y_r)- Y_x, &&  a\ge 0,\,  t(Y)>x\ge r, \\
\mathcal S^-_{r,x}(a) &:=  \mathcal S_{r,x}(a), && a\le Y_r,\, t(Y)>x\ge r\ge r_0
\end{align*}

\noindent where $t(Y):=\inf\{x\ge r_1\,:\, Y_x=0 \hbox{ and } \overline{\delta_1}(x)< 0\}$. We impose that 
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal S^+_{r,x}(a)=0  \mbox{ \rm if } x\ge \varphi_+(a,r), \qquad \mathcal S^-_{r,x}(a)=Y_x \mbox{ \rm if } x\ge \varphi_-(a,r),
\end{equation}

\noindent where, for any $a$ and $r$, 
\begin{align}
 \varphi_+(a,r) & :=\inf\{y> r\,:\, \mathcal S_{r,y}(a+ Y_r)\le Y_y  
\hbox{ and }  \overline{\delta_2}(y)\le  (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})(y)\},\\
\varphi_-(a,r) & :=\inf\{y> r\,:\, \mathcal S_{r,y}(a)\ge Y_y\hbox{ and } \overline{\delta_2}(y) \ge (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})(y)\}. \nonumber 
\end{align}

\noindent See Figure (fig:decomp of the paper). Then
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item  $\mathcal S^+$ is a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_2}\,|_{r_0}\,\overline{\delta_2} - \overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_2} -\overline{\delta_1})$ flow driven by the white noise $\mathcal W^+_Y$ killed on $\{\overline{\delta_2} \le (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})\}$ and restricted to $(-\infty,t(Y))$.
\item  The noise  $\mathcal W$ driving the SDEs of $Y$ and $\mathcal S^-$ can be replaced with $\mathcal W^-_Y$. In particular, $Y$ and $\mathcal S^-$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal W^-_Y$ and $r_1$.
\item If $Y$ is a $\ominus$-flow line, then $\mathcal W^+_Y$ is a white noise on ${\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb R}$  independent of $\mathcal W^-_Y$. 
\item Let $b\in {\mathbb R}$ and $\overline{\delta'}:= (\overline{\delta_0} \,|_b\, \overline{\delta_1})$. If $Y$ is a $\oplus$-flow line, then conditionally on 
$r_1=b$, $\mathcal W^-_Y$ is independent of $\mathcal W^+_Y$ and has the law of $\mathcal W^-$ associated by (equation eq:W- of the paper) to  the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta'})$ flow line starting at $(0,r_0)$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.25494, 'A functional central limit theorem for kernel gradient flow and infinitesimal gradient boo'] Let $\Psi,\Psi_1,\Psi_2$ be defined as
  in Equations~\eqref{eq:def-Psi}, \eqref{eq:def-Psi1}, \eqref{eq:def-Psi2}.
  Then:
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item For all fixed $(\xi^1,v)$, the mapping
    $F \mapsto \Psi_1(\xi^1,v,F,\P)$ is Fréchet differentiable on
    $\mathcal{H}$ and its gradient norm is bounded by
    $L\kappa$, where $L$ and $\kappa$ are respectively defined in
    Assumptions~\ref{ass:loss} and~\ref{ass:kernel}.
  \item For all fixed $(\bar\xi,v)$, the mapping
    $F \mapsto \Psi(\bar\xi,v,F,\P)$ is Fréchet differentiable on
    $\mathcal{H}$ and its gradient satisfies, for all $M\geq 0$,
    \[
      \sup_{\|F\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq M} \big\| \nabla_F
      \Psi(\bar{\xi},v,F,\P) \big\|_{\mathcal{H}} \;\leq \; C_M,
    \]
    for some constant $C_M>0$ that does not depend on $(\bar\xi,v)$.
    
    Furthermore, when $\P$ is replaced by $\P_n$, similar uniform
    bounds hold with constants that may depend on $n\geq 1$.
  \end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 5 (Structure of the first-order formulation: hyperbolicity and quadratic nonlinearities) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider the Einstein--Euler system under $\Tbb^2$ symmetry on $\Tbb^3$ for a general equation of state  satisfying~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}. After expressing the spacetime metric in areal gauge~\eqref{metric:areal}, consider the metric unknowns~$\amdeux, \Omega, P, Q, G, H$, together with the fluid unknowns $\mu, u$ entering the stress-energy tensor~\eqref{eq:Einsframe}. Assume furthermore that the solutions under consideration are sufficiently regular.
\bei

\item \emph{Hyperbolicity.}

\bei

\item \emph{Under the non-vacuum condition $- \Jbb \cdot \Jbb>0$,} in terms of $(\amdeux, \Omega)$ and of the unknowns $(\Jbb, \Kpar, \Lbb)$ defined in~\eqref{eq:definevar-KL} and \eqref{Jdef}, subjected to the causality inequalities~\eqref{eq:causal}, the evolution system consisting of~\eqref{eq:T2-1234-def},~\eqref{eq:T2-Euler-perp-def}, and~\eqref{eq:T2-all-suite-def} is a first-order hyperbolic system of $12$ nonlinear balance laws, supplemented with the $3$ constraints~\eqref{eq:theconstraints-def}. In addition, the wave equation for the lapse~\eqref{eq:waveconffac}, below, follows from this set of equations; in vacuum, it is a consequence of the geometry equations alone.

\hfuzz=0.3pt
\item At every non-zero null state, the two acoustic speeds and the (double) matter speed coalesce. Thus the diagonalization established on the timelike cone \emph{does not extend} uniformly to its null boundary; at $\Jbb=0$, the fluid direction is undefined.

\item If $p'(0)=0$, the limiting equations displayed in~\eqref{equa-Euler-Minko-trivial} have an explicit nontrivial Jordan structure at every non-zero null state; this is a degenerate, weakly hyperbolic regime. 

\eei 

\item \emph{Nonlinearities.}

\bei

\item The double characteristic family associated with the speed ${-\amdeux^{-1}\frac{J_1}{J_0}}$ is \emph{linearly degenerate} (even on the vacuum).  The other two nonlinear wave speeds are distinct away from the vacuum. If $p(\mu)/\mu$ tends to zero with $\mu$ tends to zero, these two nonlinear wave speeds coincide on the vacuum on which hyperbolicity is lost.  If $p(\mu)/\mu$ tends to a constant in $(0,1)$ (isothermal limit), these two nonlinear wave speeds remain distinct even on the vacuum and strict hyperbolicity holds. 

\item The metric evolution equations~\eqref{eq:T2-1234-def} and~\eqref{eq:T2-all-suite-def} and the fluid evolution equations~\eqref{eq:T2-Euler-perp-def} contain only terms that are quadratic in $(\Jbb,\Kpar,\Lbb)$, except that the fluid quadratic forms are multiplied by the bounded state-dependent coefficient $q_\Jbb$. 
They are all exactly quadratic in the isothermal case, since $q_\Jbb$ is then a constant.
\item With the exception of the lapse equations in~\eqref{eq:T2-567-def} and~\eqref{eq:evollambda-def}, all quadratic source terms involving only the variables $\Jperp, \Lbb$ are null forms\footnote{This is not the case for nonlinearities involving the variables $\Jpar, \Kpar$.}.

\eei

[Theorem 23 (Stability of two-parameter rough integrals) of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let $\mathbf{X}, \tilde{\mathbf{X}} \in  \Omega G_{p, \omega_{\mathbf{X}}}([a,b], V)$ and $\mathbf{Y}, \tilde{\mathbf{Y}} \in  \Omega G_{q, \omega_\mathbf{Y}} ([c,d], W)$. Consider the controlled paths
\[
Z \in \mathcal{D}^{p, q}_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}}\big([a, b] \times [c,d], F\big), \, \tilde{Z}\in \mathcal{D}^{p, q}_{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}, \tilde{\mathbf{Y}}}\big([a, b] \times [c,d], F\big).
\] 
Then the following estimate holds
\begin{align*}
&\left| \int_{[a,b] \times [c,d]} Z_{s, u} \, d(\mathbf{X}_s, \mathbf{Y}_u) 
      - \int_{[a,b] \times [c,d]} \tilde{Z}_{s, u} \, d(\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_s, \tilde{\mathbf{Y}}_u) \right|\\
&\qquad \leq C_{\omega_\mathbf{X}, \omega_\mathbf{Y}, p, q, Z, \tilde{Z}} 
\, \Big( D_{\omega_{\mathbf{X}}, \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}} d( Z, \tilde{Z} ) + \|\mathbf{X} - \tilde{\mathbf{X}}\|_{p} + \|\mathbf{Y} - \tilde{\mathbf{Y}}\|_{q} \Big),
\end{align*}
where $D_{\omega_{\mathbf{X}}, \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}} := \omega_{\mathbf{X}}(a,b)^{1/p} \omega_{\mathbf{Y}}(c,d)^{1/q}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stability of two-parameter rough integrals

[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] Consider a single-shelf shuffle with $n$ cards done $s$ times. If
    \[s=d+\frac{3}{2}\log_2 n,\;\;\;\;\;d\in\mathbb{R}\;\;\text{fixed}\]
    then as $n\to\infty$, we have 
    \[\text{sep}(P^s)\sim 1-\exp\left(-\frac{1}{6\cdot 4^d}\right)\]
    \begin{proof}
        We may replace $s$ shelves with $2^{s-1}$ shuffles in [FDH] by Proposition $(multishelfcorrespondence of the paper)$. Then, for some $c>0$, if $2^{s-1}=cn^{3/2}$ and $n\to\infty$, the result holds with $d=1+\log_2 c$. The above is equivalent to $s=d+\frac{3}{2}\log_2 n$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'

[Prop of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] For every natural number $k$, let $\triangle v := \boxtimes \Box^{k+1} \boxtimes \Box^{k} v$. 
    Then, there exists an APS $S$ such that $\mathsf{E}_S(\triangle)$ and $\mathsf{U}_S(\triangle)$ hold, but $\mathsf{E}_S(\boxtimes \Box^{k})$ fails.
