body:
[Prop nonexplosive-without-linear-Lyapunov of arXiv:2511.10223, 'Stochastic Reaction Networks Within Interacting Compartments with Content-Dependent Fragme'] The internal CRN in (equation eq:nonexplosive-without-linear-Lyapunov of the paper) is not explosive, but no linear Lyapunov function witnesses that it is not explosive. That is, for all $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, if $f(e,s)=c_1e+c_2s$ and $\mathcal A$ denotes the generator of $\mathcal I_\mathcal K$, then for all $c_3,c_4\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ there exists $e,s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ such that $\mathcal A f(e,s)>c_3 f(e,s)+c_4$.

Moreover, the coarse-grained model $N$ associated to (equation eq:nonexplosive-without-linear-Lyapunov of the paper) is also not explosive.
\begin{proof}
    To see that the internal CRN is not explosive, let $g(e,s)=e+\ln(s+1)$. Then
    \begin{align*}
    \mathcal A g(e,s)
    &=e(g(e+1,s)-g(e,s))+es(g(e,s+1)-g(e,s))\\
    &=e+es\ln\left(\frac{s+2}{s+1}\right) =e+es\ln\left(1+\frac1{s+1}\right)\\
    &\le e+es\frac1{s+1} \le e+e \le 2g(e,s).
    \end{align*}
    So the claim follows from Theorem (thm:lyapunov-nonexplosivity of the paper).
    
    To see that $g(e,s)=e+\log(s+1)$ cannot be replaced with a linear Lyapunov function above, fix $c_1,c_2>0$ and $c_3,c_4\ge0$, and let $f(e,s)=c_1e+c_2s$. Notice that
    \[
    \mathcal A f(e,s)=c_1e+c_2es.
    \]
    If $s$ is chosen such that $h(s):=c_2s^2+c_1s-c_3c_1s-c_3c_2s-c_4>0$ and we set $e=s$, then $\mathcal A f(e,s)>c_3 f(e,s)+c_4$. But $c_2>0$, so $h$ is a quadratic function with positive leading term and hence we can always pick such an $s$.

    Lastly, we have to show that $N$ is not explosive. For $n\in\mathcal N$, let
    \begin{align*}
        C(n)&=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} n_x, \qquad\qquad S(n)=\!\sum_{(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} sn_{(e,s)}, \qquad\qquad
        E(n)=\!\sum_{(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} en_{(e,s)}
    \end{align*}
    denote the total number of compartments, $S$ molecules, and enzymes, respectively, when in state $n$. Consider the function $V(n)=E(n)+\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)$. Then if $\mathcal L$ denotes the generator of $N$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal LV(n)
        &=\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}\Bigg[
        n_xe\big(E(n)+1-E(n)\big)
        +n_xes\big(\log(S(n)+1+C(n)+1)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\\
        &\quad\quad
        +sn_x\left(\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} \psi(x,y)\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+1+1)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\right)\Bigg]\\
        &=E(n)+\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}
        n_x(es+s)\\
        &\le E(n)+\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}
        n_x(E(n)s+s)\\
        &=E(n)+\big(E(n)S(n)+S(n)\big)\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\\
        &\le E(n)+\big(E(n)S(n)+S(n)\big)\frac1{S(n)+C(n)+1}\\
        &\le E(n)+E(n)+1\\
        &\le 2V(n)+1.
    \end{align*}
    So the remaining claim follows, as before, from Theorem (thm:lyapunov-nonexplosivity of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop nonexplosive-without-linear-Lyapunov of arXiv:2511.10223

[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2608.09840, 'Langevin dynamics along the zero set of real-analytic potentials'] Let $N$ and $\sigma$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:coarea} and let $u \colon N \to (0,\infty)$ be continuous. Define the fiber integral
\[
g(x) = \int_{\sigma^{-1}(x)} u \, d\Hcal^{n-r}, \quad x \in \sigma(N).
\]
Then every $x_0 \in \sigma(N)$ with the property that $\sigma(N)$ is an $r$-dimensional $C^1$ submanifold of $\R^d$ in some neighborhood of $x_0$ admits a neighborhood $W$ in $\R^d$ and a constant $c > 0$ such that $g \ge c$ on $W \cap \sigma(N)$.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02464, 'When does propagation of chaos in the critical Curie-Weiss model stop?'] We study increasing propagation of chaos for the critical Curie-Weiss model (i.e.\ the mean-field Ising model at critical inverse temperature $\beta=1$, with no external field). We give a simple way to see that for windows of size $k(N)\ll \sqrt N$ we still have propagation of chaos (reproving earlier results, see e.g.\cite{BAZ_chaos}), while for $k(N)$ of order $\sqrt N$ the propagation of chaos breaks down. The law of a single spin converges to $\pi$, the Bernoulli law with parameter $1/2$. If $k(N) =\alpha \sqrt N$, we give an explicit formula for the limiting distance in total variation of the law of the first $k(N)$ spins with respect to the $k$-fold product of $\pi$, as a function of $\alpha$. For even larger window sizes, the distribution of the spins has, in the thermodynamical limit, maximal distance to the $k$-fold product of $\pi$. One of the ingredients of the proof is a result about the unimodality/non-unimodality of the law of the number of positive spins among the first $k=k(N)$ spins, which may be of independent interest.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02464: When does propagation of chaos in the critical Curie-Weiss model stop?

[Proposition 8 ({\cite[Corollary~5.6) of arXiv:2609.00936, 'Extended Abstract of Counting Divisorial Contractions with Centre a $cA_n$-Singularity'] {Pae24Counting}}] 
Let $U = \operatorname{Spec} (\mathbb C[x_1, \ldots, x_n] / I)$ be an affine variety properly containing the origin. Assign positive integer weights $w_1, \ldots, w_m$ to the variables $y_1, \ldots, y_m$ of $\mathbb C^m$ and assign the weights $1, \ldots, 1$ to $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Let superscript ``an'' denote analytification. Let $\psi\colon (U^{\mathrm{an}}, \bm 0) \to (Z, \bm 0)$ be a biholomorphic map germ to a complex space subgerm $(Z, \bm 0)$ of $(\mathbb C^m, \bm 0)$. Define the variety $\hat U$ by
\[
\hat U := \operatorname{Spec} \frac{\mathbb C[x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_m]}{I + (\psi_1^{<w_1} - y_1, \ldots, \psi_m^{<w_m} - y_m)},
\]
where $\psi_j^{<w_j}$ denotes the truncation of the $j$-th coordinate power series of $\psi$ up to order $w_j - 1$. Note that $\hat U$ is isomorphic to~$U$ and let $\theta\colon (\hat U^{\mathrm{an}}, \bm 0) \to (Z, \bm 0)$ be the composition of the map germs of $\hat U^{\mathrm{an}} \to U^\mathrm{an}$ and $U^{\mathrm{an}} \to Z$. Then, both of the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\theta$ lifts to a biholomorphism around the exceptional loci of the weighted blowups, and
\item every proper birational morphism locally analytically equivalent to the weighted blowup of $Z$ is given by the weighted blowup of $\hat U$ for some local biholomorphism~$\psi\colon U \to Z$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:multipath-positive of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Let \(W\subset V\) and let \((a_i,b_i)\in W\times W\), \(1\le i\le r\),
with \(r\ge1\).  Write \(\mathbf a=(a_i)_{i=1}^r\) and
\(\mathbf b=(b_i)_{i=1}^r\).  For \(R\subset W\) and \(a,b\in W\), set \(\mathcal G_R(a,b)=0\) if either endpoint lies outside \(R\). There are unique finite coefficients
\(L_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(C)\ge0\), \(C\subset W\), such that, for every
\(R\subset W\),
\begin{equation}
        \mathbf 1_{\{a_i,b_i\in R\ \forall i\}}
        \left[\prod_{i=1}^r\mathcal G_R(a_i,b_i)\right]d_R
        =\sum_{C\subset R}L_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(C)d_{R\setminus C} .
\end{equation}
Moreover \(L_{\mathbf a,\mathbf b}(C)=0\) unless \(C\) contains all endpoints
and every connected component of \(C\) contains at least one endpoint.

body:
[Theorem 4 (Ambrosio/DiPerna-Lions) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Let $v:\mathbb R^d\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector
field satisfying
\begin{align*}
\textnormal{(R1)}\quad&
v\in L^1\bigl((0,T);BV_{\mathrm{loc}}
(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)\bigr),\\
\textnormal{(R2)}\quad&
D\!\cdot v_t=(\nabla\!\cdot v_t)\mathcal L^d
\quad\text{for a.e. }s,
\qquad
[\nabla\!\cdot v]^-
\in L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr),\\
\textnormal{(R3)}\quad&
\frac{|v|}{1+|x|}
\in
L^1\bigl((0,T);L^1(\mathbb R^d)\bigr)
+
L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr).
\end{align*}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the continuity
equation
\[
\partial_tu+\nabla\!\cdot(vu)=0,
\qquad
u(.,0)=u_0,
\]
has at most one bounded distributional solution 
$
u\in L^\infty\bigl((0,T);L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr).
$
\item
There exists a regular Lagrangian flow $Z$ associated with $v$,
unique up to $\mathcal L^d$-null sets, and
\[
Z(t,\cdot)_\#\mathcal L^d
\le
\exp\left(
\int_0^t
\bigl\|[\nabla\!\cdot v(\cdot,s)]^-\bigr\|_{L^\infty}\,ds
\right)\mathcal L^d.
\]
\item
For every nonnegative
$u_0\in L^1\cap L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the unique solution is
$
u_t\mathcal L^d
= Z(t,\cdot)_\#(u_0\mathcal L^d).$
\end{enumerate}
If, in addition,
\[
[\nabla\!\cdot v]^+
\in L^1\bigl((0,T);L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\bigr),
\]
then the reverse flow is well posed and satisfies two-sided compression bounds;
in particular $Z(t,\cdot)$ is
essentially invertible. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 76 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $U,V$ be random variables with $U,V\sim \Unif{[0,1]}$. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $U = 1-V, a.s.$,
\item $\P(U\leq s, V\leq t) = \cW(s,t) := (s+t-1)\vee 0$.
\end{enumerate}

STATUS: proof (unaudited); own-work draft; no novelty assertion. Complete implicit parametrization of all balanced opposite-head two-cycles across scalar logistic tanh factored-attention models with 0<a<b, plus exact transverse multiplier 5-2r-2/r; no factor sign flip is possible. One strictly increasing scalar equation determines the unequal negative margins. A 576-case full-Jacobian scan found no attracting candidates, as numerical evidence only.
ASSUMPTIONS: Single signed link h(s)=a+b tanh(kappa s), 0<a<b, kappa>0, eta>0, simultaneous Euclidean joint GD in (v,k,q), k^2=q^2 on the cycle, v0*v1<0. Explicit necessary and sufficient parametrization across model parameters given in proof.
SCOPE/GAP: Independent audit pending. Uniform instability of the balanced Jacobian block for unequal head magnitudes remains open; 576 floating-point samples do not settle it.

# Balanced opposite-head two-cycles: complete implicit parametrization

T328-W698-017 v1, Target 1, proof (unaudited).

Consider L(v,k,q)=log(1+exp(-v h(kq))), h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
0<a<b, kappa>0 and simultaneous Euclidean GD with fixed eta>0.
For this scalar signed link, every balanced period-two orbit whose heads have
opposite signs is covered by the following construction, up to interchanging
the two phases and simultaneously negating both factors. The construction
parametrizes cycles across the data/step parameters; for prescribed a,b,kappa,
eta these parameter equalities are necessary and sufficient, not a claim that
every prescribed model has such a cycle.

## Construction from four positive parameters

Choose 0<r<1 and T,y0,kappa>0. Define

    A=tanh T, B=tanh(r^2*T),
    D=cosh(T)^2/cosh(r^2*T)^2,
    sig(y)=1/(1+exp(-y)), f(y)=y*sig(y)^2.

There is a unique y1>0 solving

    f(y1)=f(y0)/(r*D).

Indeed f'(y)=sig(y)^2*[1+2y*(1-sig(y))]>0 on y>0,
and f increases continuously from 0 to infinity. Put

    g0=sig(y0), g1=sig(y1), c=g0/g1,
    t=y1/(y0*c),
    v0=sqrt((1-r)*(A-B)/((1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2)),
    H0=y0/v0, H1=c*H0,
    b=H0*(1+c)/(A-B), a=b*A-H0,
    eta=v0*(1+t)/(g0*H0), w=sqrt(T/kappa).

All denominators are strictly positive. Also a/b=(c*A+B)/(1+c) lies
strictly between B and A, hence 0<a<b. These parameters give the exact
period-two orbit

    (v0,w,-w) <-> (-t*v0,r*w,-r*w).

The two signed margins are -y0 and -y1. In particular the logistic factors
are exactly g0 and g1, not factors obtained from a limiting approximation.

## Verification

h(-w^2)=-H0 and h(-r^2*w^2)=H1. Thus g0*H0=g1*H1 and
the two head increments are respectively -v0*(1+t) and v0*(1+t).
Let d0=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, d1=b*kappa*sech(r^2*T)^2=D*d0.
The first factor coefficient is

    delta0=eta*v0*g0*d0
          =v0^2*(1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2/(A-B)=1-r.

For the second coefficient, the scalar equation gives

    t*(g1/g0)*D = y1*g1^2*D/(y0*g0^2)=1/r.

Consequently delta1=eta*(-t*v0)*g1*d1=-(1-r)/r=1-1/r.
On k=-q the factor multipliers 1-delta0=r and 1-delta1=1/r
return the factors exactly. The head changes sign, so the orbit is nonfixed.

## Completeness within the stated class

Balance means k^2=q^2. If k=q, the product is nonnegative, h(kq)>0,
and the head strictly increases at every finite point, so there is no finite
cycle. If k=q=0 the same argument applies. Thus a balanced cycle must lie
on k=-q with nonzero k. Interchange phases so v0>0>v1 and simultaneously
negate both factors so k0=w>0. Since delta_j=eta*v_j*g_j*h'_j,
delta0>0>delta1. The returning-factor equation is

    (1-delta0)*(1-delta1)=1.

The second factor is >1; therefore 0<1-delta0<1. Write this number r.
It follows that k1=r*w and delta1=1-1/r. In particular no factor sign flip
is possible for an opposite-head balanced two-cycle in this class.
The head update v1-v0<0 forces h0<0, and the reverse update forces h1>0.
Set H0=-h0, H1=h1, t=-v1/v0, T=kappa*w^2,
y0=v0*H0, y1=t*v0*H1. These are positive. The equal and opposite
head increments imply H1/H0=g0/g1=c, whence t=y1/(y0*c).
Dividing the two factor coefficients gives r*D*f(y1)=f(y0).
The identities h1-h0=b*(A-B), delta0=1-r and the head increment then
recover precisely the formulas for b,a,v0,eta above. This proves completeness.

## Full Jacobian test and its present limit

The normal two-step multiplier is exactly

    mu_U=(1+delta0)*(1+delta1)=(2-r)*(2-1/r)=5-2r-2/r.

It satisfies |mu_U|<1 precisely for (3-sqrt(5))/2<r<1,
equals -1 at the left endpoint, and is <-1 below it. It is zero at r=1/2.
The other two multipliers are exactly the eigenvalues of J1*J0, using
the general balanced Jacobian given in proofs/014_opposite_head_cycles.md.
This is an exact formula for the full spectrum, but no uniform inequality
for that balanced block has been proved for unequal head magnitudes.

The reproducible script scripts/asymmetric_cycles.py sampled 576 choices:
r in {.1,.2,.35,.4,.5,.65,.8,.9,.98}, T in {.1,.3,.6,.9,1.3,2,3,5},
y0 in {.01,.1,.4,1,2,4,8,16}, with kappa=1. It solved the monotone
equation by floating-point bisection and differentiated the full 3D loss.
It found zero attracting candidates; the smallest observed full spectral
radius was approximately 8.9666956. The largest relative cycle residual was
approximately 2.56e-13. These are numerical evidence, not rigorous bounds,
and cannot establish instability throughout the parametrization.

Claim 016 proves full instability and the complete second-multiplier phase
diagram on the equal-head-magnitude subfamily r=1/2,
cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2. The SINGLE remaining hard step for upgrading
the wider numerical finding to a theorem is a rigorous spectral-radius
inequality for J1*J0 throughout (r,T,y0)>0 with 0<r<1. This proof
does not claim that step or almost-everywhere factored-GD convergence.

[Lemma 31 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let $K$ be a rank-two bundle with formal Chern roots $a,b$, and let
\[
 0\to S\to\pi^*K\to Q\to0
\]
be the tautological sequence on $\PP(K)$ in the quotient convention.  Put $s=c_1(S)$ and $q=c_1(Q)$.  For every polynomial $\Phi(q,s)$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$,
\begin{equation}
 \pi_*\bigl(s^\epsilon(q+h_z)\Phi(q,s)\bigr)
 =\left.
 \partial_i\bigl(x_{i+1}^\epsilon(x_i+h_z)\Phi(x_i,x_{i+1})\bigr)
 \right|_{(x_i,x_{i+1})=(a,b)}.
\end{equation}

[Lem 10 of arXiv:2609.00719, 'On the Aleksandrov--Bakelman--Pucci estimates for the weighted $1$-Laplacian'] Let $u\in \mathrm{USC}(\R^n)$ and $u_j\in C(\R^n)$ be nonnegative. Assume that, for every $x\in\R^n$,
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(I)] there exist $x_j\to x$ such that $u_j(x_j)\to u(x)$;
            \item[(II)] for every sequence $x_j\to x$,
            \[
            \limsup_{j\to\infty}u_j(x_j)\leq u(x).
            \]
        \end{enumerate}
        Then
        \[
        \limsup_{j\to\infty}\Theta(u_j)
        \subseteq \Theta(u).
        \]

body: If A is a square matrix with every entry strictly positive, then A has a real eigenvalue r > 0, the Perron root, that is strictly greater in absolute value than every other eigenvalue of A. This r is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial and has an eigenvector with all entries strictly positive, unique up to positive scaling; no other eigenvalue admits a nonnegative eigenvector. If A is merely nonnegative and irreducible, r > 0 still exists as an eigenvalue of maximal absolute value with a positive eigenvector, though other eigenvalues may tie it in absolute value. Proved by Oskar Perron (1907) and Georg Frobenius (1912).
title: Perron-Frobenius theorem

Consider the Gaussian network and empirical FIM F_M specified in assumptions,with fixed depth L,sample count T>=1 and output dimension C>=1. Write g_(k,t)=grad_theta f_k(x_t),P=dim(theta),and F_M=(1/T)*sum_(k,t) g_(k,t)g_(k,t)^T. Let alpha>0 satisfy P/M^2->alpha,and assume explicitly that <g_(k,s),g_(kprime,t)>/M->delta_(k,kprime)*alpha*K_st,where K has diagonal kappa1 and off-diagonal kappa2,with kappa1>=kappa2>=0. All these finitely many limits hold jointly almost surely,or jointly in probability. Then lambda_max(F_M)/M -> (alpha/T)*(kappa1+(T-1)*kappa2),in the same convergence mode. The source defines kappa1 and kappa2 by the same-sample and distinct-sample order-parameter sums: kappa_j=(1/alpha)*sum_(l=1)^L alpha_(l-1)*qtilde_(j,l)*qhat_(j,l-1),where qhat_(1,l)=lim ||h_l(x_t)||^2/M_l,qtilde_(1,l)=lim ||grad_(u_l)f_k(x_t)||^2;for j=2 replace each squared norm by the corresponding inner product at distinct inputs s,t. The backward-weight decoupling is Assumption1 of the source;the explicit gradient Gram convergence is an additional hypothesis here. The output multiplicity C does not multiply this largest-eigenvalue coefficient. Fixed C,T and kappa2>=0 are essential to this stated version. No conclusion about nonzero lower-order eigenvalues when the leading coefficient vanishes,or about a growing sample count,is asserted. Draft,independent review pending.
Fixed L>=2 and fixed positive integers C,T. Widths M_l/M->alpha_l>0 for l=0,...,L-1; M_L=C. Hidden layers h_l=phi(u_l), u_l=W_l*h_(l-1)+b_l; output f=u_L is linear.
Independent Gaussian initialization W_l[i,j]~N(0,sigma_w^2/M_(l-1)) and b_l[i]~N(0,sigma_b^2), sigma_w>0 and sigma_b>0. Inputs are iid standard Gaussian. Parameters theta include all weights and biases.
phi and phi_prime have finite squared Gaussian integrals at each recursively occurring preactivation variance. The empirical FIM normalization is F=(1/T)*sum_(t=1)^T sum_(k=1)^C grad_theta f_k(x_t)*grad_theta f_k(x_t)^T.
C,T,L are fixed as M tends to infinity. P is the total number of weights and biases,alpha=sum_(l=1)^(L-1) alpha_l*alpha_(l-1),and P/M^2->alpha>0.
Explicit additional hypothesis: for every fixed k,kprime in1..C and s,t in1..T,the inner product of parameter gradients divided by M converges to delta_(k,kprime)*alpha*(kappa1 if s=t else kappa2). Convergence is either almost surely throughout,or in probability throughout.
The finite constants satisfy kappa1>=kappa2>=0. Forward and backward same-sample and distinct-sample order parameters entering the source formulas have finite deterministic limits common to each sample or sample pair. These convergence and output-decoupling statements are premises,not consequences proved here from Assumption1.

body:
[Theorem thm-intro-main of arXiv:2605.24627, 'A 4/7-limit law for the largest interpoint distance in a rotational ellipsoid'] Let $0<a<1$. Then
\[
n^{4/7}(2-M_n) \stackrel{{\cal D}}{\longrightarrow} Z,
\]
where $\stackrel{{\cal D}}{\longrightarrow}$ denotes convergence in distribution, and 
\[
\mathbb{P}(Z>t) = \exp\{-\Lambda_{a}t^{7/2}\}, \qquad t\ge 0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\Lambda_{a} = \frac{9}{64\pi}I_{a},
\]
where
\[
I_{a} = \int_A \mathbf 1 \{G(s,s',y,y',\tau)\le 1\}
\,{\rm d}s\,{\rm d}s'\,{\rm d}y\,{\rm d}y'\,{\rm d}\tau,
\]
\[
G(s,s',y,y',\tau) = \frac{s+s'}{2} + \frac{\tau^2}{4} 
- \frac{a^2}{4}(y-y')^2,
\]
and
\[
A = \{(s,s',y,y',\tau): s,s'\ge 0,\ y^2\le s,\ (y')^2\le s'\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-intro-main of arXiv:2605.24627

body:
[Lemma lem:cross-dictionary-margins of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] There exist fixed constants $c_D,g_G^0,C_S,C_G>0$ such that every dictionary
in the supplied local shell satisfies
\begin{equation}
    \left\|
        \sum_{j=1}^qh_jd_j
    \right\|_2
    \ge
    c_Ds\|h\|_2,
    \qquad
    h\in\mathbb R^q.
    
\end{equation}
For $t\in\mathbb R$, write $[t]_+=\max\{t,0\}$.
If two candidate dictionaries have quotient-dictionary distance at most
$\rho$, then two distinct size-$r$ coherent-block supports are separated by
at least
\begin{equation}
    m_S(\rho)
    =
    \left[
        \sqrt{2}\,c_D\beta_-s
        -
        C_Sr\beta_+\rho
    \right]_+,
    
\end{equation}
whereas a coherent-block mean and a separated-atom mean are separated by at
least
\begin{equation}
    m_G(\rho)
    =
    \left[
        g_G^0
        -
        C_G(r\beta_++\gamma_+)\rho
    \right]_+.
    
\end{equation}

The constants can be chosen so that $m_S(\rho)>0$ also guarantees a unique matching of the coherent atoms across the two dictionaries. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Support and local-explanation separation across nearby dictionaries

body:
[Theorem 6 (Varying environment: convergence of parameters) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of
Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}. Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a varying environment sequence with
components $(\theta_n,\lambda_n,p_n,d_n)$. Assume
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}(\theta_n,\lambda_n,p_n)=(\theta,\lambda,p)\in(0,\infty)^3,
\qquad \theta>\lambda,\ p\le1,
\]
and that $d_n\to+\infty$.  Then, for every dispersion mechanism $\Delta^{(j)}$,
$j=1,2,3,4$,
\begin{itemize}
  \item if $p>\dfrac{\theta}{\theta+\lambda}$, the process is supercritical and survives with positive probability;
  \item if $p<\dfrac{\theta}{\theta+\lambda}$, the process is subcritical and becomes extinct almost surely.
\end{itemize}

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:c0fd38f7d0050a95f86b45db4df9122b58221a436aefb71b330e6424a4e178e7","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/c0/c0fd38f7d0050a95f86b45db4df9122b58221a436aefb71b330e6424a4e178e7.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e97f6a2e479fc982d98ea30da46acade3b1f8a8696c0060e11d5d777756a1fb5","bundle_entry_key":"2605-04048-theorem-5-varying-environment-convergenc","bundle_id":"population.tex-extract-s3_026","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"tex-extract-20260907/bundle_s3_026.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:harvest.arxiv.mathematics:arxiv-2605-04048-theorem-5-varying-environment-convergenc","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Paper's own proof, opening: For the full dispersal mechanism (D1),
\[
\mu_n^{(1)} = p_n\Bigl(1+\frac{\lambda_n}{\theta_n}\Bigr),
\]
which by continuity converges to $\mu:=p(1+\lambda/\theta)$ as $n\to\infty$. Hence, the Cesàro means are so that $\frac1n S_n^{(1)}\to\log\mu$.

Now consider mechanism D4.  For any fixed integer $r\ge0$, the definition of $\Delta^{(4)}$ implies that, conditionally on $Y_n=r$, $\Delta^{(4)}(Y_n)$ is the number of occupied territories among $d_n$ when $r$ individuals are uniformly placed. [Definition def:pred_proj of arXiv:2601.09976, 'Stochastic Calculus as Operator Factorization:\\ An Operator--Covariant Derivative and Uni'] Assume that $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists of jointly measurable processes and that the predictable processes form a closed subspace of~$\mathcal{H}_X$. The \emph{predictable projection} $\Pi_X \colon \mathcal{H}_X \to \mathcal{H}_X$ is the orthogonal projection onto this subspace.

The closedness assumption is not automatic for an arbitrary energy space; it must be verified. In all examples of this paper, the predictable subspace is either all of~$\mathcal{H}_X$ (for It\^o integrals with respect to martingales and compensated Poisson processes, where $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists entirely of predictable processes) or is closed by standard results on conditional expectation.

For the integral-form energy spaces used throughout this paper---specifically, those where $u_t \in L^2(\Omega)$ for each~$t$ and the $\mathcal{H}_X$ inner product takes the form $\langle u, v \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_X} = \mathbb{E}[\int_0^T u_t v_t\, d\mu_t]$ for some positive measure $\mu$ on $[0,T]$ (possibly random, as with $d\langle X\rangle_t$)---the predictable projection admits the pointwise representation
\[
(\Pi_X u)_t = \mathbb{E}[u_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-}] \quad \text{for } t \in (0,T], \qquad (\Pi_X u)_0 = \mathbb{E}[u_0 \mid \mathcal{F}_0],
\]
where $\mathcal{F}_{t-}$ is the left-limit $\sigma$-algebra defined in Section~(sec:setup of the paper). This is the standard predictable projection of optional processes; see, e.g., [Revuz1999].

body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.

[Proposition prop:pop-hk-summatory of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For integers $m\geq0$ and $k\geq3$, write
\[
 K_{m,k}=\sum_{r=2}^{m}\kappa_{k,r},
\]
with the empty sum equal to zero when $m=0$ or $1$.
Let
\[
 I_k=\int_{\substack{c\in\mathbb R^{k-1}\ {\rm mixed}\\
                      \delta_k(c)\leq1}}w_k(c)\,dc.
\]
Then $0<I_k<\infty$ and, for fixed $k\geq3$,
\begin{equation}
 K_{h,k}=\sum_{r=2}^h\kappa_{k,r}
 \sim\frac{I_k}{2\zeta(k-1)}h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}
Here the asymptotic is as $h\to\infty$.  For $k=4$, these constants agree
with the preceding ones: $\kappa_{4,r}=\kappa_r$ and $I_4=I$.
In particular, $K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}$.

[Lemma 7 (Signed threshold coordinate) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] After orienting $a$, the function $a(c)$ changes sign at $c_*$.  More
precisely, for some finite odd integer $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 a(c)=\kappa(c-c_*)^m+O((c-c_*)^{m+1}),
 \qquad \kappa\ne0.
\end{equation}
Consequently $a$ is a strictly monotone local coordinate and its inverse is
continuous, though it need not be differentiable when $m>1$.

Fix deterministic cookie stacks beta_{z,j} in [-1,1] for z in Z^2 and j>=1. On the j-th departure from z, a walk started at x chooses each horizontal unit step with probability (1+beta_{z,j})/4 and each vertical unit step with probability (1-beta_{z,j})/4. Suppose there are common constants A,B>=0 such that at every z, sum_{j>=1}(beta_{z,j})^+<=A and sum_{j>=1}(beta_{z,j})^-<=B. If A+B<1+1/(2*pi+1), then from every starting point the walk visits every vertex infinitely often almost surely. The positive and negative budgets must be bounded separately by the same constants at all vertices; bounds on their sum at each site do not automatically give the displayed uniform A+B condition. The result allows infinitely many nonzero cookies and arbitrary spatial variation. It does not cover the exclusive-axis M(2,1,1) walk, whose repeat-departure cookies have infinite total strength. Source: Recurrence and range of the balanced excited random walk M(2,1,2), Theorem 1.2, eqs.(2)-(3), p.2; proof Section 5, pp.13-14.

body: Little Picard theorem: if f : C -> C is entire and non-constant, then the image of f is either all of C or C minus a single point, i.e. f omits at most one complex value. If moreover f is transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood of z_0 and z_0 is an essential singularity, then on every such punctured neighborhood f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely many times. The little theorem's transcendental case follows from the great one applied to g(z) = f(1/z) at its essential singularity 0.
title: Picard theorem

body:
[Defn 80 of arXiv:2608.28200, '\textbf On the Formality of Configuration Spaces of $\aka$'] A diagram consists of the data $\Gamma=(A_\Gamma,I_\Gamma,E_\Gamma,s_\Gamma,t_\Gamma, W^V_{\Gamma},W^E_{\Gamma})$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $A_\Gamma$ is a finite set of external vertices.
\item $I_\Gamma$ is a linearly ordered finite set of internal vertices, disjoint from $A_\Gamma$.

Denote by $V_\Gamma:= A_\Gamma \sqcup  I_\Gamma$ the set of all vertices.
\item $E_\Gamma$ is a linearly ordered finite set of edges.  
\item $s_\Gamma,t_\Gamma:E_\Gamma \to V_\Gamma$ are the source and the target. Both of them are endpoints of edges. 
\item $W^V_\Gamma:V_\Gamma \to \C[\ZZi ]$ is the weight of vertices.
\item $W^E_\Gamma:E_\Gamma \to \C[\partial_{1},\cdots,\partial_{n}]$ is the weight of edges. 
\end{itemize}  
We adopt the following terminology and notation:
\begin{itemize}
\item Denote the set of endpoints of an edge $e$ by $\partial e$.
\item We extend the linear order of $I_\Gamma$ to a partial order on $V_\Gamma$ by letting $a<i$ when $a\in A_\Gamma$ and $i\in I_\Gamma$. 
\item Two distinct vertices are said to be adjacent if they are the endpoints of an edge.
\item We say that the edge $e$ is oriented from $s_\Gamma(e)$ to $t_\Gamma(e)$.
\item We divide the set of edges into the following four families:
\begin{itemize}
    \item a loop is an edge whose endpoints are identical;
    \item a chord is an edge between two distinct external vertices;
    \item a dead end is an edge that is not a loop and such that at least one of its endpoints is internal and has only one adjacent vertex;
    \item a contractible edge is an edge that is neither a chord, nor a loop, nor a dead end.
\end{itemize}

\item The {valence} of a vertex is the number of edges for which the vertex is
an endpoint, with loops adding two to the valence.
\item An edge $e$ is {simple} if there exists no other edge with the same set of endpoints.
\item {Double edges} are distinct edges with the same set of endpoints. 
\item Two vertices $v$ and $w$ are {connected} if there exists a path of edges joining them (ignoring orientations). 
\item Given a finite set $A$, a  {diagram on $A$} is a diagram $\Gamma$ such that $A_\Gamma=A$.
\item A diagram on $A$ is a {unit} if it has no internal vertices or edges.  We denote a unit by $\boldsymbol{1}$. 
\item Two diagrams  $\Gamma$ and  $\Gamma'$ are {isomorphic} if $E_\Gamma=E_{\Gamma'}$ and there exist two order-preserving bijections $\phi_E\colon E_\Gamma\cong E_{\Gamma'}$ and $\phi_I\colon I_\Gamma\cong I_{\Gamma'}$. 
\item We will abuse notation by denoting a diagram and its isomorphism class by the same letter $\Gamma$.
\end{itemize}
title: Definition 80 of arXiv:2608.28200

body:
[Theorem thm:main1 of arXiv:2412.03511, 'Near-optimal shattering in the Ising pure $p$-spin and \\ rarity of solutions returned by '] Consider the pure $p$-spin case $\xi(x) = x^p$.
For all $\varepsilon>0$, there exists an integer $p_0=p_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for all $p \ge p_0$ and all $(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{(2 \log p) /p} \le \beta \le (1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{2\log 2}$, there exits a random collection of subsets $\mathcal{C}_1,\cdots,\mathcal{C}_m \subset \{-1,+1\}^N$ (measurable with respect to $\bm{G}$) with the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Small diameter: $\max_{\bm{\sigma}_1,\bm{\sigma}_2 \in \mathcal{C}_i} d_H(\bm{\sigma}_1,\bm{\sigma}_2) \le rN$ for all $i \le m$.
\item Pairwise separation: $\min_{1\le i \neq j \le m} d_H(\mathcal{C}_i,\mathcal{C}_j) \ge R N$. 
\item Small Gibbs mass: $ \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} \max_{1\le i\le m} \mu_{\beta,\bm{G}}(\mathcal{C}_i) \le e^{-cN}$.  
\item Collective coverage of the Gibbs measure: $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\mu_{\beta,\bm{G}}\big(\bigcup_{i=1}^m \mathcal{C}_i\big) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}$.
\end{enumerate}
In the above, $d_H$ is the Hamming distance, $c = c(\varepsilon)>0$ and there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon)>0$ such that one can take $r = 1/p^{1+\delta}$ and $R = \delta/p$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A metric space is a set X with a function d : X x X -> R such that d(x,y) >= 0 with equality iff x = y (identity of indiscernibles), d(x,y) = d(y,x) (symmetry), and d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z) (triangle inequality). Completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges in X.

[Lemma lem:star of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Fix an atom $i$ and set $P_{ij}=\frac12p_jd_{ij}$ for $j\ne i$. Then
$\sum_jP_{ij}=1$, the valid star coefficients $B_{ij}$ lie on a real
two-dimensional affine plane through
$m_i$ with $\lVert m_i\rVert^2=\frac12|z_i|^2$, and
$\sum_jP_{ij}B_{ij}=m_i$; their variance is
$V_i=E+\frac{|z_i|^2}2-L_i$ where
$L_i=\sum_{j:t_j=t_i}p_j|z_j-z_i|^2\ge0$. Consequently there exist two star
neighbours whose segment contains a point $\delta$ with
\[
  \Wnorm\delta^2\ \le\ \frac E4+\frac{5|z_i|^2}8-\frac{L_i}4 ,
\]
and $\delta$ is a closure point of three-point selections
(Lemma~(lem:closure of the paper)). Choosing $i$ with $|z_i|^2\le E$:
\begin{equation}
  \inf_{\substack{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3\\ |\mu|<1}}C(q)\ \le\ \frac{7E}8,
  \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Gamma_3\le\frac78 .
\end{equation}

body:
[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Write \(D(\cE)^*\) for the continuous anti-dual of the form domain.
With the preceding first-slot-linear convention, the standard Gelfand
triple is
\[
                 D(\cE)\subset L^2(\mathfrak m)\subset D(\cE)^*.
\]
Let $u:Z\to\C$ be holomorphic and globally Lipschitz.  For $s\le0$ set
\begin{equation}
                           U(s,x)=u(\Psi_{-s}x).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
                         \|U(s)\|_{L^2(\mathfrak m)}\le Ce^{-s/2},
                         \qquad s\le0,
\end{equation}
and on every finite interval $[s_0,s_1]\subset(-\infty,0]$,
\begin{equation}
 U\in L^2([s_0,s_1];D(\cE)),\qquad
 \partial_sU+A_{\rm form}U=0\quad\text{in }D(\cE)^*,
\end{equation}
where $\langle A_{\rm form}v,\phi\rangle=\cE(v,\phi)$ is the form
operator.  On $\Dom A$, $A_{\rm form}$ agrees with the self-adjoint
operator $A$.
Moreover $s\mapsto U(s)$ is continuous into $L^2(\mathfrak m)$ and
\begin{equation}
                              U(0)=e^{sA}U(s),
                              \qquad s<0.
\end{equation}

[Proposition prop:simultaneous-appearance of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Given an $L$-block-step at block-step $i$, the edge(s) in the current block-step must have appeared altogether (potentially with some other edge) in a previous $F$-step, or there is a local-gap (potentially from a previous step).

 In other words, unless there is a local-gap (potentially from a previous step), there is a block-step $t<i$ s.t. $E(\tau_i) \subseteq E(\tau_t)$, and moreover, $\tau_t$ is an $F$ block-step.
 
 Formally, at least one vertex making a final appearance at the current block-step $i$ is a block-witness vertex for some previous block-step, particularly step-$t$.

Definition 1 (printed p.6) models training tasks by a centered Gaussian mixture on low-dimensional subspaces; its task-diversity notion concerns function classes and subspace overlap rather than merely counting a finite fixed task pool. For the paper's reduced linear-attention model, infinite training context and isotropic initialization, Proposition 1 (p.8), equation (9) and Lemma 1 (p.9) give a spectral reduction of separately trained query/key matrices and scalar value parameter. In particular the active squared spectral weights balance the scalar squared under the stated balanced initialization. This is prior architecture for finite-pool selector analysis. This scope card does not assert its assumptions cover unconstrained off-diagonal blocks or an empirically noncentered finite task distribution. Theorems 1-3 (pp.15-17) concern optimal-model subspace generalization under the source's covariance-regularization then training-context then test-context limits; they are not a raw-coordinate fixed-M gradient-flow selector.

[Lemma lem:finite-chaos-brownian-probe of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Fix $\alpha\geq0$.  For every $\delta_{\rm pr}>0$ there exist $n\geq2$,
$\varphi_{\rm pr}\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$, and a smooth field $q$ on
$[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d$ with
\begin{equation*}
 h_n(\xi):=\frac{\operatorname{He}_n(\xi_1)}{\sqrt{n!}},
 \qquad
 \Theta_n(s):=s^{n/2}\int_s^1
 \tau^{-n/2}\varphi_{\rm pr}(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau,
 \qquad
 q(s,y):=\Theta_n(s)h_n(y/\sqrt s),\qquad 0<s\leq1,
\end{equation*}
where $\operatorname{He}_n$ is the probabilists' Hermite polynomial.  The
associated source is
\begin{equation*}
 F_0^{\rm tan}:=-\left(\partial_s+\frac12\Delta_y\right)q
 =\varphi_{\rm pr}(s)h_n(y/\sqrt s)\not\equiv0
\end{equation*}
The corresponding Hessian estimate is
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert D_y^2q\right\rVert_{L^2(s^\alpha\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\gamma_s)}
 \geq(C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}}-\delta_{\rm pr})
 \norm{F_0^{\rm tan}}_{L^2(s^\alpha\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\gamma_s)}.
 
\end{equation}
The field vanishes on a terminal strip, and all its derivatives are
uniformly of polynomial growth in the spatial variable.

\end{align}

body:
Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space and T a trace-class operator on H. List the nonzero eigenvalues lambda_1, lambda_2, ... of T according to their algebraic multiplicities (each finite, by the Riesz-Schauder theorem; the list may be finite or empty). Then sum_n |lambda_n| <= ||T||_1 < infinity and tr T = sum_n lambda_n. Self-adjointness is not assumed; the theorem is exactly what makes the trace computable from the spectrum of a non-normal operator.
H is a separable complex Hilbert space
T is trace class on H
eigenvalues are counted with algebraic (not geometric) multiplicity
no self-adjointness or normality is assumed

Order a basis of generalized eigenvectors along Jordan chains so that the span of each initial segment is T-invariant, and apply Gram-Schmidt: the resulting orthonormal basis (u_n) of M puts T|_M in upper triangular form with diagonal entries <T u_n, u_n> = lambda_n. Complete by an orthonormal basis (v_m) of the orthogonal complement of M. Computing the (basis-independent) trace in the basis (u_n) together with (v_m) gives tr T = sum_n lambda_n + tr Q, where Q is the compression of T to the orthogonal complement of M, a trace-class operator that is quasinilpotent, since a nonzero eigenvalue of Q would produce a generalized eigenvector of T not accounted for in M. Step 3. A quasinilpotent trace-class Q has tr Q = 0. Its Fredholm determinant d(z) = det(I + zQ) is entire, has no zeros (the zeros of the determinant occur at -1/mu for the nonzero eigenvalues mu of Q, and there are none), satisfies the bound |d(z)| <= product over n of (1 + |z| s_n(Q)), whose logarithm is o(|z|) as |z| -> infinity because sum_n s_n(Q) < infinity, and has d'(0) = tr Q. body:
[Corollary cor:semilinear-additive of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Consider semilinear SPDEs with additive noise,
\[
  \mathrm{d}X(t) = [AX(t) + F(X(t))]\,\mathrm{d}t + Q^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}W(t),
\]
where $A$ generates an analytic semigroup on $H$, $Q^{1/2} \in L_2(U,H)$, and $F: V \to V^*$ is twice continuously Fr\'echet differentiable with $F'_u, F''_{uu}$ satisfying the growth and integrability conditions of Assumptions \textup{(D1)--(D3)} (so that $\mathcal{A}(t,u) := -[Au + F(u)]$ fits the abstract framework of Assumptions (ass:LR of the paper)--(ass:diff2 of the paper)). Assume that the hypotheses of Theorem~(thm:main of the paper), Part~II, hold for the given deterministic direction $h \in H$, namely the structural Assumptions~(ass:SC of the paper) and~(ass:SC-raised of the paper), all three clauses of Assumption~(ass:nondeg of the paper) (the range and moment conditions \textup{(i)}--\textup{(ii)} at the chosen H\"older-triangle pair $(q, p^*)$, and the Cameron--Martin compatibility \textup{(iii)}), and the fixed-Tikhonov substitution regularity~(hyp:iii-F-prime of the paper).
Then $\mathcal{B}'_u = 0$, $\mathcal{B}''_{uu} = 0$, the Malliavin--second variation equation (equation eq:second-var of the paper) has no stochastic integral term, the correction terms involve only $F''_{uu}$ (not $\mathcal{B}''_{uu}$), and the formula reads
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \delta_U(v_h) &= \bigl[\delta_U\bigl(r \mapsto \Phi_r^{*}z\bigr)\bigr]_{z = \gamma_t^{\dagger}h}\\
  &\quad + \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int_0^t \operatorname{Tr}_U\bigl[\Phi_r^{*}\,(\gamma_t+\varepsilon I)^{-1}\,[\mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t]\,(\gamma_t+\varepsilon I)^{-1}h\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}r,
\end{aligned}
\]
with $\Phi_r = \mathcal{D}_r X(t)$. The first line must be read as ``first take the frozen-$z$ divergence, then substitute $z = \gamma_t^{\dagger}h$''; it is not the composed divergence $\delta_U(r \mapsto \Phi_r^{*}\gamma_t^{\dagger}h)$, which already absorbs the trace correction (Lemma~(lemma:HS-kernel of the paper)(iv)). The frozen-$z$ divergence is genuinely anticipating unless $F = 0$, in which case it reduces to an It\^o integral. If the random evolution family generated by $A + F'(X(\cdot))$ admits an a.s.\ bounded realisation $Y(t,r) \in L(H)$, an additional structural input, not a consequence of analyticity of $S(t)$ alone, then $\Phi_r^{*} = (Q^{1/2})^{*}Y(t,r)^{*}$ and the frozen-$z$ field may be written in that factored form; otherwise the factorisation is shorthand for the Hilbert--Schmidt kernel $\Phi_r$.

\medskip\noindent The Cameron--Martin hypothesis carries conditional content. Clause~\textup{(iii)} of Assumption~(ass:nondeg of the paper) is a genuine joint convergence-and-integrability condition on the quadruple $(\gamma_t, \mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t, \Phi_r, h)$ and is not an automatic consequence of $A$ being analytic ``via parabolic regularisation''. Even in the additive case $\mathcal{B} = Q^{1/2}$ state-independent, the first variation $Y(t,r)$ is random whenever the drift is nonlinear, hence $\mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t \neq 0$ in general, and the trace integrand $\mathcal{I}^{(\varepsilon)}_r$ does not vanish identically. Its verification is therefore a real task. It can be carried out, in principle, via parabolic maximal-regularity bounds on the linearised semigroup $\{S_F(t,r)\}$ generated by $A + F'(X(\cdot))$ at the relevant operating point $(q, p^*)$ on the H\"older triangle, but it requires explicit input on the spectral structure of $\gamma_t$ relative to $h$. We record it as an explicit hypothesis to make this dependence transparent. The fully linear case ($F = 0$, $A$ linear with $\mathcal{B}$ deterministic) is the only subcase in which it is automatic, with $\mathcal{I}^{(0)} \equiv 0$ and $\Psi \equiv 0$ (cf.\ Remark~(rem:CM-compat-role of the paper)).
title: Corollary cor:semilinear-additive of arXiv:2608.21805

[Theorem 21 (Sharp uniform weak-Schatten link output) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $1<r<\infty$.  Uniformly over all five Hilbert spaces in
\eqref{eq:link-definition}, every
\[
 K\in\Sch_{r,\infty}(X,A\otimes Z),
 \qquad
 L\in\Sch_{r,\infty}(B\otimes Z,Y)
\]
satisfies
\begin{align}
 \norm{\operatorname{Link}_Z(L,K)}
  _{\Sch_{r,\infty}(\log\Sch)^{-1/r}}
 &\le C_r
 \norm L_{r,\infty}^{*}\norm K_{r,\infty}^{*}
 \notag\\
 &\le C_r
 \norm L_{\Sch_{r,\infty}}\norm K_{\Sch_{r,\infty}}.
 
\end{align}
The assertion holds on the full weak ideals, not only on their
finite-rank closures.  Within the targets
$\Sch_{r,\infty}(\log\Sch)^{-\alpha}$, the enlargement exponent
$\alpha=1/r$ is optimal uniformly over dimensions and contracted Hilbert
spaces.

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The integrals of measurable functions $f:X\to\mathbb R_+$ have the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f\leq g$ implies $\int f\leq\int g$.

\item $E\subset F$ implies $\int_Ef\leq\int_Ff$.

\item $\int f+g=\int f+\int g$.

\item $\int\lambda f=\lambda\int f$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 2 (Krein criterion for subdensities) of arXiv:2607.00132, 'On a moment determinacy conjecture of Bertoin and Yor'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with moments of all positive orders. Suppose that there exists a non-zero absolutely continuous submeasure
\[
 \nu(\dd x)=h(x)\,\dd x\leq \mu(\dd x)
\]
such that $\nu$ has moments of all positive orders and
\begin{equation}
 \int_c^\infty \frac{-\log h(x^2)}{1+x^2}\,\dd x<\infty,
 \qquad
 \text{ for some $c>0$,}
\end{equation}
where $h$ is positive on $(c^2,\infty)$. Then $\mu$ is moment-indeterminate.

Let $\boldsymbol{f}(z) = (f_l(z))_{l = 1}^{L}$ be functions such that $f_l(z)$ is holomorphic for $z$ in some $\N$-independent compact neighborhood of $[\alpha_{k_l} - \eps,\beta_{k_l} + \eps]$ where it is bounded independently of $\N$, for any $l \in [L]$. Let $\textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}[\boldsymbol{f}]$ be a $L$-dimensional random Gaussian vector with covariance
\[
\textnormal{\textsf{Cov}}_{l_1,l_2}[\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{f}] = \oint_{\gamma_{l_1}} \oint_{\gamma_{l_1}} \frac{\dd z_1\dd z_2}{(2\ii\pi)^2} \mathcal{F}_{l_1,l_2}(z_1,z_2) f_{l_1}(z_1) f_{l_2}(z_2)
\]
in terms of the fundamental solution \eqref{FFFFFFFFFFF} associated to the bands of $\mu$ and the matrix $(\theta_{h_{l_1},h_{l_2}})_{l_1,l_2 = 1}^{L}$. Then, as  $\N \rightarrow \infty$ we have
\[
\bigg( \textnormal{\textsf{Lin}}_{k_l}[f_l] - \N \int_{\alpha_{k_l}}^{\beta_{k_l}} f_l(x)\mu_{h_l}(x)\dd x \bigg)_{l = 1}^{L} \,\, \mathop{\sim}^{\textnormal{d}}\,\,\textnormal{\textbf{\textsf{Gau\ss{}}}}[\boldsymbol{f}] + \bigg( \sum_{m = 1}^{L} \big(\textnormal{\textsf{Gau\ss{}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z},m} - \N \hat{n}^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_m\big) \cdot  \omega_{k_l,m}[f_l]\bigg)_{l = 1}^{L}.
\]
where the discrete Gaussian $\textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z}} = \textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z}}[\Qu,\L,\boldsymbol{u}]$ is the same as in Theorem~\ref{Theorem_CLT_for_filling_fractionsi}. [Definition def:ising-cavity of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] On the tree of Definition~(def:ising-rpc of the paper), let
		$B_s^i(\alpha)$, $1\le i\le N$, and $Y(s,\alpha)$ be centered
		continuous Gaussian martingales indexed by $s\in[0,1]$ and the
		leaves $\alpha$. The two families are independent of each other,
		of $H_N$, and of the Poisson point processes defining the
		cascade. Their covariances are
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{E} B_s^i(\alpha)B_t^j(\beta)
			&=
			\delta_{ij}\,
			\xi'\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge
			s_{\alpha\wedge\beta}\bigr),\\
			\mathbb{E} Y(s,\alpha)Y(t,\beta)
			&=
			N\vartheta\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge
			s_{\alpha\wedge\beta}\bigr).
		\end{align*}
		For $\mathbf{m}\in[-1,1]^N$, with
		\[
		q_\mathbf{m}:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N m_i^2,
		\]
		define the multiscale cavity field by
		\[
		Z(\mathbf{m},\alpha)
		:=
		\sum_{i=1}^N m_i B_{q_\mathbf{m}}^i(\alpha).
		\]
		We call $Y(q,\alpha)$ the Onsager field at self-overlap $q$.
title: Multiscale cavity field and Onsager field

[Corollary cor:three-bc-unmarked-length-bridge of arXiv:2607.04264, 'Macroscopic Feynman Cycles and Poisson--Kingman Universality in Bose Condensation'] Let \(b \in \{\mathrm{per}, D, N\}\), and assume
\(N_L / V_L \to \rho > \rho_{\mathrm{c}}\).  Then
\[
    \Xi_{L,N_L}^{b,\mathrm{len}}
    \Longrightarrow
    \overline{\Xi}^{\, \rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}}}
    \qquad
    \text{in }
    \mathcal{N}_\ell\bigl([0,1] \times (0,\infty)\bigr),
\]
where \(\overline{\Xi}^{\, \rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}}}\) is the Gamma bridge of endpoint \( \rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}}\): the
Poisson point process $\overline{\Xi}$ on \([0,1] \times (0,\infty)\) with intensity
\(du\, dx/x\), conditioned in the density sense on
\[
    \int_{[0,1] \times (0,\infty)} x\, \overline{\Xi}(du,dx) =  \rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}}.
\]
Moreover, if \(X_{L,1}^{\downarrow} \geq X_{L,2}^{\downarrow}
\geq \cdots\) are the ranked atoms of the length coordinate of
\(\Xi_{L,N_L}^{b,\mathrm{len}}\), then
\[
    \bigl(X_{L,1}^{\downarrow}, X_{L,2}^{\downarrow}, \ldots\bigr)
    \Longrightarrow
     (\rho - \rho_{\mathrm{c}})\, \bigl(P_1^{\downarrow}, P_2^{\downarrow}, \ldots\bigr),
\]
where \((P_i^{\downarrow})_{i \geq 1} \sim \mathrm{PD}(0,1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unmarked length bridge

[Lem e:drift of arXiv:2411.10586, 'A convergence framework for Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble\\ via pole evolution'] For any $w\in {\mathbb C}\setminus {\mathbb R}$, the drift term in (equation eq:dms2 of the paper)
\begin{align}\begin{split}
    & \zeta\,\partial_w\Bigl( (E +\chi w)\,(m^{(n)}_{\zeta t})^2(E +\chi w)
      +(\chi w+2\sqrt n(\sqrt m+\sqrt n))\, m^{(n)}_{\zeta t}(E +\chi w)\Bigr)\,{\rm d} t\\
    &\quad +\frac{2-\beta}{\beta E}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
      \frac{(E +\chi \widetilde \lambda^{(n)}_i(t))\,{\rm d} t}{(\widetilde \lambda^{(n)}_i(t)-w)^3}.
\end{split}\end{align}
equals
\[
\frac12\,\partial_w\bigl(\Delta^{(n)}_t(w)+\sqrt w\bigr)^2-\frac12
+
\frac{2-\beta}{\beta}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{(\widetilde\lambda^{(n)}_i(t)-w)^3}+{\mathcal E}^{(n)}_t(w),
\]
where 
\[
|{\mathcal E}^{(n)}_t(w)|,\; |\partial_w{\mathcal E}^{(n)}_t(w)| \lesssim n^{-1/3}(1+|\Delta^{(n)}_t(w)+\sqrt w|)^2.
\]

[Corollary of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let $\hat{f}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}$ and $\hat{f}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}$ be the estimators of a density $f$ as defined in Proposition (prop:density-robust of the paper).
    Assume that the hypotheses of Proposition (prop:density-robust of the paper) are satisfied.
    Further assume that $f$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz and $\operatorname{supp}(f) \subseteq [0,1]^d$, and that \(\phi_2\) satisfies (equation eq:phi_2_close_condition of the paper).
    Then there exist random probability densities
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(1)}$ and
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(2)}$, defined on a common probability space,
    such that, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
    \[
    \hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x)
    \overset{(d)}{=}
    \hat{f}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x),
    \qquad i=1,2,
    \]
    and such that for constants $C(\phi_1, d)$ and \(\tilde{C}(\phi_1,d)\) depending only on $\phi_1$ and $d$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb{E} \left[\int_{[0,1]^d} \left|\hat{g}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}(x) - \hat{g}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}(x)\right| \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x \right] \\
    & \leq \min\left\{\frac{\gamma^{d/2} \|f\|_{\infty}^{1/2} \left(\mathrm{vol}(\Pi_1)^{1/2} + \mathrm{vol}(\Pi_2)^{1/2}\right)}{n^{1/2}} + \frac{L \tilde{C}(\phi_1, d)}{\gamma}W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}, C(\phi_1, d)W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}\right\}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition l:dotprodbound of arXiv:2411.04116, 'Poisson genericity in numeration systems with exponentially mixing probabilities'] Let $X_1,X_2,\dots $ a sequence of random variables defined on $(\mathbb X, \mathcal{F},\mathbb P)$ taking values on alphabet $\Omega$. Let   $\Delta$ be the matrix of $\eta$-mixing coefficients with $\|\Delta\|<\infty$.  Let $c=(c_i)_{i\ge 1}\in \ell^2$ and $\varphi:\Omega^\mathbb N \to \mathbb R$ 
a bounded function that is also $c$-Lipschitz. 
Then, the Azuma--Hoeffding coefficients $d=\left(d_i\right)_{i\ge 1}$ satisfy, for each $i\geq 1 $, 
\begin{align}
   0\le d_i \leq \sum_{j\geq i} c_j \eta_{ij}.
\end{align}
In particular, $\|d\|\le \|\Delta\|\|c\|$.

body:
Coja-Oghlan cover-counting upper bound for sparse random graph colourability: there is a nonnegative error function e(q) tending to zero as q tends to infinity such that, for all sufficiently large fixed integers q and every fixed c>(2q-1)log q-1+e(q), G(n,c/n) is not q-colourable with probability tending to one as n tends to infinity. The original theorem is stated for G(n,m) with average degree 2m/n; the same fixed-degree conclusion follows for the binomial model by edge-count concentration and monotonicity, leaving a fixed strict margin. Equivalently, the limsup of the average-degree sharp-threshold sequence is at most (2q-1)log q-1+o_q(1). Natural logs are used. No convergence of the threshold sequence is assumed, and an unspecified o_q(1) term gives no certified numerical bound at q=3.
q a sufficiently large fixed integer
c fixed and strictly above the bound
n tends to infinity first; error tends to zero as q grows

body:
[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2506.10476, 'Construction of ergodic \textsc{idla} forests in $\mathbb{Z}^d$'] Let $d \geq 2$. The infinite-volume \textsc{idla} forests $\fdag{\infty}$ and $(\fdag{n})_{n\geq 0}$ satisfy the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Almost surely, the set of vertices of $\fdag{\infty}$ satisfies $V(\fdag{\infty}) = \mathbb{Z}^d$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are invariant w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are $\alpha$-mixing, that is for all $n\geq 0$, for all events $\mathcal{A},\ \mathcal{B}$, 
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B} \right)
	\] 
	and
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B} \right).
	\] 
	Consequently, the distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are ergodic, w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 1 (L\'evy's theorem) of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] Let $f:U\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a non constant
analytic function and $(Z_{t})_{t\geq0}$ be a planar Brownian motion
running inside $U$. Then there is a planar Brownian motion $W_{t}$
such that $f(Z_{t})=W_{\sigma(t)}$ with 
\[
\sigma(t)=\int^{t}_{0}\vert f'(Z_{s})\vert^{2}ds
\]
and $t\in[0,\tau_{U}]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary coro:diffusregu of arXiv:2411.10235, '\textbf{Smooth transport map via diffusion process}'] Let $p : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a probability density function of the form
\[
p(x) = \exp\left( -\frac{\|x\|^2}{2} + a(x) \right),
\]
such that \( a \in H^\beta_K(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathbb{R}) \) with \( \beta \geq 1 \) and \( K > 0 \). Then, for all \( t \in [0, 1) \) we have
\[
\sum_{k = 0}^{\lfloor \beta \rfloor} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} \|\nabla^k s(t,x)\| \leq Ce^{-t}(1+t^{-1/2})
\quad \text{and} \quad
\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} \|\nabla^{\lfloor \beta \rfloor +1} \log s(t,x)\| \leq Ce^{-t}(1 +t^{(\beta - \lfloor \beta \rfloor)/2 - 1}).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary coro:diffusregu of arXiv:2411.10235

body:
[Lemma 14 (Asymptotics via Taylor Expansion) of arXiv:2608.14143, 'Mod-$\phi$ convergence for random variables with cyclotomic generating functions'] Let $s_N \in \N$ be a sequence of natural numbers and, for each $N\in\N$, let $(a_{N,j})_{j=1}^N$ be a sequence of natural numbers. Let $h(w, z) := \log\bigl(\frac{1-e^{zw}}{-zw}\bigr)$ for $w \neq 0$ and $h(0, z):=0$. For each $N \in \N$, set $\delta_{N,j} := a_{N,j}/s_N$. Assume that $\max_{1\le j \le N} \delta_{N,j} \to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ and that the limit
\[
\Sigma := \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{j=1}^N \delta_{N,j}
\]
exists in $\R$. Then, for every compact set $K\subset\C$, the sum $S_N^a(z) = \sum_{j=1}^N h(a_{N,j}/s_N, z)$ admits the asymptotic expansion
\[
S_N^a(z) = \frac{z}{2}\,\Sigma + o(1),
\]
uniformly for $z\in K$.

[Lemma le:bounds-W-l-one-step of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider the setup of Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper). 
  For $l\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $\bar e\in E_{l-1}$, and $e'\in E_l$, 
  we have
  \begin{align}
    
    &{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le 2^{-\alpha}{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
&{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]^2
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),\\
    
    &{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}]\le\min\{{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2,2{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]+{c_2}\}
  \end{align}
  with the constants $C_\alpha$ and ${c_2}$ from Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper).
  For $\alpha\in[0,\frac12)$,
  the bound  in (equation eq:bound-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) is stronger than
  the bound in (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]>2^{-\alpha}C_\alpha^{-1}$.
  Similarly, the minimum in bound (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-log of the paper) equals
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2$ if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]\ge -\log 2-{c_2}$.
  Note that the expectations do not depend on the choice of $\bar e$ and
  $e'$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Induction step for moments of effective weights

body: [Lemma lem:intersections_times of arXiv:2411.13133, 'Connectivity of the adjacency graph of\\ complementary components of the $\SLE$ Fan'] Fix $\kappa \in (0,4)$ and let $h$ be a whole-plane GFF with values modulo a global multiple of $2\pi\chi$. Fix $\delta, p \in (0,1)$. Then,  there exists $\theta_0 \in (0,1)$ depending only on $\kappa , \delta$ an $p$ such that the following holds with probability at least $1 - p$ for any fixed $\theta \in (0, \theta_0)$. For all $t \in (0, \tau_0(\mathbf{D})]$ there exist $t_1, t_2, t'_1, t'_2$ such that $0 < t_1 < t < t_2 < \tau_0(\mathbf{D}_\delta)$ and $0 < t'_1 < t'_2$, and for each $j = 1,2$, $\eta_0(t_j) = \eta_\theta(t'_j)$ and at this point $\eta_\theta$ hits $\eta_0$ on the left side of $\eta_0$ with angle gap $\theta$. Furthermore, for any $s \in [t_1, t_2]$ we have $|\eta_0(s) - \eta_0(t)| < \delta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let F be C, R or Q, r >= 3 an integer and 0 < eps <= 1, and let xi be uniform on {-1,1}^n. (Thm 1.1) There is C = C(r, eps) such that: if f in F[x_1,...,x_n] is a quadratic polynomial all of whose coefficients have absolute value <= 1 and sup_x P(f(xi) = x) >= C (log n)^{r/2} / n^{1 - 2/(r+2)}, then there is a quadratic form h of rank < r such that the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of f - h is at most eps n^2. (Thm 1.2) If instead the degree-2 coefficients of f lie in a fixed finite set S (C = C(r, eps, S)), the same hypothesis gives h of rank < r differing from f in at most eps n^2 coefficients. With r = 3: point probabilities much larger than n^{-3/5} force f to be close to a form of rank <= 2, which over C splits into two linear factors.

Assumes: Rademacher variables; coefficients bounded by 1 (Thm 1.1) or taken from a finite set (Thm 1.2)

[Proposition 54 (Composition bound) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge1$. Let $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ be finitary codings with coding radii
$r_1$ and $r_2$, and let $Y_2=\varphi_2(\varphi_1(X))$, where $X$ is i.i.d.
Assume
\[
\E\big((2r_1+1)^{4d}\big)<\infty
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\E\big((2r_2+1)^{4d}\big)<\infty.
\]
Then $Y_2$ satisfies a Gaussian concentration bound with constant
\[
K_d\,
\big(\E\big((2 r_2+1)^{4d}\big)\big)^{1/2}\,
\big(\E\big((2 r_1+1)^{4d}\big)\big)^{1/2},
\]
where $K_d$ depends only on the dimension. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Composition bound

[Prop 31 ({\cite[Proposition~3.8) of arXiv:2609.01389, 'K-stability and birational rigidity of Fano 3-fold weighted complete intersections'] {CO}}]

With the notation and assumptions as above, let $\msp \in Z \subset Y \subset X$ be a flag of type $\mathrm{IIa}$.
Then,
\[
\delta_{\msp} (X) \ge
\min \left\{ 4 l_Y, \ \frac{1}{S (V_{\bullet, \bullet}^Y; \Gamma)}, \ \frac{1}{r_{\msp} S (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}; \msp)} \right\},
\]
where
\[
\begin{split}
S (V_{\bullet, \bullet}^Y; \Gamma) &= \frac{3}{(A^3)} \int_0^{\frac{1}{l_Y}} \left(\int_0^{\frac{\nu - \mu}{\nu} t (u)} \left( (2 \nu + \lambda - \mu) t (u)^2 - 2 (\nu + \lambda) t (u) v + \lambda v^2 \right) d v \right. \\
& \hspace{3cm} \left.+ \int_{\frac{\nu - \mu}{\nu} t (u)}^{t (u)} \frac{\nu^2 + \lambda \mu}{\mu} (t (u) - v)^2 d v \right) d u, \\
S (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}; \msp) &= \frac{3}{(A^3)} \int_0^{l_Y} \left( \int_0^{\frac{\nu-\mu}{\nu} t (u)} ((\nu+\lambda) t(u) - \lambda v)^2 d v  \right. \\
& \left. \hspace{2cm} + \int_{\frac{\nu-\mu}{\nu} t (u)}^{t(u)} \left( \frac{\nu^2 + \lambda \mu}{\mu} \right)^2 (t(u) - v)^2 d v \right) d u + F_{\msp} (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}),
\end{split}
\]
with $t (u) = (1 - l_Y u)/l_H$ and
\[
F_{\msp} (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}) = \frac{1}{4 l_Y l_H^3 (A^3)} \cdot \frac{\mu(\nu^2 + \lambda \mu)}{\nu^2} \cdot \ord_{\msp} (\Delta|_{\Gamma}).
\]

Author-derived counterexample, independent review pending: let f be majority of three independent bits, mu=Bernoulli(epsilon)^3, nu=Bernoulli(1-epsilon)^3 with 0<epsilon<1/2. Each endpoint exterior makes a cell section nonconstant with probability 2 epsilon(1-epsilon), and each cell TV is 1-2 epsilon. Substituting endpoint sensitivities into a telescoping bound would give 6 epsilon(1-epsilon)(1-2 epsilon), tending to zero, whereas E_nu f-E_mu f=1-6 epsilon^2+4 epsilon^3 tends to one. For replacement order 1,2,3, the actual hybrid sensitivities are 2 epsilon(1-epsilon), (1-epsilon)^2+epsilon^2, 2 epsilon(1-epsilon); their TV-weighted sum equals the true difference. At epsilon=1/100 the false bound is 14553/250000 and the difference is 249851/250000. The valid inequality with actual hybrid laws is not refuted.

[Definition 17 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] For $0\le r\le k$, write $\pi^k_r:J^k\to J^r$ for the natural truncation.
By convention, we set $J^r=0$ and $\pi^k_r=0$ when $r<0$.
By Theorem \ref{t.Taylor}, the vector space $J^k_h$ for $h \in \sH$ is equal to the vector space of polynomials of the form   $$ \sum_{|I| = 0}^{ k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I $$ with coefficients $c_I \in \C$. Thus an element $\sigma \in \sO(J^k)_h$, namely,  a local section $\sigma$ of the bundle $J^k$ near $h$, can be written as $$ \sigma(g) =  \sum_{|I| = 0}^{k} \sigma_I(g) \ g^*(xyt)^I $$ for  $\sigma_I \in \sO_{\sH, h}$, which we write simply as $$ \sigma =  \sum_{|I| = 0}^{k} \sigma_I  \ g^*(xyt)^I.$$ For each $1 \leq a \leq m$, define the differential operator $D_{X_a}$ (resp. $D_{Y_a}$)  that sends $\sigma \in \sO(J^k)_h$ to an element of  $\sO(J^{k-1})_h$ as follows. 
\begin{eqnarray*} 
D_{X_a} \sigma & := & \sum_{|I|=0}^{k-1} (X_a \sigma_I - (i_a +1) \sigma_{I^{+a}} - \frac{p+1}{2} \sigma_{I_{-a}}) g^*(xyt)^I \\
D_{Y_a} \sigma & := & \sum_{|I|=0}^{k-1} (Y_a \sigma_I - (j_a +1) \sigma_{I_{+a}} + \frac{p+1}{2} \sigma_{I^{-a}}) g^*(xyt)^I.
\end{eqnarray*}
Also define the differential operator $D_{T}$  that sends  $\sigma \in \sO(J^k)_h$ to an element of  $\sO(J^{k-2})_h$ as follows. 
$$ D_T \sigma \ = \  \sum_{|I|=0}^{k-2} (T \sigma_I - (p+1) \sigma_{I^{\sharp}}) g^*(xyt)^I.$$

body: [Lemma lem:spreadof2 of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] Fix a big box $B$. Assume that $B$ is successful and that it is connected by a path of successful big boxes to a $2$-ignited successful big box. Then $B$ has the property that the center box of every $q$-box in all four of the crossings of $B$ by good $q$-boxes  will eventually be completely occupied by $2$s. If, in addition, $B$ is centrally successful, then the center boxes in its path guaranteed by (CS1)--(CS2) is also completely occupied by $2$s.

[Cor of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] Fix $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$
and let $r = (\lambda/n)^{1/d}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\lambda > \lambda_c$,
    then with high probability as $n \to \infty$, the natural map $H_1(\mathcal{C}) \to H_1(M)$ is surjective.
    If $\lambda < \lambda_c$,
    with high probability
    it is the zero map.
    \item If $\lambda > \lambda_c$,
    there exists $1 \le Q' < \infty$
    such that $H_1(M) \cong H_1(\mathcal{C})/H_1^{Q' r|\log r|}(\mathcal{C})$
    with high probability as $n \to \infty$.
    \item For fixed $\lambda < \infty$,
    there exists $q(\lambda) > 0$
    such that, with high probability as $n \to \infty$,
    the natural map
    $H_1(\mathcal{C})/H_1^{qr|\log r|}(\mathcal{C}) \to H_1(M)$
    has nontrivial kernel (in particular, it is not an isomorphism).
    In this case, the natural map
    $H_1(\mathcal{C}) \to H_1(M)$ 
    is also not an isomorphism.\footnote{This last result also follows from Bobrowski [Bobrowski22].}
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Ppn 90 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recalling \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym} and Definitions \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}--\ref{d:measure.classes.sym}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) \subseteq \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, we can find $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ with $\sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu$.
It was shown in the \hyperlink{p:thm.control.problems.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}} that $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$, so $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$.
Therefore, for any $\epsilon>0$ we can find $L>0$ and controls 
    \beq
        
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \eeq
such that (recalling that $\sym$ is a contraction) we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu, \mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
        \le\bbW_2\Big(\tilde \mu, \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
         \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
We see from Definitions~\ref{d:SDE.classification} and \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}
that the sets of controls $\Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ and $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ are in fact identical, so the controls \eqref{e:Lip.general.in.IAMP.sym.controls} belong to $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$, and 
    \[
        \mu \in \cB_\epsilon\Big(\cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)\,.
    \]
    Since for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L > 0$ so that this holds, we conclude $\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
    As this holds for all $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition def: associated bp of arXiv:2411.02898, '\vspace{-1.5cm}The connectivity and phase transition in inhomogeneous random graphs of fin'] Given a random graph model $\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}} = \ensuremath{\mathbb{G}} (n, m, \bm{a}, \bm{c}, p(n))$ with $p(n) = \lambda / n$, we associate a multi-type branching process $\bm{Z}_t^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(k)$ of $m$ types of particles, where $(k)$ indicates that the process starts with a single particle of type $k$. A type $l$ particle will have offspring distribution \[ \textrm{Poi}(\lambda a_1 c_{l1} ) \otimes \dots \otimes \textrm{Poi}(\lambda a_m c_{lm}). \] We write $q_k$ as the extinction probability of $\bm{Z}^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}_t(k)$.
title: Definition def: associated bp of arXiv:2411.02898

  $z_0 \sim \mu_1$ and $z'_0 \sim \mu_2$, with $z_0, z'_0, W, W''$ all mutually
  independent. Then for every $\delta_\star \in (0,1)$ and every $R \geqslant R_\star$
  there exists a $T_\star(\delta_\star, R) >0$ deterministic such that
  \begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{P}(  \| z_{T_\star} - z_{T_\star}' \| \leqslant \delta_\star ,  \ \text{ and } \ z_{T_\star},z_{T_\star}' \in \mathcal{C}_R  ) > 0 .
  \end{equation*}

[Dfn 1. dfn: BTM of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [The Bouchaud trap model] 
  Fix an electrical network $G$.
  Let $\{\xi_{x}^{G}\}_{x \in V_{G}}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with $\xi_{x}^{G} \stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=} \xi$.
  Set $\nu_{G} \coloneqq \sum_{x \in V_{G}} \xi_{x}^{G} \delta_{x}$,
  which is a random measure on $V_{G}$.
  Conditional on $\nu_{G}$,
  the (symmetric) Bouchaud trap model (BTM) is defined as the continuous-time Markov chain $X_{G}^{\nu_{G}}$. 
  The random measure $\nu_{G}$ is called a \textit{trap}.

body: Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with curvature tensor R. The Ricci curvature is the symmetric bilinear form Ric obtained by tracing the curvature tensor over one pair of indices: Ric(Y,Z) = trace of the linear map X |-> R(X,Y)Z. For a unit tangent vector v in T_pM, extend v to an orthonormal basis v, e_1,...,e_{n-1} of T_pM; then Ric(v,v) = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} K(sigma_i), where sigma_i is the 2-plane spanned by v and e_i, i.e. Ric(v,v) is (n-1) times the average sectional curvature of the 2-planes containing v. For general (nonzero, not necessarily unit) v, Ric(v,v) = |v|^2 Ric(v/|v|, v/|v|) by homogeneity. A further trace of Ric against the metric gives the scalar curvature.
title: Ricci Curvature

[Definition 1 (\cite{ABS2025}) of arXiv:2608.30859, 'Conservation Laws with Discontinuous Flux:\\ A First Application to Traffic Flow'] For a given couple $(\bar u(x), \bar\theta(x))$, a set of points 
        \[\bar{y}_1 < \bar{y}_2 < \cdots < \bar{y}_N,
        \]
        is a \emph{set of interfaces} for $(\bar u, \bar \theta)$ if it contains all the jumps in $\bar \theta$ and, for any open interval $J_i=(y_i, y_{i+1}), i \in \{0, \cdots, N\}$:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item If $\bar \theta(x)=1$ on $J_i$, then $\bar u(x)$ is monotone increasing.
            \item If $\bar \theta(x)=0$ on $J_i$, then $\bar u(x)$ is monotone decreasing.
        \end{itemize}

Let H and K be Hilbert spaces and T: H -> K compact. Let s_1 >= s_2 >= ... > 0 be the nonzero singular values of T, repeated according to multiplicity (a finite list or a sequence tending to 0). Then there are orthonormal systems (e_n) in H and (f_n) in K, indexed by the same set, such that T x = sum_n s_n <x, e_n> f_n for every x in H, the series converging in K; moreover the series converges in operator norm, with ||T - sum_{n <= N} s_n <., e_n> f_n|| = s_{N+1}. Here (e_n) is an orthonormal basis of (ker T)^perp, (f_n) is an orthonormal basis of the closure of ran T, T e_n = s_n f_n, T* f_n = s_n e_n, and |T| x = sum_n s_n <x, e_n> e_n. T is Hilbert-Schmidt iff sum_n s_n^2 < infinity and trace class iff sum_n s_n < infinity.
H and K are Hilbert spaces
T: H -> K is compact
singular values are listed in nonincreasing order with multiplicity

body:
[Lemma 6 (Aldous meeting-time comparison) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a finite irreducible reversible continuous-time chain
with stationary law $\pi$, and write $P^t$ for its transition semigroup. Let
$\tau_{\rm meet}$ be the first time two independent copies of the chain occupy
the same state. Put
\begin{equation}
        t^*_{\rm mix}:=\inf\left\{t\ge0:
        \max_x\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\TV}\le \frac1{2e}\right\},
\end{equation}
and let
\[
        T_M:=\max_{x,y}\E_{x,y}\tau_{\rm meet} .
\]
If $H_i$ denotes the hitting time of state $i$ by one copy of the chain, then
there is a universal constant $K_A<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
        T_M
        \le
        K_A\left(\sum_i
        \frac{\pi_i}{t^*_{\rm mix}\vee \E_\pi H_i}\right)^{-1} .
\end{equation}
It follows that, for continuous-time simple random walk with jump rate $1$ on a
finite connected multigraph $G$,
\begin{equation}
        t_{\rm meet}(G)
        \le K'_A\bigl(\tmix(G)+\Kemeny(G)\bigr)
\end{equation}
for another universal constant $K'_A$.

body:
[Lemma equivalence of monomials of arXiv:2609.04072, 'Oort's conjecture for split unitary Shimura varieties'] For two distinct tuples $(i,l,f),(i',l',f')\in \llbracket 1,g\rrbracket\times \llbracket0,N-1\rrbracket\times \mathfrak S_J$, we have $$P_{i,l,f}=P_{i',l',f'}$$ if and only if the following conditions are all satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item There exists a (necessarily unique) $k_0\in \llbracket 1,g'\rrbracket$ such that $r_{k_0}=0$,
	\item $l=l'=0$,
	\item $f'=f\circ \tau_{(0,k_0)}$ where $\tau_{(0,k_0)}$ denotes the transposition exchanging $0$ and $k_0$,
	\item $i=f(0)$ and $i'=f(k_0)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, if $0\notin \{r_1,\dots,r_{g'}\}$, the monomials $P_{i,l,f}$ are pairwise distinct.

[Prop 2. prop: atom convergence from simple measure convergence of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $\nu, \nu_{1}, \nu_{2}, \cdots$ be simple measures on $S$.
  For each compact subset $K$ of $S$,
  consider the following condition.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (VC), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
      Write $\{x_{i}\}_{i \in I_{K}} = \At(\nu) \cap K$ for the atoms lying in $K$.
      (NB. $I_{K}$ is a finite set.)
      Then, for all sufficiently large $n$,
      we can write $\At(\nu_{n}) \cap K = \{x_{i}^{(n)} \mid i \in I_{K}\}$ 
      in such a way that $x_{i}^{(n)} \to x_{i}$ for each $i \in I_{K}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then, the statements below are equivalent with each other.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      The measures $\nu_{n}$ converge to $\nu$ vaguely.
    \item 
      Any compact subset $K$ of $S$ with $\nu(\partial K) = 0$ 
      satisfies (2. prop: characterization of vague convergence of simple measures of the paper).
    \item 
      There exists an increasing sequence $(D_{k})_{k \geq 1}$ of relatively compact open subsets of $S$ 
      such that $\bigcup_{k \geq 1} D_{k} = S$, $\mu(\partial D_{K}) = 0$ for each $k$, 
      and each $\closure(D_{k})$ satisfies (2. prop: characterization of vague convergence of simple measures of the paper).
  \end{enumerate}

[Lemma 18 (Binary polynomial positivity patterns) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $r,n,d_{\mathrm{pol}}\in\N^+$ with $n\ge r$.  Let
$p_1,\ldots,p_{n}$ be arbitrary real polynomials in $r$ variables,
each of total degree at most $d_{\mathrm{pol}}$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \Bigl\lvert
 \bigl\{
 \left(
  \one_{\{p_1(\bmmu)>0\}},\ldots,
  \one_{\{p_n(\bmmu)>0\}}
 \right):
 \bmmu\in\R^r
 \bigr\}
 \Bigr\rvert
 \le
 \left(\frac{4ed_{\mathrm{pol}}n}{r}\right)^r.
\end{equation}
The list may contain repeated polynomials or the zero polynomial.

[Definition of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Let $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be arbitrary maps.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We say that $f$ is \emph{$\mathbf{p}$-convex} if $f=h\circ\mathbf{p}$ is the composition of $\mathbf{p}$ 
followed by  a convex function $h\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$.

\item
We define the \emph{$\mathbf{p}$-convex envelope} $\env_\mathbf{p} f\colon X\to[-\infty,+\infty]$
of $f$ pointwise by 
\[
\env_\mathbf{p} f(x) := \sup\{h(x): h\leq f, \text{$h$ is $\mathbf{p}$-convex\,}\},
\qquad x\in X.
\]
As before, inequalities of functions are understood pointwise.
\end{enumerate}
