# Finite-Lp clipped score transfer with compact covariance repair

Status: proof (unaudited). Target 2 conditional lemma. No new hard seed,
dimension exponent, fixed-endpoint result, or priority claim is asserted.

Let d>=1, 2<=p<infinity, 0<e<=1, m=ceil(p), D=d+2m. For arbitrary
probability laws P,H on R^d, write P_sigma=P*N(0,sigma^2 I), and similarly
for H and Q=(1-eta)P+eta H. Suppose a fixed jointly measurable field
a_sigma obeys E_Psigma||a_sigma-s_Psigma||^p <= (e/4)^p/sigma^p
for every sigma>0. Put
 B=4D/e, eta=[e/(2(B+sqrt(D)))]^p,
 f_sigma=projection onto the ball of radius B/sigma of a_sigma.
Then, at every sigma>0,
 E_Qsigma||f_sigma-s_Qsigma||^p <= 2^(1-p)e^p/sigma^p <= e^p/sigma^p.
One query to a simulates a query to f. No moment assumption on H is
needed for this assertion. For fixed finite p and inverse-polynomial e,
eta is inverse polynomial in d. The statement is not uniform as p grows.

1. Mixture convexity. Let p_sigma,h_sigma denote the positive smooth
component densities, q_sigma=(1-eta)p_sigma+eta h_sigma, and
w=eta h_sigma/q_sigma. Differentiating the Gaussian convolutions gives
 s_Q=(1-w)s_P+w s_H.
For any measurable f, convexity of the p-th power of Euclidean norm gives
 ||f-s_Q||^p <= (1-w)||f-s_P||^p+w||f-s_H||^p.
Integration, using q_sigma(1-w)=(1-eta)p_sigma and q_sigma w=eta h_sigma,
therefore yields
 E_Qsigma||f-s_Q||^p <= (1-eta)E_Psigma||f-s_P||^p
                          +eta E_Hsigma||f-s_H||^p.       (A)
This posterior identity is used in the proof only. The implemented field
f does not evaluate densities, component scores, or posterior weights.

2. Gaussian score moments. For any probability law L and X=Y+sigma Z,
Z standard Gaussian independent of Y, s_Lsigma(X)=-E[Z|X]/sigma.
Conditional Jensen gives ||s_Lsigma||_Lr <= ||Z||_Lr/sigma for r>=1.
The elementary Gaussian radial moment formula gives
 E||Z||^(2m)=product_{j=0}^{m-1}(d+2j) <= D^m.
Monotonicity of probability-space Lr norms then gives
 ||Z||_L(2p)<=sqrt(D), and ||Z||_Lp<=sqrt(D).
Gaussian convolution differentiation and the conditional expectation
identity hold for arbitrary L: the derivatives of the Gaussian kernel
are bounded and integrable against a probability measure. These facts
do not require moments of Y. All component scores have the finite norms
used below; bounded f has finite component error norms as well.

3. Clipping. Nonexpansiveness of Euclidean projection Pi_R gives
 ||Pi_R(a)-s|| <= ||a-s||+||Pi_R(s)-s||.
For R=B/sigma,
 E||Pi_R(s_P)-s_P||^p <= E||s_P||^(2p)/R^p.
By Step 2 the p-th root is at most D/(B sigma). Minkowski thus gives
 ||f-s_P||_Lp(P_sigma) <= (e/4+D/B)/sigma = e/(2sigma).
The deterministic cap and Step 2 also give
 ||f-s_H||_Lp(H_sigma) <= (B+sqrt(D))/sigma.
Insert these bounds into (A). The two weighted terms are bounded by
 (e/2)^p/sigma^p and eta(B+sqrt(D))^p/sigma^p=(e/2)^p/sigma^p.
This proves the announced bound. Projection is jointly measurable and
uses only public parameters, so the simulation preserves adaptive rounds.

4. Compact repair. Suppose additionally P is supported in the unit ball
and Cov(P)<=I/d. The parameter eta obeys eta<=1/(2d): indeed
 e/[2(B+sqrt(D))]<=1/(8D), so eta<=1/(64D^2)<=1/(2d).
Choose the public law H uniform on the cube [-c,c]^d,
 c=sqrt(3/(eta d)). Then Cov(H)=I/(eta d), EH=0,
 E||H||^2=1/eta, and its support radius is sqrt(3/eta).
Writing mu=EP and Sigma=Cov(P),
 Cov(Q)=I/d+(1-eta)Sigma+eta(1-eta)mu mu^T.
As ||mu||<=1, it follows that I/d<=Cov(Q)<=3I/d and E||Q||^2<=2.
Q has bounded support; for fixed p and inverse-polynomial e its support
radius is polynomial, unlike the unbounded Gaussian repair used in C03.

Let alpha=sqrt(eta/3) and Q'=law(alpha Y), Y~Q. This public rescaling
puts Q' in the unit ball, keeps covariance condition number <=3, and
gives E||Q'||^2<=2eta/3. Its field at new noise sigma'>0 is
 alpha^-1 f_(sigma'/alpha)(x/alpha).
The p-th power error scales by alpha^-p while the denominator becomes
(sigma'/alpha)^p. Thus the SAME relative e/sigma' error promise holds.
Queries and TV distances are preserved under the invertible rescaling.

5. Hardness and endpoint qualifications. Any seed TV lower bound r
against the supplied field a transfers to Q with lower bound r-eta,
with the same instance probability and query rounds, by (A)'s legal
field construction and TV(P,Q)<=eta. The seed must actually supply the
Lp guarantee stated above. An L2-only seed is NOT promoted to p>2.
Scalar rescaling transfers that conclusion to Q'. Smoothed targets are
Gaussian convolutions of compactly supported laws; an endpoint comparison
still needs its own seed TV bound. In particular this lemma does not
repair C04's loss of late box labels at an inverse-polynomial endpoint.
Taking p=2 permits the existing box seed; arbitrary fixed p requires a
seed with the corresponding accuracy guarantee. No such new seed is
constructed here. The missing super-square-root mechanism remains open.

## Version 2: exact OU applicability and progress classification

This is a conditional relative-score transfer, not a Target 2 lower
bound in a uniform absolute OU-error model. Its earlier "moved" label
must not be interpreted as establishing a scored move of that problem.
The finite-Lp and compact-support lemma remains a proof (unaudited).

For a base law Q, the OU process is
 X_t=exp(-t)Y+sqrt(1-exp(-2t)) Z.
Write sigma(t)=sqrt(exp(2t)-1). The corresponding field is
 g_t(x)=exp(t) f_sigma(t)(exp(t)x).
The exact density scaling gives s_OU,t(x)=exp(t)s_Q,sigma(t)(exp(t)x).

For the row's p=2 convention this is a squared-error certificate

On a specified query time range t>=delta>0, the relative bound DOES
suffice for uniform root-mean-square error epsilon_score when

promise alone supplies no such seed guarantee. C05 supplies a concrete
failure for the particular earlier field; C06 states an alternative
conditional transfer at an independently specified intrinsic floor.

body:
[Prop 7 (One-cap model) of arXiv:2609.03296, 'Nonuniqueness of Model Potentials and Weak Geodesic Rays'] For \(0<\rho<1\), define
\[
 b_\rho(w)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,
  & |w|^2\leq (1-\rho)/\rho,\\[4pt]
  \dfrac12
  \left(
   \begin{aligned}
    &-\log(1+|w|^2)
     +(1-\rho)\log|w|^2\\
    &-\rho\log\rho
     -(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho)
   \end{aligned}
  \right),
  & |w|^2\geq (1-\rho)/\rho.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(b_\rho\) extends to a normalized positive-mass
\(\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}\)-model potential. Its unique pole is \(\infty\), its
contact region (equivalently, zero-contact set) is
\[
 C_\rho
 =
 \left\{|w|^2\leq\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}\right\},
\]
and
\[
 \omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\ddc b_\rho
 =
 \one_{C_\rho}\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\rho\delta_\infty.
 \tag{2.2}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \left\langle\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\ddc b_\rho\right\rangle
 =
 \one_{C_\rho}\omega_{\mathrm{FS}},
 \qquad
 \int_{\CP^1}
 \left\langle\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\ddc b_\rho\right\rangle
 =
 1-\rho>0.
\]

[Lemma 19 (Canonical Besov traces in the completed intersections) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $I=[t_0,t_1]$ be compact and let $\alpha,r\in\R$.  Consider the closure of
smooth finite-spatial-block paths in
\[
 C_IH^\alpha\cap L_I^\infty B_{2,\infty}^r
\]
with the intersection norm and the uniform little-Besov convention
\eqref{eq:uniform-little-besov-tail}.  Every element of this closure has a
unique representative in
\[
 C\bigl(I;b_{2,\infty}^r\bigr),
\]
and the endpoint evaluations are bounded.  The canonical
$C_IH^\alpha$ representative satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{t\in I}\|f(t)\|_{b_{2,\infty}^r}
 \le \|f\|_{L_I^\infty B_{2,\infty}^r},
 \qquad
 f_n\longrightarrow f\ \text{in the intersection norm}
 \Longrightarrow
 f_n\longrightarrow f\ \text{in }C_Ib_{2,\infty}^r.
\end{equation}
In particular, if the $H^\alpha$ trace of $f$ vanishes at an endpoint, then
its $b_{2,\infty}^r$ trace vanishes there as well.

[Definition def:geometry of arXiv:2411.08018, 'Last passage percolation in hierarchical environments'] We introduce the following notation:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item For $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $a\prec b$, we denote by $\mathsf{Rect}(a,b)$ the rectangle whose bottom-left and top-right corners are $a$ and $b$ 
    respectively.\\

    \noindent In what follows we fix $a\prec b$ and write $R \coloneqq \mathsf{Rect}(a,b)$.\\

    \item We denote by $\mathsf{Diag}(R)$ the diagonal of $R$ between the bottom-left and top-right corners of $R$.
    In other words, $\mathsf{Diag}(R)$ is the line segment with endpoints $a$ and $b$.
    \item We denote by $\mathsf{Slope}(R)$ the slope of $\mathsf{Diag}(R)$.
    \item We will often abuse notation by writing $\mathsf{Slope}(a,b) \coloneqq \mathsf{Slope}(\mathsf{Rect}(a,b))$, 
    so that $\mathsf{Slope}(a,b)$ equals the slope of the line segment with endpoints $a$ and $b$:
    \[
        \mathsf{Slope}(a,b) = \frac{b_2-a_2}{b_1-a_1}.
    \]
    \item 
    For $r\in(0,1)$ we define
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{Cyl}_r(R) \coloneqq \bigl\{ (x,y)\in R : |y-\mathsf{Slope}(R)x| \le r(b_2-a_2) \bigr\},
    \end{equation*}
    see Figure (fig:geometry of the paper).
    A straightforward calculation shows that  
    \footnote{For instance, $\mathsf{Cyl}_r(R)$ can be expressed as the disjoint union of a parallelogram of area $2r(1-r)|R|$ and two right triangles of area $\frac12r^2|R|$.}
    \[
        |\mathsf{Cyl}_r(R)| = (2-r)r|R|.
    \] 
    In particular, since $r\in(0,1)$ we get
    \begin{align}
        |\mathsf{Cyl}_r(R)|\ge r|R|.
    \end{align}
\end{enumerate}
title: Rectangles,  slopes, and cylinders

body:
[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] The phase $\gamma$ is $C^1$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}
\gamma'
=
\mu\varphi\cos^2\gamma+\varphi^{-1}\sin^2\gamma>0.
\end{equation}
Thus $\gamma$ is strictly increasing, and the zeros of $u$ are precisely
the points where $\gamma\in\frac{\pi}{2}+\pi\mathbb Z$. Moreover,
$\gamma(D^-)$ exists and is finite; if $u$ satisfies the natural condition at
$D$, then $\gamma(D^-)\in\pi\mathbb Z$.

body: In number theory, the modularity theorem states that elliptic curves over the field of rational numbers are related to modular forms in a particular way. Andrew Wiles and Richard Taylor proved the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves, which was enough to imply Fermat's Last Theorem (FLT). Later, a series of papers by Wiles's former students Brian Conrad, Fred Diamond and Richard Taylor, culminating in a joint paper with Christophe Breuil, extended Wiles's techniques to prove the full modularity theorem in 2001. Before that, the statement was known as the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture, Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture, or the modularity conjecture for elliptic curves.
title: Modularity theorem

[Theorem 2 (Higher-dimensional affine-cover pressure) of arXiv:2607.07014, '2607.07014'] Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a compact convex polytope, and let \((\Phi_{\omega_n})_{n\ge1}\) be i.i.d. random piecewise affine self-maps of \(K\). Set \(\Phi_n:=\Phi_{\omega_n}\circ\cdots\circ\Phi_{\omega_1}\) and \(R_n:=R_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Phi_n;K)\). Assume that \(R_n\) is measurable for every \(n\ge1\), and that 
\[\sup_{\omega}R_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Phi_{\omega};K)\le B\] 
for some deterministic \(B\ge1\). Then the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-pressure} remain valid after replacing \(N_n\), \(X_n\), \(\Lambda\), \(I_\pm\), and \(\log 2\) by \(R_n\), \(Y_n:=n^{-1}\log R_n\), \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{cov}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{cov},\pm}\), and \(\log B\), respectively, where
\[
\Lambda_{\mathrm{cov}}(q):=\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1}\log\mathbb E[R_n^q]
\]
and \(I_{\mathrm{cov},\pm}\) are defined from \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{cov}}\) exactly as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-pressure}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Higher-dimensional affine-cover pressure

body:
[Lemma lem:distance-identity of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Let \(I=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) for some \(N\in\mathbb N\), or let
		\(I=\mathbb N\).  Let \((X_i,d_i,\mu_i)\), \(i\in I\), be an ordered
		family of pairwise disjoint metric probability spaces, and write
		\(\nu_i=\operatorname{Law}(d_i(U_i,V_i))\), where \(U_i,V_i\) are independent with
		law \(\mu_i\).  In each of the following cases, let \(d\) be a metric on the indicated
		disjoint union whose restriction to each component is its given metric,
		and assume that all components are Borel subsets of the resulting metric
		space.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
			\item The ordered family may be augmented by one additional component
			$(X_\ast,d_\ast,\mu_\ast)$.  This single component is placed after all
			components $X_i$, $i\in I$. Let $p_i>0$, $i\in I$.  If $X_\ast$ is present, let
			$p_\ast>0$, assume that $p_\ast+\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1$,
			and put
			\[
			\mu=\sum_{i\in I}p_i\mu_i+p_\ast\mu_\ast,
			\qquad
			\nu_\ast=\operatorname{Law}(d_\ast(U_\ast,V_\ast)),
			\]
			where $U_\ast$ and $V_\ast$ are independent with law $\mu_\ast$.
			If $X_\ast$ is absent, assume that
			$\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1$, put
			$\mu=\sum_{i\in I}p_i\mu_i$, set $p_\ast=0$, and let
			$\nu_\ast$ be the zero measure on $\mathbb R_+$.
			
			Let $\phi_i:X_i\to\mathbb R_+$, $i\in I$, be measurable.  Suppose that
			$d(x,y)=\phi_i(x)$ whenever $x\in X_i$ and $y$ belongs to a later
			component, and put $\eta_i=(\phi_i)_\#\mu_i$.  If $U$ and $V$ are
			independent with law $\mu$, then
			\[
			\operatorname{Law}(d(U,V))
			=
			p_\ast^2\nu_\ast
			+\sum_{i\in I}p_i^2\nu_i
			+2\sum_{i\in I}p_i\Big(
			p_\ast+\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\j>i}}p_j
			\Big)\eta_i.
			\]
			
			\item Let $(X_0,d_0,\mu_0)$ be an additional initial component, which
			is placed before $X_i$ for every $i\in I$.  Let
			$p_i>0$, $i\in I\cup\{0\}$, and assume that $p_0+\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1$.
			Put
			\[
			\mu=p_0\mu_0+\sum_{i\in I}p_i\mu_i,
			\qquad
			\nu_0=\operatorname{Law}(d_0(U_0,V_0)),
			\]
			where $U_0$ and $V_0$ are independent with law $\mu_0$.
			
			Let $\phi_i:X_i\to\mathbb R_+$, $i\in I$, be measurable and suppose that
			$d(x,y)=\phi_i(x)$ whenever $x\in X_i$ and $y$ belongs to an earlier
			component.  If $U$ and $V$ are independent with law $\mu$, then
			\[
			\operatorname{Law}(d(U,V))
			=
			p_0^2\nu_0
			+\sum_{i\in I}p_i^2\nu_i
			+2\sum_{i\in I}p_i\Big(
			p_0+\sum_{\substack{j\in I\\j<i}}p_j
			\Big)(\phi_i)_\#\mu_i.
			\]
		\end{enumerate}

[Corollary Priority dynamics is a zero-range process of arXiv:2607.22908, 'Epidemic Phase Transitions in the Zero-Range Process'] Let $\eta_0 \in \mathbb{N}_0^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be an
  initial configuration drawn from $\mu_\rho$ for some $\rho > 0$, and let $(\xi_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be
  the slot-priority dynamics of (def:priority of the paper) started from any priority assignment compatible
  with $\eta_0$. Define $\eta_t(x) = n(\xi_t, x)$ as the number of occupied slots at site $x$ at
  time $t$.

  Then $(\eta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ has the law of the zero-range process on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with rate function $g$ and initial condition $\eta_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Priority dynamics is a zero-range process

[Corollary 57 of arXiv:2512.05466, 'Stochastic Flows and Marked Stable Processes'] Let $z< 0$, and consider the interval partition  of the interval $[0,\cR_{z,0} (0-)]$ given by 
\[
\beta_{z}:=
\{ (\cR_{r,0}(a-), \cB_{r,0}(a)) \colon  
 \cT_{(a,r)}\text{ a spindle, } \, \cB_{r,0}(a)\le \cR_{z,0} (0-)).  
\]
Then $\beta_{z}\eqdis G \gamma$, where $G$ has Gamma distribution $(\alpha, \frac{1}{2|z|})$ and $\gamma$ is a Poisson--Dirichlet interval partition with parameter $(\alpha,\alpha)$, independent of each other.

[Corollary 7 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Introduce a measure (Green's measure) on Borel 
subsets $\Gamma$ of $\bR^{d+1}$
\index{$S$@Miscelenea!Green's measure}
by the formula
$$
G(\Gamma)=
E_{\cF_{\tau}}\int_{\tau}^{\gamma}e^{-\phi_{\tau,t}}\kappa_{t}
I_{\Gamma}(\sft_{t},x_{t})\,dA_{t}.
$$
Assume that $A,B<\infty$ and set $p'=p/(p-1),q'=q/(q-1)$.
 Then $G(\Gamma)$ is absolutely continuous and
its  density $G(t,x)$ is such that, if $p\geq q$,
$$
\Big(\int_{\bR} \Big(\int_{\bR^{d}}G^{p'}(t,x)\,dx\Big)^{q'/p'}
dt\Big)^{1/q'}
$$
and, if $p\leq q$,
$$
\Big(\int_{\bR^{d}}\Big(\int_{\bR} G^{q'}(t,x)\,dt\Big)^{p'/q'}
dx\Big)^{1/q'}
$$
is dominated by
$$
  N(d)(B^{2}+A)^{ d/(2p)}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 7 of arXiv:2605.03236

body: [Def nodal family of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] For integers $g, n\geq 0$, a family of nodal curves of genus $g$ with $n$ marked points over a noetherian scheme $B$ is a flat proper morphism $\pi:C \rightarrow B$ admitting $n$ sections $s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n$, whose geometric fibers are nodal connected curves of arithmetic genus $g$.

 Then
for all $ x\in \mathbb R^d$, the derivatives $ \partial ^{\alpha }F(x),\alpha \in \mathcal I$ form a non-degenerate Gaussian vector, i.e. $ \det( \mathsf{Cov} (V(x))>0$.
Also, for $ \delta >0,$
\begin{align*}
\inf_{ | x-y | >\delta } | \det( \mathsf{Cov} \left(V(x,y)\right)) | >0.

[Theorem 7 (Fluctuation theorem) of arXiv:2607.18690, '2607.18690'] Assume \eqref{eq:mainhyp} and suppose that
\begin{equation}
        \mathcal{E}_t\to\mathcal{E}_\infty,
        \qquad
        \frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t\nu_s^\top\nu_s\to \mathcal{C} .
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
        \frac{X_t-\Exp[X_t]}{\sqrt t}
        \Rightarrow
        N(0,\sigma^2J),
        \qquad
        \sigma^2
        :=
        \Tr\!\left(\mathcal{C}\mathcal{E}_\infty\Sigma\mathcal{E}_\infty^\top\right), \text{ and }J=\1\1^\top.
\end{equation}
The limiting Gaussian law is supported on the line $\R\1$.
title: Fluctuation theorem

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] There exist sequences $(A_i)_{i}, (J_i)_{i}, (\mathcal{L}_i)_{i}$ with the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[left=0pt,label=(\alph*)]
    \item $A_i\subset\R_+^{2i}$ is a Borel set (in fact a polyhedron) with
    \[
    \int_{A_i } e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}} dt_1\dots dt_{2i} \leq \frac{1}{i!}\,.
    \]
    \item  $J_i\subset \mathbb Z_+^{2i}$ is an index set.
    \item  $\mathcal{L}_i$ is a mapping
    \[
    \mathcal{L}_i: \mathcal P_d \times A_i \to \C\langle X_{j,I}:j\in[1,d], I\in J_i \rangle
    \]
    where 
        \begin{itemize}
            \item for each fixed $T\in A_i$, $\mathcal{L}_i(\cdot, T)$ is a linear map, 
            \item for each fixed $Q\in \mathcal P_d$, the coefficients of $\mathcal{L}_i(Q,\cdot)$ are measurable (in fact simple) functions on $A_i$,
            \item given $M$ a monomial with coefficient $1$, for each fixed $T\in A_i$, $\mathcal{L}_i(M, T)$ is a sum of monomials with  coefficient $1$.
        \end{itemize}
    \item ($\frac1{N^2}$-Expansion).
    For any $Q\in \PP_d$ and $s\geq 1$,
	\begin{align} 
		&\E\left[ \ts_N\Big( Q(\bs{X}^N) \Big) \right] 
        = \tau(Q(\bs x^0)) + \sum_{i=1}^{s-1} \frac{\alpha_i(Q)}{N^{2i}}
        + \frac{\tilde \alpha^N_s(Q)}{N^{2s}}
	\end{align}
    with coefficients given by
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_i(Q) &:= \frac{1}{2^i} \int_{A_i } e^{-t_{2i}-\dots-t_{1}} \tau\Big( \left[\mathcal{L}_i(Q,T_i)\right](\bs x^{T_i}) \Big)\ dt_1\dots dt_{2i} \\
        \tilde \alpha_s^N(Q) &:= \frac{1}{2^s} \int_{A_s} e^{-t_{2s}-\dots-t_{1}} \E\left[\tau_N\Big( \left[\mathcal{L}_s(Q,T_s)\right] (\bs X^{N,T_s}) \Big)\right]\ dt_1\dots dt_{2s}\,
    \end{align*}
    (using the notation $T_i=(t_1,\dots, t_{2i})$ of Definition \eqref{tech1}).
    \item (Complexity). 
        If $Q=(P^*P)^k$, then for any $T\in A_i$, $\mathcal{L}_i(Q,T)$ is the sum of at most 
           $ 
            d^{2i} \times \left( 2k\times  c(P) \right)^{4i} 
            $
        $P$-monomials $M$ (with $n=i$) such that $p(M) = 2k+4i$ and $q(M) = 2k$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 25 of arXiv:2511.10535

[Theorem 66 (Least quadratic state for nondominated Hilbert semimartingales) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $\Smax$ be the nondominated Hilbert semimartingale model class of
\Cref{sec:canonicalization}.  For $1/3<\eta<1/2$, put
$\tau_0=(\eta;\mathcal S_2,\mathcal S_1)$.  The quadratic response
specification $\mathfrak Q_2(H)$ admits the total $\Smax$-causal
reconstruction
\[
 \mathcal A_2:\Omega_H\longrightarrow
 \mathsf Z_{\eta;\mathcal S_2,1}(H),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{ch}_{\tau_0}(\mathcal A_2)=(X,A,Q),
\]
without an additional accessibility hypothesis.  The total quasi-sure state
constructed in Part~II is the unique least sufficient state for
$\mathfrak Q_2(H)$ on $\Smax$: a causal source realizes the complete quadratic
program if and only if it admits a stable-causal readout of $\mathcal A_2$.
Its area and covariance coordinates have the
$\mathcal S_2/\mathcal S_1$ state geometry selected by Brownian calibration
and the corresponding orthogonal direct-sum laws.  Every stable-causal derived
representation of the complete quadratic program factors through this state.

[Theorem deviation bds of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] Let $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a usual random walk started at $o$ with step distribution $\mu$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] For any $D\geq 0$ and $n\geq 0$ sufficiently large, there exists $C_D>1$ such that 
\[ C_D^{-1} {\rm e} ^{-D} \leq \mathbb{P}_{o}\big[d_{{\mathcal G}}\big(Y_n, [o,Y_{\infty})\big)\geq D\big]\leq C_D {\rm e} ^{-D}.\]
The constants $C_D$ are bounded in $D$. 

\item[(2)] This means in particular that for $n>0$ big enough also
\[ \mathbb{P}_{o}\big[\big(Y_n,Y_{\infty}\big)^{{\mathcal G}}_{o}< D\big]\ \lesssim {\rm e} ^{-D}\]
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 11 (Realizability of prescribed torsion-angle data) of arXiv:2609.00673, '2609.00673'] Fix torsion angles
\[
\phi_i\in(-\pi,\pi],\qquad 1\le i\le n-2,
\]
and define
\[
\beta_1=0,\qquad \beta_{i+1}=\pi-\phi_i-\beta_i.
\]
There exists a non-orthogonal discrete general helix having these torsion angles and some turning angles in $(0,\pi)$ if and only if
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^{n-1}
\left\{
\psi\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z:
\cos\bigl((-1)^{i-1}\psi+\beta_i\bigr)>0
\right\}
\ne\varnothing.
\]
Thus arbitrary turning-angle data can be realized after a suitable choice of torsion angles, as in Corollary~\ref{cor:turning-bound}, but prescribed torsion-angle data need not be realizable.

u, \mu)$. There exist smooth functions $\ell(t)$ and $m(t)$ such that $\gamma'(t) = \ell(t) \mu(t)$, $
u'(t) = m(t) \mu(t)$, and $\mu'(t) = \ell(t) \gamma(t) - m(t) 
u(t)$. The ratio $\kappa_g(t) = m(t)/\ell(t)$ is the hyperbolic geodesic curvature of $\gamma$.
(\gamma, 
u) is a smooth Legendre curve
Frame (\gamma, 
u, \mu) is pseudo-orthonormal in R^{1,2}_1

[Theorem See~\Cref{thm:convergence_nonsimple_cle} for a more detailed statement of arXiv:2609.04138, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ I:\\ subsequential limits of the non-simple C'] For all $\kappa\in(4,8)$, consider a $\CLE_\kappa$ in the unit disk $\BD$ equipped with the graph distance $D^\kappa$, where two distinct loops are adjacent if and only if they intersect. Then, for every sequence $\kappa_n \downarrow 4$, there exists a sequence $\ka_{\kappa_n} \uparrow \infty$ such that, along a subsequence, 
		\[
		\left( \ka_{\kappa_n}^{-1}D^{\kappa_n} (\SCL^{\kappa_n}(x), \SCL^{\kappa_n}(y))\right)_{x,y \in \BD \cap \BQ^2} \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits_{n\to \infty}^{(\mathrm{d})}
		\left( D (\SCL(x), \SCL(y))\right)_{x,y \in \BD \cap \BQ^2},
		\]
		for the product topology, where $D$ is a distance on the set of loops of a $\CLE_4$ in $\BD$, and where $\SCL^{\kappa_n}(x)$ (resp.\ $\SCL(x)$) is the loop of the $\CLE_{\kappa_n}$ (resp.\ $\CLE_4$) that surrounds $x$. Moreover, the above convergence also holds for the distances to $\partial \BD$, and the distances $D(\partial \BD, \SCL(x))$ for $x \in \BD \cap \BQ^2$ have the law of the times at which the uniform exploration discovers each loop $\SCL(x)$. Finally, the limiting metric $D$ depends on the $\CLE_4$ in a conformally invariant and local manner. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: See~\Cref{thm:convergence_nonsimple_cle} for a more detailed statement

[Corollary 91 (Causal consistency and gluing of horizons) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Fix a tuple $\Xi$ satisfying Definition~\ref{def:Xi-assumptions} and fix the Cauchy data.  If $0<T_1<T_2$ and fixed points
$Z^{(T_j)}\in\mathcal Z_{T_j}$ exist, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak R_{T_1}Z^{(T_2)}=Z^{(T_1)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, let $\tau$ be measurable and suppose that for every rational
$q\in(0,1]$ a strongly measurable fixed point $Z^{(q)}$ is given on
$\{q<\tau\}$, extended by $0$ outside this event.  Then these fixed points
glue uniquely to a solution on $[0,\tau)$ in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:random-interval-solution}.  For every deterministic
$T\in(0,1]$, its restriction to $[0,T]$ on $\{T<\tau\}$ admits a strongly
measurable $\mathcal Z_T$-valued representative.

[Proposition prop:appenC4 of arXiv:2509.23086, 'On Optimal Markovian Couplings of L\'evy Processes'] We have $\mu_n \xrightarrow{\Lambda} \mu$ if and only if (equation def:weak-conv of the paper) holds for all bounded Lipschitz test functions $\varphi\in C_b(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying 
	\[
	|\varphi(x)| \le C \min\{1,|x|^2\}, 
	\qquad 
	|\nabla \varphi(x)| \le C|x| \quad \text{(Lebesgue a.e.)}
	\]
	for some constant $C \ge 0$.

	By assumption, (equation def:weak-conv of the paper) holds for every bounded Lipschitz function $\varphi$ satisfying the above growth bounds. In particular, it applies to functions $\varphi$ that vanish inside some ball $B_r(0)$, since in that case we can find constants $C,C'\ge 0$ with

[Definition 20 (Hyperbolic and de Sitter involutes \cite{ZP2026}) of arXiv:2608.26823, 'Evolutes, involutes and parallels of Legendre curves in hyperbolic and de Sitter 2-spaces '] \rm
Let $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow\Delta_1$ be a spacelike Legendre curve  with curvature $(m_h,n_h)$ and  $t_0\in I$.
Then the \textit{hyperbolic involute}  $ HI_{t_0}(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow H^2$  of    $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)$  is defined as  
\begin{equation}\notag
HI_{t_0}(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)(t)=  \cosh\left(\int_{t_0}^t{m_h(t)}{\rm d}t\right)\bgamma_h(t)-\sinh\left(\int_{t_0}^t{m_h(t)}{\rm d}t\right)\bgamma_h^s(t).
\end{equation} 
The \textit{de Sitter involute} $ DI_{t_0}(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d):I\rightarrow S_1^2$   of $(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)$  is defined as  
\begin{equation}\notag
DI_{t_0}(\bgamma_h,\bgamma_h^d)(t)=  \sinh\left(\int_{t_0}^t{m_h(t)}{\rm d}t\right)\bgamma_h(t)-\cosh\left(\int_{t_0}^t{m_h(t)}{\rm d}t\right)\bgamma_h^s(t).
\end{equation}
title: Hyperbolic and de Sitter involutes \cite{ZP2026}

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2604.15191, 'Quantitative Stability of Many-Marginal Schr\"odinger Bridge'] For $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$,  $\phi, \chi \in \mathcal{C}(\mathbb{T}^d)$, we have
\begin{align*}
\frac{\dd}{\dd\lambda} \m T_\mu^\varepsilon [\phi + \lambda\chi](y)
&= -\frac{\int_{\mb T^d}e^{\frac{\phi(x) + \lambda\chi(x) - c_\varepsilon(x, y)}{\varepsilon}}\chi(x)\,\dd\mu(x)}{\int_{\mb T^d}e^{\frac{\phi(x) + \lambda\chi(x) - c_\varepsilon(x,y)}{\varepsilon}}\,\dd\mu(x)} = -\mb E_{X\sim\pi_y[\phi + \lambda\chi]}[\chi(X)],\\
\frac{\dd^2}{\dd\lambda^2} \m T_\mu^\varepsilon[\phi + \lambda\chi](y)
&= -\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\mb V_{X\sim\pi_y[\phi + \lambda\chi]}[\chi(X)].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Polyanskiy-Wu Proposition1, two-sided regular-density case. Let U,V be random vectors in R^n, n>=1, with finite full second moments. Suppose their Lebesgue densities p_U,p_V are strictly positive and continuously differentiable, and share constants c1>0,c2>=0 satisfying ||gradient log p_j(x)||<=c1*||x||+c2 for every x in R^n and j=U,V. Use natural logarithms for differential entropy h and relative entropy D. Define W2(P,Q)=inf_couplings (E||A-B||^2)^(1/2) and Delta=[(c1/2)*(sqrt(E||U||^2)+sqrt(E||V||^2))+c2]*W2(P_U,P_V). Then both differential entropies and both relative entropies are finite, |h(U)-h(V)|<=Delta, and D(P_U||P_V)+D(P_V||P_U)<=2*Delta. No independence between U and V is required; the statement depends only on their marginal laws. This extracts the common-regularity conclusion of source equations9-10, with all moment norms noncentered.
Strictly positive C1 densities on R^n with common linear score-growth constants c1>0,c2>=0.

[Lemma lem-local-expansion of arXiv:2605.24627, 'A 4/7-limit law for the largest interpoint distance in a rotational ellipsoid'] Let $x=x(\theta,\delta,w)$ and $y=x(\theta+\pi+\psi,\delta',w')$. Then, as $\delta,\delta',\psi,w,w'\to 0$, we have
\[
2-\|x-y\| = \frac{\delta+\delta'}{2} + \frac{\psi^2}{4}
- \frac{a^2}{4}(w-w')^2 + r(\delta,\delta',\psi,w,w'),
\] 
where
\[
r(\delta,\delta',\psi,w,w') =
o\bigl(\delta+\delta'+\psi^2+w^2+(w')^2\bigr).
\]

The remainder is uniform in $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Local expansion

body: In mathematics, the gamma function, denoted by $\Gamma$ (capital Greek letter gamma), is the most common extension of the factorial function to complex numbers. First studied by Daniel Bernoulli, the gamma function is defined for all complex numbers $z$ except non-positive integers, and satisfied $\Gamma (n)=(n-1)!$ for every positive integer $n$. The gamma function can be defined via a convergent improper integral for complex numbers with positive real part: $\Gamma (z)=\int _{0}^{\infty }t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,\ \qquad \Re (z)>0.$ The gamma function then is defined in the complex plane as the analytic continuation of this integral function: it is a meromorphic function which is holomorphic except at zero and the negative integers, where it has simple poles.

[Theorem 33 (Distributional CLT for the kernel-weighted measure) of arXiv:2604.20634, 'Distributional Statistical Models:\\ \large Weak Moments, Cumulants, and a Central Limit T'] Under the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:weak-clt}, suppose additionally
that each~$X_i$ has a nonnegative density $f\in L^1(\R)$ with
$\varphi\ge 0$ and $\int_\R f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx = 1$.  Define the
kernel-weighted probability density $h := \varphi f$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The function $h$ is a probability density with finite moments of all
orders.

\item The mean and variance of~$h$ coincide with the first two weak
cumulants:
$\mu_h = {}^{(\varphi)}\kappa_1$ and $\sigma_h^2 = {}^{(\varphi)}\kappa_2$.

\item The classical characteristic function of~$h$ is the weak
characteristic function: $\widehat{h}(t) = {}^{(\varphi)}\phi(t)$.

\item Let $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d.\ with density~$h$ and set
\[
\bar{Z}_n
\;=\;
\frac{Y_1+\cdots+Y_n - n\,{}^{(\varphi)}\kappa_1}
     {\sqrt{n\,{}^{(\varphi)}\kappa_2}}.
\]
Then $\bar{Z}_n$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$:
for every $a\in\R$,
\[
P(\bar{Z}_n \le a)
\;\longrightarrow\;
\Phi(a),
\]
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 4 (Duflo (1997), Corollary 2.1.10) of arXiv:2606.21111, 'On Elephant Random Walk with Delayed Amnesia'] Let $\{M_n,\mathcal{F}_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a real, square-integrable vector martingale whose predictable quadratic variation is $\{\langle M\rangle_n\}_{n\ge 0}$. Also, let the following assumptions hold for a deterministic real sequence $\{a_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ which increases to $\infty$:\\
\noindent {(i)} $a_n^{-1}\langle M\rangle_n\xrightarrow{p}\Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ is a deterministic symmetric positive semi-definite matrix, and\\
\noindent {(ii)} Lindeberg's condition is satisfied, that is, for all $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation*}
a_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}(\parallel M_k-M_{k-1}\parallel^2 \mathbb{I}_{\{\parallel M_k-M_{k-1}\parallel \ge \varepsilon \sqrt{a_n}\}}|\mathcal{F}_{k-1})\xrightarrow{p} 0.
\end{equation*}
Then, $a_n^{-1/2}M_n\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Cor 56 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and consider the kernel
\[
b_m := \mathbb E\!\Big[
|B_\infty(0,r^{(n)}_0)\cap B_\infty(m,r^{(n)}_{m})|
\Big],
\qquad m\in\mathbb Z^d.
\]
Let $f^{(L)}$ be a local observable such that
$\delta_k f^{(L)}=\delta>0$ for $k\in\Lambda_L$ and
$\delta_k f^{(L)}=0$ otherwise.
Then
\[
\liminf_{L\to\infty}
\frac{\mathbb E\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\big(c_i^{(n)}(X)\big)^2}
{\|\delta f^{(L)}\|_2^2}
=
\|b\|_1 .
\]

Consequently the universal bound
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\big(c_i^{(n)}(X)\big)^2
\le
\|\delta f\|_2^2\,\|b\|_1
\]
is sharp: neither the prefactor nor the functional $\|b\|_1$
can be replaced by a strictly smaller universal quantity. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor 56 of arXiv:2602.14618

Let G be a transient connected locally finite network with strictly positive conductances, and I its canonical random interlacement Poisson process on time-shift classes of doubly infinite random-walk trajectories times R, with intensity nu tensor Lebesgue measure. Fix a deterministic t in R. For each vertex v, let tau_t(v)>t be the first interlacement arrival level after t whose trajectory visits v; in that trajectory take the oriented edge e_t(v) used on its first entry to v. Reverse each such edge. The set AB_t(I)={-e_t(v): v in V} has the law of the oriented wired uniform spanning forest: each vertex has one outgoing edge, and forgetting all orientations gives the WUSF. The choice of the first entry is well-defined for a transient doubly infinite trajectory. This is a fixed-time statement; it does not assert simultaneous absence of exceptional times for all real t. Source: Interlacements and the Wired Uniform Spanning Forest, Theorem 1.1, p.2; proof Section 4, Lemma 4.1, pp.11-12.

[Lem 7 of arXiv:2605.30779, '2605.30779'] Let \(\mathcal G_\star\) denote either \(\mathcal G^{(\beta)}\) defined in \eqref{eq:airy_green_beta_limit}, or \(\mathcal G^{(\beta)}_{\Theta}\) defined in \eqref{eq:defn_Airy_Green_multiple}.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item  
    Almost surely,
    \[
      \lim_{\substack{|w|\to\infty\\ \Re w\ge0}}
      \bigl|\mathcal G_\star(w)+\sqrt w\bigr|=0,
    \]
    where the square root is the principal branch, positive on \((0,\infty)\). Consequently,
    \[
      \mathcal G_\star(x)\longrightarrow-\infty,
      \qquad x\to+\infty.
    \]
  \item   
    If, in addition, \(\beta\in\{1,2\}\), then, along the positive real axis,
    \begin{equation*} 
      \begin{pmatrix}
        x^{1/4}\bigl(\mathcal G_\star(x)+\sqrt{x}\bigr)\\[0.4em]
        x^{1/4}\left(
        -\dfrac{1}{\mathcal G_\star'(x)}-2\sqrt{x}
        \right)
      \end{pmatrix}
      \Longrightarrow
      \mathcal N\!\left(
        \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
        \frac1\beta
        \begin{pmatrix}
          1&-1\\
          -1&2
        \end{pmatrix}
      \right).
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, almost surely,
    \[
      \mathcal G_\star'(x)
      =
      -\frac1{2\sqrt{x}}+o(x^{-1}),
      \qquad
      \mathcal G_\star''(x)
      =
      \frac1{4x^{3/2}}+o(x^{-2}).
    \]
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem JSJ of arXiv:2609.00233, 'A survey on mapping class groups of 3-manifolds'] Suppose that $M$ is a compact, oriented, irreducible  3-manifold with $\partial M \cong \bigsqcup^k T^2$ for some $k \geq 0$.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item There is an $m \geq 0$ and a submanifold $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m T_i \subseteq M$ such that for every $i$, $T_i \subseteq M$ is an incompressible torus, and each component of $M$ cut along $\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m T_i$ is Seifert fibred or atoroidal.
\item Any two minimal submanifolds with the above property are isotopic.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $X$ be a centered Gaussian measure on a real separable Hilbert space $K$ with covariance operator $Q_X$. For a test function $h \in C_b^2(K)$, the infinite-dimensional Stein equation is the partial differential equation $\operatorname{Tr}(Q_X D^2 U(x)) - \langle x, D U(x) \rangle_K = h(x) - \mathbb{E}[h(X)]$, whose unique smooth solution is given by the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup integral $U(x) = -\int_0^1 \frac{1}{2t} (\mathbb{E}[h(\sqrt{t} x + \sqrt{1-t} X)] - \mathbb{E}[h(X)]) \mathrm{d}t$.
K is a real separable Hilbert space
Q_X is trace-class
h \in C_b^2(K)
title: Infinite-Dimensional Stein Equation for Gaussian Measure

Y:( [0,T] \times \Omega \times U , \mathfrak B_T  \otimes {\mathfrak F} \otimes  \mathfrak U ) \to (M,\mathfrak M) , \quad (t,\omega,u) \mapsto Y^u(t,\omega)
$$
is called {\em $\mathfrak U$-optional} 
 if it is $\mathfrak O \otimes \mathfrak U  /  \mathfrak M$-measurable where $\mathfrak O$ denotes the optional $\sigma$-field on $[0,T] \times \Omega$. We say that $Y$ has a {\em $\mathfrak U$-optional version} if there exists  $ ^{\circ}Y$
 which is $\mathfrak U$-optional and {\em indistinguishable} from  $Y$, in the sense that, for all $u \in U$, the processes $ ^{\circ} Y^u$ and $Y^u$ are indistinguishable.

body:
Moser's inequality reads $\sup_{Q^-}u\le C\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $Q^-$ strictly earlier than $Q^+$. Three hypotheses are load-bearing, and all three fail for the naive elliptic-style statement. (1) No inequality at a single time: on $\mathbb R^n$ the positive solution $u_k(x,t)=e^{kx_1+k^2t}$ has, on $B_1\times\{t\}$, $\sup u_k/\inf u_k=e^{2k}\to\infty$, so $\sup_{B_1\times\{t\}}u\le C\inf_{B_1\times\{t\}}u$ cannot hold with $C$ independent of the solution; the same family (or the shifted heat kernel $\Phi(x-y,t+\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$) shows that even the elliptic Harnack constant for the Laplacian does not transfer. (2) The time direction cannot be reversed: $\sup_{Q^+}u\le C\inf_{Q^-}u$ is false, since $u_k$ grows like $e^{k^2t}$; information propagates forward in time only. Intuitively, a heat distribution can be large now and tiny in the past. (3) Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder is needed, not just on $Q^-\cup Q^+$: the inequality is applied to $u$ and to $\sup u-u$ in the derivation of Holder continuity, and both must be nonnegative on the full cylinder $B_{2r}\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Also parabolic, not Euclidean, scaling governs the geometry: the cylinder for radius $r$ must have time length comparable to $r^2$, so an auditor should check that a cited Harnack inequality is applied on cylinders of the correct aspect ratio, with the two sub-cylinders separated in time by a fixed multiple of $r^2$.
The two cylinders must be separated in time, past on the left of the inequality
Nonnegativity is required on the entire cylinder
Time-slice and reversed-time versions are false
Cylinders must respect the parabolic scaling t ~ r^2
title: Pitfall: The Parabolic Harnack Inequality needs a time lag, the right time direction, and nonnegativity

[Definition def_arw_using_stacks of arXiv:2605.06887, 'Law of large numbers for activated random walk on villages'] For each $x \in V$ we start with
  $\lfloor \sigma_x n \rfloor$ houses in village $x$ with one sleepy particle in them. 
  In each operation below we always execute the instructions of each stack in ascending order: $j=1,2,\dots$ 
  

\begin{enumerate}

\item  For each $x \in V$, $\lfloor \nu_x n \rfloor$ many immigrants arrive at the airport of village $x$ and use the first $\lfloor \nu_x n \rfloor$ taxi tickets  $\gamma_{j,x}, \, j=1,\dots, \lfloor \nu_x n \rfloor$ to distribute themselves in the houses of village $x$.

\item 
Each active particle in village $x$ has a clock with rate $1+\lambda_x$. When the first clock rings (in any of the houses of any of the villages), say in house $i$ of village $x$, we reveal the next unused landlord notice $\kappa_{j, (x,i)}$ of house $(x,i)$ and evolve the system by making that active particle sleep or jump accordingly. Note that if the instruction is a sleep and the house $(x,i)$ has at least one other (active) particle in it, then nothing happens (the particle tries to sleep and is then instantly re-awoken). 

\item  If the revealed landlord notice $\kappa$  was a jump instruction, then this particle goes to the airport of its current village $x$, grabs the next airplane ticket $\zeta_{j',x}$ and
flies to a village (or the graveyard state $\dagger$) accordingly.
If the airplane arrived at village $y$
then it moves to a house in village $y$ according to the next taxi ticket $\gamma_{j'', y}$.

\item We repeat steps (stacks_def_ii of the paper) and (stacks_def_iii of the paper) until all particles have either jumped to the graveyard state or went to sleep.
 \end{enumerate}
title: Construction of VARW using stacks

body:
For a finite simple graph G and integer k>=1, its strong k-core is the maximal vertex set S for which each vertex in S together with its outside neighbourhood N(S) has at least k neighbours in S. Initially colour every vertex black. While a black or blue vertex has fewer than k black neighbours, colour it red and colour all its black neighbours blue. The final black set is the strong k-core, the blue set is its outside neighbourhood, and the red set is the complement of those two sets. Each red step creates at most k-1 new blue vertices; this is a bound on new births, not final blue degree. For k=4, each red/blue component has at least one quarter of its vertices red, and these red vertices have no neighbour outside that component.

Let d>=2 and N>=2 be integers and C={x_1,...,x_N} a set of N distinct points on the unit sphere S^(d-1) in R^d. For an integer t>=0, C is a spherical t-design if (1/N)sum_(x in C)p(x)=integral_(S^(d-1))p(x)d sigma_d(x) for every real polynomial p on R^d of total degree at most t, where sigma_d is normalized uniform surface measure. If m>=1 is the number of distinct inner products <x,y> with x,y in C and x!=y, then C is sharp when it is a spherical (2m-1)-design. This is Definition1.1 of Cohn-Kumar math/0607446v2, printedp101/PDFp3. The case m=1 is included: an antipodal pair is a sharp configuration. This definition concerns a set of distinct, equally weighted points.

t nonnegative integer for a t-design

[Lemma 18 (Quantitative positivity) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\YY, \YY' \in \XXA$ be sets, let $\delta \in (0,1)$ be a number with
$\pi(\XX\setminus\YY') \le \delta/4$, and let
\[
  s : \XX \times \XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty), \qquad (x,y) \longmapsto s(y \mid x),
\]
be a $\XXA \otimes \XXA$-measurable map such that
\[
  \pi\bigl( \{ x \in \YY : s(y \mid x) = 0 \} \bigr) \;\le\; \frac{\delta}{4}
  \qquad\text{for every } y \in \YY' .
\]
Then there exist a number $\eta \in (0,1]$ and a set $G \in \XXA$ with
$\pi(G) \ge \tfrac12$ such that
\[
  \int_{L} s(y \mid x)\, \pi(\dd x) \;\ge\; \frac{\eta\delta}{2}
  \qquad
  \text{for every } y \in G \text{ and every } L \in \XXA \text{ with }
  L \subseteq \YY \text{ and } \pi(L) \ge \delta .
\]

[Thm zetaM_Fourier_An of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] We have
$$
\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=\frac{K_{\lambda,\mu}+K_{\lambda',\mu}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda}, \quad\widehat{\xi_M^c}(\lambda)=\frac{K_{\lambda,\mu}-K_{\lambda',\mu}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda},
$$
where
$$
\mu=\mu_M:=(n-M,1,1,\dots,1)\vdash n,
$$
and $K_{\alpha,\mu}$ denotes the Kostka number.

Moreover, if $\lambda_1<n-M$ and $l(\lambda)<n-M$, then $\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=\widehat{\xi_M^c}(\lambda)=0$. If $\lambda_1\ge n-M$, we have
$$\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=\binom{M}{\,n-\lambda_1\,}\frac{
d_{\lambda^*}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda},\quad\widehat{\xi_M^c}(\lambda)=\binom{M}{\,n-\lambda_1\,}\frac{
d_{\lambda^*}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda}.$$
If $l(\lambda)\ge n-M$, we have
$$\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda)=\binom{M}{\,n-l(\lambda)\,}\frac{d_{\lambda^\bullet}}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda},\quad\widehat{\xi_M^c}(\lambda)=-\binom{M}{\,n-l(\lambda)\,}\frac{d_{\lambda^\bullet}
}{d_\lambda}\,\Id_{d_\lambda}.$$
title: Fourier transform of $\xi_M$ and $\xi_M^c$

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be a sequence of independent random variables with \mathbb{E}[X_n] = 0 and \sigma_n^2 = \mathbb{E}[X_n^2] < \infty. Let s_n^2 = \sum_{k=1}^n \sigma_k^2. [Cor primitivecounts of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Let $r>0$ and let $M_r(L)$ be the number of primitive sign classes with $\|\bm u\|\le r$.
Let
$$
\mu_r=\frac{v_nr^n}{2\zeta(n)}.
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb E_{\mu_n}M_r(L)=\mu_r,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_n}(M_r(L))=\mu_r.
$$
Let $L_n$ be distributed according to $\mu_n$ on $\mathbb X_n$.
In particular, if $r_n>0$ and $v_nr_n^n/(2\zeta(n))\to\infty$, then
$$
\frac{M_{r_n}(L_n)}{v_nr_n^n/(2\zeta(n))}\to1
$$
in probability.
For fixed $\rho>1$,
$$
\frac{M_{\rho\operatorname{GH}_n}(L_n)}{\rho^n/(2\zeta(n))}\to1
$$
in probability.

body:
[Theorem 1 (Stein recursion for products of disjoint principal minors) of arXiv:2607.03984, 'On Wilks' problem: Exact recursive formulas via Stein's method for the joint moments of di'] Let $d\in\N$, let $p_1,\ldots,p_d\in\N$, set $p\leqdef p_1 + \cdots + p_d$, and let $\mathfrak{W}=(\mathfrak{W}_{rs})_{1 \leq r,s \leq d}\sim \mathcal{W}_p(\alpha,\Sigma)$, where $\alpha\in (p-1,\infty)$ and $\Sigma\in \mathcal{S}_{++}^p$. For every $\bb{n}=(n_1,\ldots,n_d)\in\N_0^d$, let
\[
P_{\bb{n}}(S) = \prod_{r=1}^d |S_{rr}|^{n_r}, \qquad m_{\bb{n}} = \sum_{r=1}^d n_r p_r.
\]
If $m_{\bb{n}}=0$, then $\EE[P_{\bb{n}}(\mathfrak{W})]=1$. If $m_{\bb{n}}\geq 1$, define recursively
\[
P_{\bb{n}}^{(0)} \leqdef P_{\bb{n}}, \qquad P_{\bb{n}}^{(r + 1)} \leqdef \frac{1}{m_{\bb{n}}-r}\mathcal{R}_{\alpha,\Sigma}P_{\bb{n}}^{(r)}, \qquad r\in\{0,\ldots,m_{\bb{n}}-1\}.
\]
Then $\smash{P_{\bb{n}}^{(r)}\in\mathcal{H}_{m_{\bb{n}}-r}}$ for every $r\in\{0,\ldots,m_{\bb{n}}\}$, the polynomial $\smash{P_{\bb{n}}^{(m_{\bb{n}})}}$ is constant, and
\begin{equation}
\EE\left[\prod_{r=1}^d |\mathfrak{W}_{rr}|^{n_r}\right] = \EE[P_{\bb{n}}^{(0)}(\mathfrak{W})] = \EE[P_{\bb{n}}^{(1)}(\mathfrak{W})] = \cdots = \EE[P_{\bb{n}}^{(m_{\bb{n}})}(\mathfrak{W})] = P_{\bb{n}}^{(m_{\bb{n}})}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
\EE\left[\prod_{r=1}^d |\mathfrak{W}_{rr}|^{n_r}\right] = \frac{1}{m_{\bb{n}}!}\left(\mathcal{R}_{\alpha,\Sigma}^{m_{\bb{n}}}P_{\bb{n}}\right)(S),
\end{equation}
for any $S\in \mathcal{S}^p$, because $\mathcal{R}_{\alpha,\Sigma}^{m_{\bb{n}}}P_{\bb{n}}$ is a constant polynomial.
title: Stein recursion for products of disjoint principal minors

[Proposition expvar of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let  $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$  be a {\em stationary} marked point process  
   on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{K}$ with non-null, finite intensity
     $\rho$.  Let $\xi : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a translation invariant marking function.
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item  
Let $\xi$ be fast \textnormal{BL}-localizing on all finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ as in 
(equation Lp-stab of the paper) for $p = 1$ and 
assume $\xi$
also
satisfies  a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-moment condition on {\em finite windows} 
as at~(equation e:xinpmomcopied of the paper) for {\em some} $\varepsilon > 0$. Then for almost all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ as $n\to\infty$ the Palm distributional limit of $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)$, 
given by  $\Upsilon_{\0}$
in (equation e.xil-0 of the paper), exists and for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\Big| n^{-1} \mathbb{E}  \mu_n^\xi(f) -  \rho \mathbb{E} [\Upsilon_{\0}]\int_{W_1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d} x\Big| = O(n^{-1/d}).
\end{equation}
If $\xi$ satisfies (equation Lp-stab of the paper)  for $p=1$ with
$\varphi_{1}$ only decreasing to zero, then the right-hand side of (equation expasy of the paper) is $o(1)$.

 
\item   
Assume $\xi$ is fast  \textnormal{BL}-localizing on finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$  as in (equation Lp-stab of the paper) for $p \in \{1,2\}$  and assume 
$\xi$ satisfies a $(2 + \varepsilon)$-moment condition on finite windows as at~(equation e:xinpmomcopied of the paper) for some $\varepsilon > 0$. 
Then for \(\rho^{(2)}\)-almost all \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^d\) as $n\to\infty$ the Palm distributional limit of $(\xi(\tilde{x}_1,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n),\xi(\tilde{x}_2,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n))$
given by $\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}=(\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[1],\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[2])$, $z=x_2-x_1$,
in (equation e.xil-xy of the paper) exists.

Further, if $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ has  summable exponential $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations as in Definition~(def.A2 of the paper) then for all $f \in  \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \,\mu_n^{\xi}(f) =  \sigma^2(\Upsilon) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2 \,\mathrm{d} x \in [0,\infty),
\end{equation}
whereas for all $f, g \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}

\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-1}  {\rm{Cov}} ( \mu_n^{\xi}(f) , \mu_n^{\xi}(g) )  =  \sigma^2(\Upsilon) \int_{W_1} f(x) g(x) \,\mathrm{d} x,
\end{equation}

where 

\begin{align}  
\sigma^2(\Upsilon) =
\rho\mathbb {E} [\Upsilon_{\0}^2]  \ + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left( \mathbb {E} \Bigl[\Upsilon_{
(\0,z)}[1]\Upsilon_{(\0,z)}[2]\Bigr] \rho^{(2)}(\0,z) - \rho^2\mathbb {E} [\Upsilon_{\0}]^2 \right) \mathrm{d} z \in [0, \infty).
\end{align}

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

 |V_{n+1} \wedge V_n| > |V_n \wedge V_{n-1}|,

[Definition 1 (Quasi-Feller kernel) of arXiv:2606.23222, 'A Route to Harris ergodicity for Non-Feller Markov Kernels'] A Markov kernel \(P\) on \(S\) is called quasi-Feller if there exist a Polish
space \(W\), a measurable map \(H:S\to W\), and a Markov kernel \(Q\) from
\(W\) to \(S\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item for every \(f\in C_b(S)\), the function
    \[
            Qf(w)=\int_S f(y)Q(w,dy)
    \]
    belongs to \(C_b(W)\);
    \item for every \(f\in C_b(S)\),
    \[
            Pf=Qf\circ H;
    \]
    \item if \(D_H\) denotes the set of discontinuity points of \(H\), then
\[
        Q(w,D_H)=0,
        \qquad
        w\in \bigcup_{K\subset S\ \mathrm{compact}} \overline{H(K)} .
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:circuit-output of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For every $\zeta\in\mathscr P_\tau$,
\[
 \left\|n^{-F(\tau)}
 \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}(\zeta)
 \right\|_{\tau,\varepsilon}
 \le \|\zeta\|_{\mathscr P_\tau},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}
 =n^{F(\tau)}\operatorname{Contr}^{\rm norm}_{\Gamma,\tau}.
\tag{2.3.17}
\]
The same estimate holds with arbitrary typed gaps and retained output
ports.  Inserting prescribed maps multiplies the right side by at most
the product of their operator norms, provided they contain no hidden
unnormalized cup or cap.

Status: proof draft (unaudited). No novelty or priority claim. This theorem concerns a selected balanced width-two orbit; it does not establish a general-data canonical escape limit.

## Theorem
Let M be invertible and Sigma symmetric positive definite, both 2x2. Let B,A be SQUARE 2x2 factors solving gradient flow for C(BA)=tr((BA-M)Sigma(BA-M)^T)/2. Suppose initially
  B^T B=AA^T,
  B and A are invertible,
  sign det(BA)=sign det M,
  C(BA)<C(0).
Then the factors converge to finite limits B*,A* with B*A*=M. No isotropy or commutation assumption is imposed, and no assumption of an initially best-rank-one saddle is made.

## 1. Global boundedness, analytic convergence, and finite-time full rank
The balance K=B^T B-AA^T is conserved, hence remains zero. Loss decreases and Sigma positive definite bounds P=BA. The exact invariant identity
  ||B^T B||F^2+||AA^T||F^2=2||BA||F^2+||K||F^2
bounds both factors when w=2; their trace norms are bounded by the corresponding Frobenius norms times sqrt(2). Thus the forward polynomial ODE is global and bounded.

The bounded analytic gradient trajectory has a finite-length tail and converges to a stationary factor pair, by the elementary local Lojasiewicz argument given in C002: at a cluster point choose a local analytic gradient inequality, integrate the square-root energy dissipation to bound remaining length, and trap the late trajectory inside that neighborhood. This is the analytic convergence ingredient, not an inference that boundedness alone implies a point limit.

Put W=A^T and U=(B;W). The stacked flow is U'=-H(P-M)U, with H(D)=[[0,D Sigma],[Sigma D^T,0]]. On every finite time interval the linear fundamental matrix of this prescribed continuous coefficient is invertible, so U keeps column rank two. If Wc=0, balance gives ||Bc||^2=c^T B^T Bc=c^T W^T Wc=0, hence Uc=0 and c=0. Thus W and B stay invertible at every finite time. Define O=B W^(-1). Balance gives O^T O=I, and its constant determinant is
  delta=sign det O=sign det(BA)=sign det M.
This equality of signs does not assert det(BA) is constant in magnitude.

## 2. Classify possible limiting ranks
Balance passes to the limit, so B*,W* have the same Gram matrix and the same rank. If that rank is zero then both vanish, contradicting C(P*)<=C(P(0))<C(0). If their common rank is two, stationarity and invertibility give G*=(B*W*^T-M)Sigma=0, hence B*W*^T=M.

It remains to rule out common rank one. Their equal rank-one Gram matrices imply
  B*=b h^T, W*=a h^T,
where ||h||=1 and ||a||=||b||=rho>0. Then P*=ba^T, and stationarity gives G*a=0 and G*^T b=0. Since M has rank two, G* cannot be zero; it has rank exactly one.

## 3. A rank-one limit forces increasing determinant, a contradiction
Choose oriented orthonormal frames L=[b/rho,J2 b/rho], R=[a/rho,J2 a/rho], J2=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. In these frames G*=L diag(0,gamma)R^T, with gamma!=0. Let Hinv=R^T Sigma^(-1)R. From M=P*-G*Sigma^(-1), direct determinant expansion yields
  det M=-rho^2 gamma (Hinv)22.
Since (Hinv)22>0, delta=sign det M=-sign gamma.

Although B*,W* are singular, O(t) still converges: choose any index j with h_j!=0. For all late times the nonzero jth columns w_j(t),b_j(t) converge to nonzero multiples of a,b. An orthogonal 2x2 map of fixed determinant delta is uniquely determined by its action on one nonzero vector. Explicitly
  O(t)=L_j(t)diag(1,delta)R_j(t)^T,
using the oriented normalized column frames. Hence O(t)->O*=L diag(1,delta)R^T. If h_j<0, both oriented frames change sign together and the same formula results.

The exact input-factor equation is W'=-G^T O W. Since W is invertible at every finite time, Jacobi's formula gives
  d/dt log|det W|=-tr(G^T O).
At the alleged rank-one endpoint this coefficient tends to
  -tr(G*^T O*)=-delta gamma=|gamma|>0.
Therefore for all sufficiently late times |det W| grows at least exponentially with positive rate |gamma|/2. This contradicts the previously established boundedness of W (and also its rank-one limit). Thus common rank one is impossible. Only common rank two remains, and its stationary product equals M. QED, subject to independent analytic audit.

## Why the energy hypothesis cannot be omitted
In dimension two the same graph determinant component contains the negative map as well as the positive one. Let M=diag(3,1), Sigma=I, choose W(0)=c I with c>0 and B(0)=-W(0). Then O=-I has determinant +1=sign det M and balance is exact, but P=-WW^T. The coordinate-diagonal invariant flow has positive diagonal w_i satisfying w_i'=-(m_i+w_i^2)w_i, so W and B tend to zero. Its initial loss is greater than C(0), outside the theorem. Thus determinant orientation alone is insufficient and cannot be used to drop the strict energy hypothesis.

## Canonical escape connection and remaining obligation
At any nonzero balanced rank-one critical factor zstar and its positive residual vector v, the two columns zstar,sqrt(eta)v form a balanced J-null rank-two plane. Their graph determinant is sign det M by the same endpoint determinant identity. For eta sufficiently small their loss is below C(0), because the critical rank-one product has strictly lower loss than zero and the perturbation is small. The finite-eta balanced outgoing factor flows therefore meet this theorem.

For a limiting canonical escape orbit, one must ALSO ensure it remains a nonconstant rank-two factor realization in this component, with loss below C(0) at a finite time. These are expected from its nonzero normal mode, but are not supplied merely by taking limits of rank-two finite-eta orbits: rank can drop in a limit. The pending dominant Gram escape proof must verify the canonical normal-mode expansion, balanced realization and nonzero normal coefficient before invoking this endpoint theorem. Do not interchange the eta limit and t->infinity based on finite-eta convergence alone.

For the final connection paragraph, the strict critical energy inequality is exact: C(P)-C(0)=-tr(P Sigma P^T)/2+<G,P>. At any rank-one stationary product <G,P>=b^T G a=0; nonzero P and positive-definite Sigma make C(P)<C(0). This does not assume that P is best rank one.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:34bc22cb3481f5c38302f01d1fa56a8cf139f838fb0e985f87f9681f103548ce","revision_digest":"sha256:7f7355b46f9a74f292fdcd8da948418090dd4840d067411c51d863dcc85295b8","source_id":"own-work:w704:T232-w704-C010:v2","source_revision":"v2-as-read-2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Def Def_Exch of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $(\xi_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of random variables.
Given $n\in \mathbb{N}$, the random variables $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are called {\sl exchangeable} if for any permutation $\sigma$ of $(1,2,\ldots,n)$,
 the law of $(\xi_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,\xi_{\sigma(n)})$ coincides with that of $(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$.
The sequence $(\xi_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb{N}}$ is called exchangeable if, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
 the random variables $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ are exchangeable.
title: Def Def_Exch of arXiv:2606.22183

[Proposition prop:hybrid-gap of arXiv:2608.10184, 'The sharp SAT/UNSAT phase transition in random ellipsoid fitting'] There are constants $e_\gamma,c_\gamma>0$, depending only on $\gamma$, such that for every $0\le r\le k_d$, with
probability at least $1-e^{-c_\gamma d^2}$,
\begin{equation}
\inf_{(H,B,b)}\
\mathscr{L}_n\bigl(\mathsf{K}(H,b)+\mathsf{R}(B)\bigr)\ge e_\gamma,
\end{equation}
where the infimum is over all $H\succeq 0$, $B\succeq 0$, and $b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $1/4\le\|H\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2+\|B\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2\le4$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Hybrid model risk gap

[Definition def-P-weighted of arXiv:2605.03385, 'Quantum Loewner evolution in quantum natural time: phases and Markov properties'] Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \beta \in (-2,2)$ and $\ell > 0$. 
    Let $P_{\alpha, \beta, \ell}$ be the probability measure defined by
    \[\frac{dP_{\alpha, \beta, \ell}}{d \mathrm{LF}^{(\alpha,0)}_{\mathbb{D}, \ell}} (\phi) = Z_{\alpha,\beta,\ell}^{-1} \mathcal{L}^\beta_\phi(\partial \mathbb{D}), \qquad Z_{\alpha,\beta,\ell} := \mathrm{LF}^{(\alpha,0)}_{\mathbb{D}, \ell}[\mathcal{L}^\beta_\phi(\partial \mathbb{D})].\]
    In other words, $P_{\alpha, \beta, \ell}$ is obtained from $\mathrm{LF}^{(\alpha, 0)}_{\mathbb{D}, \ell}$ by weighting by the boundary $\beta/2$-GMC measure and    normalizing to be a probability measure.
title: Definition def-P-weighted of arXiv:2605.03385

body: A group is cyclic if it is generated by a single element g (every element is a power g^k). Up to isomorphism the cyclic groups are the integers Z (infinite order) and Z/nZ (order n). Every subgroup and every quotient of a cyclic group is cyclic; a finite cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n. A finite group is cyclic iff it has an element whose order equals the group's order.
title: Cyclic Group

			\sup_{z \in K}\big|U_{t}(z) - 2\pi^{2}\big|

			e^{-2t}\,\sup_{z \in K}\big(1 + V(z)^{2}\big)^{2}
			\sup_{|s - \frac12| \le \delta_{K}(t)}
			\big|U_{0}(s) - 2\pi^{2}\big|,
			
		\end{equation}
		with $\delta_{K}(t) \to 0$; in particular $U_{t} \to 2\pi^{2}$
		locally uniformly at the exact exponential rate $e^{-2t}$ provided
		the centered potential does not vanish at the median,
		$\mathfrak{U}_{0}(\tfrac12) \neq 0$, equivalently
		$U_{0}(\tfrac12) \neq 2\pi^{2}$, the
		degenerate case relaxing faster, at $o(e^{-2t})$, with
		asymptotic profile
		\begin{equation}
			e^{2t}\big(U_{t}(z) - 2\pi^{2}\big)
			\;\longrightarrow\;
			\big(1 + V(z)^{2}\big)^{2}\,
			\big(U_{0}(\tfrac12) - 2\pi^{2}\big)
			
		\end{equation}
		whenever $U_{0}$ is continuous at $\tfrac12$. Equivalently, in
		curvature form: along the canonical flow the projective curvature of
		every law relaxes locally uniformly in rank to the Cauchy value
		$-2\pi^{2}$ at rate $e^{-2t}$, and the limit retains no memory of
		the initial law beyond the single number visible in the
		profile~(equation eq:nohair-profile of the paper).

$$\xymatrix@R=16pt@C=16pt{
&K_N^+\ar[rr]&&U_N^+\\
H_N^+\ar[rr]\ar[ur]&&O_N^+\ar[ur]\\
&K_N\ar[rr]\ar[uu]&&U_N\ar[uu]\\
H_N\ar[uu]\ar[ur]\ar[rr]&&O_N\ar[uu]\ar[ur]
}$$
which correspond via Tannakian duality to the following categories of partitions,
$$\xymatrix@R=18pt@C=2pt{
&\mathcal{NC}_{even}\ar[dl]\ar[dd]&&\mathcal {NC}_2\ar[dl]\ar[ll]\ar[dd]\\
NC_{even}\ar[dd]&&NC_2\ar[dd]\ar[ll]\\
&\mathcal P_{even}\ar[dl]&&\mathcal P_2\ar[dl]\ar[ll]\\
P_{even}&&P_2\ar[ll]
}$$
and whose asymptotic laws of truncated characters are the main limiting laws:
$$\xymatrix@R=18pt@C=20pt{
&\mathfrak B_t\ar@{-}[rr]\ar@{-}[dd]&&\Gamma_t\ar@{-}[dd]\\
\beta_t\ar@{-}[rr]\ar@{-}[dd]\ar@{-}[ur]&&\gamma_t\ar@{-}[dd]\ar@{-}[ur]\\
&B_t\ar@{-}[rr]\ar@{-}[uu]&&G_t\ar@{.}[uu]\\
b_t\ar@{-}[uu]\ar@{-}[ur]\ar@{-}[rr]&&g_t\ar@{-}[uu]\ar@{-}[ur]
}$$
Moreover, under very strong axioms for everything, we have uniqueness too.

[Lemma soussolution of arXiv:2508.02416, 'On the surjectivity of the conditional expectation\\ given a real random variable'] Let \( A \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]) \), $m\ge 3$ and 
$
k \in \{2,\dots, \frac{4^{m}}{2} - 3\}.
$
There exists a Borel set \( A_m^k \subset A \cap I_m^k \) and a non-negative measurable function \( g_{A_m^k} \) such that
\begin{itemize}\small
    \item[(i)] \(\mu(dx)\text{-a.e.,} \quad \int_{\mathbb{R}} g_{A_m^k}(y)\,\pi_{X=x}(dy) = \mathbf{1}_{A_m^k}(x),\)
    \item[(ii)] \(\{y \in \mathbb{R} : g_{A_m^k}(y)>0 \} \subset \left[2^{-m} - 4^{-(m+1)},\, 2^{-m} - 4^{-(2m+1)} \right],\)
    \item[(iii)] \(\lambda(A_m^k) \geq 2\lambda(A \cap I_m^k) - \alpha_m.\)
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 9 (Approximation against test functions) of arXiv:2604.23461, 'Scaling limit of Sinkhorn-rescaled Random Matrices \\ via Stability of Static Schrödinger '] Suppose Assumptions \ref{assump:random_matrix}--\ref{assump:bounded_cost} hold. For any bounded test function $g \in L^{\infty}([0,1]^2)$ and any $D > 0$, denote $\tau = (D+1)\log(m \vee n) + \log 4$, and let $\eps_{\textup{pot}}$ be as defined in Theorem \ref{thm:first_approximation_rescaled} evaluated at this $\tau$. Assume the dimensions are sufficiently large such that $\eps_{\textup{pot}} \le 1$. Then there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that with probability at least
		\[
		1 - 2(m \vee n)^{-D} - m^2 \exp(-c\,\Phi_{\bLambda}) - 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\bLambda\|_1^2/2}{mn\sigma^2+R\|\bLambda\|_1}\right),
		\]
		the integration error against $g$ is bounded by
		\begin{align}
			\left|\int_{[0,1]^2} g\!\left(\varphi_{\X^{\r,\c}} - \varphi_{\bLambda^{\r,\c}}\right) dx\, dy\right| \le 2\|g\|_{\infty} \eps_{\textup{pot}} e^{2K} + \frac{\|g\|_{\infty} e^{2K}}{\|\bLambda\|_1} \left( \sigma\sqrt{2mn\tau} + 2R\tau \right),
		\end{align}
		where $\varphi_{\X^{\r,\c}}(x,y) = \frac{mn}{N}\X^{\r,\c}(\lceil mx \rceil, \lceil ny \rceil)$ and $\varphi_{\bLambda^{\r,\c}}(x,y) = \frac{mn}{N}\bLambda^{\r,\c}(\lceil mx \rceil, \lceil ny \rceil)$ are the piecewise constant extensions to the unit square. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Approximation against test functions

body: [Lemma Griffith of arXiv:2508.12464, 'On the Fitness Landscape in the $\NK$ Model'] Let $(F_{N})_{N\geq 1}$ be a sequence of convex and differentiable functions defined on $[0,\infty).$ Assume that $f(x):=\lim_{N\to\infty}F_{N}(x)$ exists for all $x\in [0,\infty).$ If $f$ is differentiable at some $x_0\in (0,\infty),$ then $\lim_{N\to\infty}F_{N}'(x_0)=f'(x_0).$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Prop 43 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $l\in \N_0$.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item If $c\in \R, f,g\in \dC l$, then $cf+g\in \dC l$ and $\der^\al(cf+g) = c\der^\al f + \der^\al g$ for $|\al|\leq l$.
\item If $n\in \N$ and $f_1,\dots, f_n\in \dC l$, then $\bigotimes_{i=1}^n f_i\in \dC l$ and 
\[\der^\al \left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n f_i\right) = \sum_{\be_1 + \dots + \be_n = \al} \frac{\al!}{\be_1! \cdots \be_n!} \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \der^{\be_i} f_i, \quad |\al|\leq l \text{ (Leibniz)}.\]
\item $f,g\in \dC l$, then $g\circ f\in \dC l$ and 
\[\der^\al(g\circ f) = \sum_{k=1}^{|\al|} \sum_{\cB\in \prttn \al k} \frac{\al!}{\cB!} \innp{\nabla^k g\circ f}{\der^\cB f}, \quad |\al|\leq l \ \text{ (Faa di Bruno)}.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 43 of arXiv:2511.20322

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The number of possibilities of choosing $k$ objects among $n$ objects is
$$\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$$
called binomial number, where $n!=1\cdot2\cdot3\ldots(n-2)(n-1)n$, called ``factorial $n$''.

body: [Lemma l:gluing of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal S$ be a (non-killed) ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow.  The restriction of $\mathcal S$ to the closure of each $A_i$ gives a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow, call it $\mathcal S^i$.  Let $x>r$ and $a\ge 0$. Let $i\le j$ such that $\inf A_i\le r<\sup A_i$, and $\inf A_j < x\le \sup A_j$. We can define by induction $t_i:=r$, $a_i:=a$, and for $j \ge k> i$, $a_k:=\mathcal S^{k-1}_{t_{k-1},t_k}(a_{k-1})$, $t_{k}:=\inf A_k$. Almost surely for all $r\le x$ and $a\ge 0$, $\mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=\mathcal S^j_{t_{j},x}(a_j)$.

body:
[Defn 11 (Weak and strong convergence) of arXiv:2507.00346, 'The strong convergence phenomenon'] Let $\boldsymbol{X}^N=(X_1^N,\ldots,X_r^N)$ be a sequence of
$r$-tuples of random matrices, and let 
$\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ be an $r$-tuple of elements
of a $C^*$-probability space $(\mathcal{A},\tau)$.
\smallskip
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\itemsep\medskipamount
\item 
$\boldsymbol{X}^N$ is said to \emph{converge weakly} to 
$\boldsymbol{x}$ if
for every $P\in\mathbb{C}\langle x_1,\ldots,x_{2r}\rangle$
\begin{equation}

	\lim_{N\to\infty} \ntr(P(\boldsymbol{X}^N,\boldsymbol{X}^{N*}))
	= \tau(P(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{*}))
	\quad\text{in probability}.
\end{equation}
\item 
$\boldsymbol{X}^N$ is said to \emph{converge strongly} to 
$\boldsymbol{x}$ if
for every $P\in\mathbb{C}\langle x_1,\ldots,x_{2r}\rangle$
\begin{equation}

	\lim_{N\to\infty} \|P(\boldsymbol{X}^N,\boldsymbol{X}^{N*})\|
	= \|P(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{*})\|
	\quad\text{in probability}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
title: Weak and strong convergence

[Corollary coro of arXiv:2412.02486, 'On the curvatures of \\ random complex submanifolds'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~(theorem1 of the paper),
	for any $\epsilon \in (0,1]$,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item (holomorphic bisectional curvature) if 
		$3r\geq 2n-1$ and  $0<\eta < \epsilon (3r-2n+2),$
			there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$
			\density(\hbc_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}.$$
		\item (holomorphic sectional curvature) If $2r\geq n$ and $0<\eta < \epsilon(2r-n+1)$,
			there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$
		\density(\hc_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}.$$
		\item (Ricci curvature) If  $0<\eta < \epsilon(r(n-r)-(n-r-1))$, 	there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$		
		\density(\ricci_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}
		.$$
		\item (Scalar curvature) 
		If  $0<\eta < \epsilon(\frac{1}2r(n-r)(n-r+1))$, 	there exists a sequence of sections $(s_d)_{d\geq d_0}$ with $s_d\in H^0(M,E\otimes L^d)$ such that $Z(s_d)\subset M$ is a smooth $(n-r)$-submanifold and
		$$	
		\density(\scal_{Z(s)}<-d^{1-\epsilon})>1-d^{-\eta}
		.$$
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let phi : G -> H be a group homomorphism. Then the kernel K = ker(phi) is a normal subgroup of G, the image phi(G) is a subgroup of H, and the map G/K -> phi(G), g K |-> phi(g), is a well-defined group isomorphism. Consequently every homomorphic image of G is isomorphic to a quotient of G by a normal subgroup, and |G| = |K| . |phi(G)| when G is finite. The same statement holds word for word for rings (kernel an ideal, image a subring) and for modules over a ring (kernel and image submodules); the second and third isomorphism theorems, H N / N congruent to H / (H cap N) for H a subgroup and N normal, and (G/N) / (M/N) congruent to G/M for normal subgroups N and M of G with N contained in M, are its corollaries.

[Def PSCR of arXiv:2607.19511, 'A Conditional Probability Hierarchy for Stochastic Choice\footnote{We thank Samson Abramsk'] Fix a stochastic choice rule $c: {\cal G} \to \Delta(\Omega)$. Suppose there is a selection $s$ such that, for each $G \in \cal G$ and $F \in \cal F$: 
\begin{equation}~
c_G(F)=\mathbf{1}_F(s(G)).
\end{equation}
That is, each $c_G(\cdot)$ is the Dirac measure concentrated on $s(G)$.  We call such a stochastic choice rule a \textbf{point stochastic choice rule}.
title: Def PSCR of arXiv:2607.19511

[Theorem 33 (Crossing probability) of arXiv:2607.27786, 'Gaussian free field in annulus: \\BPZ equations and crossing probabilities for level lines'] Fix $r>0$ and an even number $n=2N$. 
For $\bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta}\in\LX_n$, we write $\bs{x}=\ee^{\ii\bs{\alpha}}$ and $\bs{y}=\ee^{\ii\bs{\beta}-r}$. 
Let $\varphiann{n}$ be the bounded harmonic function in annulus $\A_r$ with alternating boundary data~\eqref{eqn::boundarydata}.
Suppose $\Gamma$ is Dirichlet GFF in annulus $\A_r$. 
Let $\gamma^j$ be the level line of $\Gamma+\varphiann{n}$ starting from $x_{j}$ for $1\le j\le n$ and denote $\bs{\gamma}=(\gamma^1, \ldots, \gamma^n)$.
We define $\cross(\bs{\gamma})$ and $\wind(\bs{\gamma})$ as in~\eqref{eqn::crossingevent_def} and~\eqref{eqn::windingevent_def}. 
We have 
\begin{align}
&\PP[\cross(\bs{\gamma}), \wind(\bs{\gamma})=(m;\ell)]=\frac{\LZcro{n}^{(\ell)}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \beta_{2m+1}, \ldots, \beta_{2m+n})}{\LZann{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta})}, \quad \text{for $m\in\{1, \ldots, N\}$ and $\ell\in\Z$};\\
&\PP[\cross(\bs{\gamma})]=\sum_{m=1}^N\frac{\LZcro{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \beta_{2m+1}, \ldots, \beta_{2m+n})}{\LZann{n}(r; \bs{\alpha}, \bs{\beta})}.
\end{align}
where $\LZann{n}, \LZcro{n}^{(\ell)}, \LZcro{n}$ are partition functions defined in~\eqref{eqn::LZann_def}-\eqref{eqn::LZcro_def}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Crossing probability

[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] For every $\alpha\in(0,1]$, the radial part of the spectrum
\eqref{eq:spindle-spec}, namely the eigenvalues with $m=0$, is
$\{j(j+1):j\ge0\},$
independently of $\alpha$, with eigenfunctions $P_j(\cos t)$. Moreover,
$\Area(\Sph^2_\alpha)=4\pi\alpha,$
and, with normalized area measures,
\[
\Bigl(\Sph^2_\alpha,d_{g_\alpha},
\frac{\vol_{g_\alpha}}{\Area(\Sph^2_\alpha)}\Bigr)
\longrightarrow
\Bigl([0,\pi],|\cdot|,\tfrac12\sin t\,dt\Bigr)
\]
in the mGH topology as $\alpha\to0$. The limit is the Legendre model up to
the constant factor $\tfrac12$ in the measure, which does not affect its
operator or spectrum.

[Proposition 105 (Brownian registration trilemma) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Fix $t>0$ and assume the polynomial covariance hypothesis
\eqref{eq:brownian-polynomial-covariance}.  No realization can simultaneously
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item equal the raw Chen-local area $A_t^C(\omega)$;
\item arise from a bounded functional agreeing with point evaluation on all
      active second-chaos coordinates;
\item be positively spectrally faithful to $K_{C,t}$, in the sense that some
      $a,c>0$ satisfy
      \[
       N_{A_t^C}(au)\ge cN_{K_{C,t}}(u)
      \]
      for all sufficiently small $u$ on an event of positive probability.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the valid assignments are typed:
\[
 \mathcal B_{\rm ann}=K_{C,t},\qquad
 \mathcal B_{\rm que}=A_t^C(\omega),\qquad
 \mathcal B_{\rm aux}=\mathfrak D_T(B^C(\omega)).
\]
Relations between them are covariance, radonification, or nonlinear response
transforms, not operator identifications.

If $D$ is $f$-pseudo-effective, we define the non-nef locus $\NNef(D/S)$ of $D$ over $S$ as
\[ \NNef(D/S) := \bigcup_{v} \overline{c_{X}(v)}, \]
where $v$ runs through all divisorial valuations over $X$ satisfying $v_{\num}(D/S)>0$.
If $D$ is not $f$-pseudo-effective, we set $\NNef(D/S) := X$.

[Corollary coro:Wegner_orbital of arXiv:2604.20215, '\bf Edge Universality for Inhomogeneous Random Matrices II: Markov Chain Comparison and Cr'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] \textbf{Frozen regime:} Given   any  fixed integer $D\geq 2$,  if
         \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \ll 1\), then for any fixed integer  $k\geq 1$ with $s_N=M^{-2/3}$,
       $ (T_{s_N})_*  R_{N,\lambda}\bigl(dx_1,\dots,dx_k\bigr)$
        converges vaguely to the corresponding limits  of $D$ independent GUE/GOE matrices.

    \item[(ii)] \textbf{Skellam regime:} Given   any  fixed integer $D\geq 2$,  if
         \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \to \mu \in (0,\infty)\) with $s_N=M^{-2/3}$, then
       $ (T_{s_N})_*  R_{N,\lambda}\bigl(dx_1,\dots,dx_k\bigr)$converges vaguely to a new point process \(R^{\mathrm{(Skellam)}}_{\mu;k}(dy_1,\ldots,dy_k)\) defined by definition (def:skellam_process of the paper) that interpolates between Airy and Poisson  statistics.

    \item[(iii)] \textbf{Diffusive regime:}  If $d=1$, \(M^{\frac13}\lambda \gg 1\),
       then  the $k$-point correlation measure  converges
       to those of the corresponding $1d$ 2-stable random band matrix with effective bandwidth $W=\sqrt{\lambda}M$ and $N=DM$.
\end{enumerate}

[Definition def:halfcross of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $B=Q\times[s,s+h]$ with $Q=y+[-w,w]^d$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $T(B)$ is the event that there is an open path contained in $B$ whose trace has duration
  at least $h/2$.
\item For $1\le i\le d$, $S^+_i(B)$ is the event that there is an open path contained in $B^+$
  whose trace starts at a point with $x_i\le y_i+\vartheta w$ and later reaches a point with
  $x_i\ge y_i+w$; and $S^-_i(B)$ is its mirror image, obtained by replacing $x_i-y_i$ by
  $y_i-x_i$.
\end{itemize}
The \emph{half-crossing event} of $B$ is
$H(B)=T(B)\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^d\big(S^+_i(B)\cup S^-_i(B)\big)$.
title: Half-crossings

body: Let X and Y be Banach spaces and let T : X -> Y be a linear map. If the graph of T, consisting of all pairs (x, Tx) for x in X, is a closed subset of the product space X times Y (with the product topology), then T is automatically continuous (bounded). Equivalently, if x_n -> x in X and Tx_n -> y in Y together force y = Tx for every such sequence, then T is bounded. The theorem follows from the open mapping theorem and can fail if either X or Y is not complete.
title: Closed graph theorem

body: In probability theory, concentration inequalities provide mathematical bounds on the probability of a random variable deviating from some value. The deviation or other function of the random variable can be thought of as a secondary random variable. The simplest example of the concentration of such a secondary random variable is the CDF of the first random variable which concentrates the probability to unity. If an analytic form of the CDF is available this provides a concentration equality that provides the exact probability of concentration. It is precisely when the CDF is difficult to calculate or even the exact form of the first random variable is unknown that the applicable concentration inequalities provide useful insight.

$|J|\le K_d$,
\begin{equation}
w\bigl(\mathcal{K}_{\kappa_1}\cap\ker\mathcal{W}_J\cap\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{F}}\bigr)
\ge w\bigl(\mathcal{K}_{\kappa_0}\cap\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{F}}\bigr)-o(d)
\ge(\sqrt\alpha+3\eta)d.
\end{equation}
The $o(d)$ term may depend on the fixed $C_0$ but is uniform in $J$. In particular, the compact set
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{D}_J:=\sqrt d\, \bigl(\mathcal{K}_{\kappa_1}\cap\ker\mathcal{W}_J\cap\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{F}}\bigr)
\end{equation}
is nonempty and satisfies
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{W}_J(S)=0,\qquad
\kappa_1^{-1} I_d \preceq S\preceq\kappa_1 I_d
\quad(S\in\mathcal{D}_J).

Current q,r in (0,1], valid Gaussian Gram; fresh iid Gaussian rows and tanh; n integer >=1769472(1+K), finite K,Lambda>=0. Uses C017 joint-norm mgf, C002 scalar drift, C010 conditional variance and C015 centered fourth moment (the latter components unaudited).
